articles.title: In-hospital management and disposition outcomes for patients with mild traumatic brain injury and isolated traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVE**: This study aims to review the in-hospital management and disposition of patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI) and a Glasgow coma score (GCS) ≥ 13 with isolated traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage.

**MATERIALS AND METHODS**: Retrospective single-center cohort study, using prospectively collected data from patient charts. All patients admitted to a neurosurgical department at a Danish university hospital, after TBI with radiological confirmed intracranial haemorrhage and GCS ≥ 13, were included. Data on the type of haemorrhage was collected. The outcomes of interest were length of hospital stay (LOS), repeated head CT (RHCT), discharge to in-patient rehabilitation, and neurosurgical intervention. Relative risk (RR) for discharge to inpatient rehabilitation and RHCT was calculated with traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage (tSAH) as reference for acute subdural haemorrhage (aSDH), traumatic intracerebral haemorrhage (tICH) and epidural haemorrhage (EDH) as a pooled category.

**RESULTS**: In the period April 1st, 2022, to December 31

**CONCLUSION**: Patients admitted with mild TBI and isolated tSAH have a shorter LOS, lower risk of RHCT, and a lower risk of requiring inpatient rehabilitation at discharge, compared to patients with mild TBI and other types of intracranial haemorrhage. However, the current study is limited to a single-center retrospective design.

articles.title: Expanding minimally invasive options in emergency general surgery: a multicentre evaluation of a novel MIS platform.
articles.abstract:
**PURPOSE**: Emergency general surgery (EGS) carries elevated morbidity, and minimally invasive surgery (MIS) may reduce surgical trauma but remains limited by staffing, logistical, and technical barriers. The Maestro

**METHODS**: This multicentre retrospective study compared 24 Maestro-assisted EGS cases (July 2024-April 2025) with 25 consecutive conventional laparoscopic cases performed by the same surgical team. Outcomes analysed included surgery time, conversion rate, postoperative complications, length of stay, and 30-day mortality. Analysis was stratified by procedure type: appendectomy, emergency colectomy, and small bowel obstruction surgery. Additional Maestro cases without baseline comparators were reported descriptively.

**RESULTS**: Within comparable procedure groups, Maestro-assisted cases showed shorter surgery times: appendectomy (33.5 [31.5-42.3] vs. 76.0 [70.0-81.0] min, p = 0.002), emergency colectomy (135.0 [122.0-165.0] vs. 197.5 [159.3-220.0] min, p = 0.08), and small bowel obstruction (107.0 [28.0-110.0] vs. 108.0 [90.8-127.5] min, p = 0.54). No Maestro cases required conversion to open surgery, compared with 3 of 25 baseline cases (12%). Complication rates and length of stay were similar between groups. No device-related adverse events occurred.

**CONCLUSION**: In this preliminary procedure-stratified analysis, Maestro-assisted EGS was associated with shorter surgery times and a trend toward shorter length of stay and lower conversion rates in complex procedures such as colectomy, while maintaining comparable safety outcomes. The platform appeared adaptable across diverse emergency indications and may support minimally invasive approaches in emergency settings. Larger, prospective studies will be necessary to confirm these observations and define the role of collaborative robotic platforms in emergency surgical care.

articles.title: Beyond the national average: Demographically stratified estimates of resource utilization for trauma systems planning.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Trauma systems are planned for populations, but resources are consumed by individual patients whose needs vary by age, sex, and injury pattern. To estimate the resources a population will need, existing tools often apply simple national averages of what admissions consume, creating a potential mismatch between the resources needed and those available. We compared simple population size-based estimates against estimates stratified by patient demographics.

**METHODS**: Using the American College of Surgeons Trauma Quality Programs Participant Use Files (2022-2024), we conducted a retrospective analysis of adult admissions to 502 Level I/II trauma centers. Per-admission estimates for seven resources were derived from pooled 2022-2023 admissions using three approaches: simple estimates based on population size, singularly stratified estimates by age, sex, or payer alone, and jointly stratified estimates combining all three. Estimates were applied to held-out 2024 admissions and percent error calculated, with a 2017-2019 sensitivity analysis.

**RESULTS**: Among 1,803,746 derivation and 947,281 validation admissions, the simple estimate fell outside 10% of observed utilization in 40 of 63 subgroup and metric combinations, 21 higher than observed and 19 lower. Blood product estimates were 236% higher than observed among Medicare-covered patients. Stratifying on one characteristic corrected error chiefly within its own subgroups (59 of 63 within 10%). Applied jointly, age, sex, and payer brought 62 of 63 combinations within 10%, reducing median absolute error from 13.8% to 3.0%.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Simple estimates differed from observed resource use by 10% or more for nearly every patient group examined, failing in both directions in a manner no single adjustment can correct. Stratification by age, sex, and payer, characteristics knowable before injury, substantially reduced this error.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Prognostic/Epidemiological; Level III.

articles.title: Early inflammatory response is associated with antibiotic treatment outcomes in acute phlegmonous appendicitis: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Acute phlegmonous appendicitis is considered an intermediate inflammatory subtype between uncomplicated and complicated appendicitis. Although nonoperative management is increasingly accepted for uncomplicated appendicitis, evidence for phlegmonous appendicitis remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate the 1-year success rate of antibiotic treatment and identify early factors associated with treatment outcomes.

**METHODS**: This retrospective study included 476 patients with CT-defined acute phlegmonous appendicitis treated at Zhongshan Hospital between January 2021 and June 2025. Patients with incomplete follow-up were excluded from the primary analysis. Of these patients, 374 initially received antibiotic therapy, and the primary endpoint was the 1-year success rate of antibiotic treatment. Clinical characteristics, appendicolith status, and changes in inflammatory markers during the first 24 h were analyzed. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify factors associated with successful antibiotic treatment, and a nomogram was developed and internally validated. The model was considered exploratory and requires external validation before clinical application.

**RESULTS**: The complete-case 1-year treatment success rate among the 374 patients receiving antibiotic therapy was 50.3% (188/374; 95% CI 45.2-55.3%). Patients with appendicoliths had a significantly lower success rate than those without appendicoliths (31.3%; 95% CI 21.5-43.2% vs. 54.4%; 95% CI 48.8-59.9%, P < 0.001). Baseline clinical characteristics showed limited association with treatment outcomes, whereas early inflammatory marker changes were more closely associated with outcomes. Multivariable analysis demonstrated that a WBC count decrease ≥ 20% (OR 1.92, 95% CI 1.08-3.42, P = 0.027) and a neutrophil percentage (N%) decrease ≥ 6% (OR 3.65, 95% CI 2.08-6.39, P < 0.001) within the first 24 h were independently associated with higher odds of successful antibiotic treatment. In contrast, the presence of appendicolith was independently associated with lower odds of successful antibiotic treatment (OR 0.46, 95% CI 0.25-0.85, P = 0.013). A nomogram incorporating these three variables demonstrated moderate discrimination (AUC = 0.738).

**CONCLUSIONS**: Approximately half of patients with acute phlegmonous appendicitis achieved successful treatment with antibiotics. Early reductions in inflammatory markers were associated with treatment outcomes and may provide information for early risk stratification. A nomogram incorporating appendicolith status and early inflammatory marker changes may estimate the likelihood of treatment success; however, this model was considered exploratory and requires external validation.

articles.title: Reversed airflow during asynchronous volume controlled mechanical ventilation in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: a physiological observational study.
articles.abstract:
**AIM**: Chest compressions during the inspiratory phase of a ventilation can force air out of the lungs, so-called reversed airflow. Human data on this phenomenon during mechanical ventilation are lacking. We aimed to quantify its frequency and magnitude during asynchronous mechanical ventilation in intubated adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients receiving continuous chest compressions.

**METHODS**: This single-centre descriptive cross-sectional study used prospectively collected data from patients treated by a physician-staffed prehospital team. After tracheal intubation, patients were ventilated with an Oxylog 3000 transport ventilator in volume-controlled mode without positive end-expiratory pressure, during continuous manual chest compressions. Intratracheal pressures recorded via two catheters allowed calculation of airflow and ventilation parameters during the first minute after intubation. Reversed airflow was defined as expiratory airflow during the inspiratory phase of a mechanical breath. Continuous data are reported as median (first-third quartile).

**RESULTS**: Twelve patients were included (median age 68 years [62-75]; 7 [58.3%] male), of whom 5 (41.7%) achieved sustained return of spontaneous circulation. Reversed airflow occurred in 10 (83.3%; 95% CI 55.2-95.3) patients and in 141 of 172 (82.0%; 95% CI 75.6-87.0) analysed ventilations. The median reversed-airflow volume was 61 mL [42-80] per episode. Median ventilation rate was 14 breaths/min [13-16], gross inspiratory tidal volume 324 mL [305-345], minute ventilation 4.8 L/min [3.8-5.9], and peak inspiratory pressure 46 cmH

**CONCLUSION**: Reversed airflow occurred frequently during asynchronous volume-controlled mechanical ventilation with the Oxylog 3000 in intubated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients receiving continuous manual chest compressions. Its physiological and clinical implications require further investigation.

articles.title: Development of a 3D CT-based convolutional neural network for automated detection and classification of acetabular fractures.
articles.abstract:
**PURPOSE**: This proof-of-concept study aimed to develop and evaluate one of the first three-dimensional (3D) CT-based convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for acetabular fracture recognition and Letournel classification. The objectives were to assess fracture detection, fracture classification, and compare CNN performance with that of orthopaedic trauma surgeons.

**METHODS**: In this multicentre retrospective cohort study, CT data from six level-1 trauma centres were used. Fractures were annotated in 3D Slicer using a cubic region of interest and labelled according to the Letournel classification. Data were split into 80% for training and 20% for internal validation, with two Australian hospitals used for external validation. A DenseNet-121 model implemented in the MONAI framework was trained for 100 epochs using data augmentation. Performance was evaluated using AUC, accuracy, recall, and precision.

**RESULTS**: A total of 929 patients with 939 acetabular fractures and 782 healthy contralateral sides were included. The CNN achieved an accuracy, recall, and precision of 91% for fracture recognition. Fracture classification proved more challenging, with the best performance for distinguishing elementary from associated fractures (accuracy 75%, recall 75%, precision 76%) and lower performance for the ten-category Letournel classification. Posterior wall fractures showed the best individual classification performance (accuracy 85%, recall 85%, precision 55%). Overall, the CNN performed worse than orthopaedic trauma surgeons, with the largest differences observed for the full Letournel classification.

**CONCLUSION**: This study establishes a foundation for the automated classification of complex musculoskeletal injuries from three-dimensional CT imaging, with acetabular fractures serving as a representative use case. This CNN accurately detected acetabular fractures but showed limited performance for detailed Letournel classification, particularly for rare and complex fracture patterns. Although automated fracture recognition appears feasible, further improvements are required before clinical implementation.

articles.title: Intensive care unit versus ward admission in the elderly patient with one or more rib fractures: Are we too conservative?
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: Standardized protocols are often created to triage admission destination of elderly patients with rib fractures. The aim of this study was to assess risk factors for the occurrence of complications and unplanned intensive care unit admission and evaluate adherence to our institution's rib fracture admission algorithm. We hypothesized that adherence to the algorithm was good and that the algorithm correctly identified patients at risk of complications or ward failure.

**METHODS**: A retrospective study was performed of all patients aged ≥ 65 years admitted with rib fractures between October 1, 2018 and December 31, 2020. Primary outcome was algorithm-adherent triage to the ICU or ward. Subgroup analysis was performed of patients with and without complications. A logistic stepwise regression model was made to identify independent risk factors for adverse in-hospital outcomes.

**RESULTS**: In total, 202 patients were included. A total of 152 patients were correctly triaged following the admission algorithm (75.2%) of whom 124 (61.3%) were triaged to the ICU and 78 (38.6%) were triaged to the ward. 16 of 124 patients (12.9%) were triaged to the ICU in nonadherence with the algorithm, and 31 of 78 patients (39.7%) were triaged to the ward in nonadherence with the algorithm. After logistic regression modeling, age ≥ 77 years, the presence of solid organ injury, and a BPC-18 ≥ 2 were found to improve the algorithm by capturing more complications. After adding these factors, the algorithm captured 94.3% of complications.

**CONCLUSION**: Adherence to the algorithm was modest at 75%. Over one in four patients developed one or more complications, but the rib fracture-related complication rate was low (3%). Following the algorithm, ward failure rate was low (3%). The addition of specific injury-related variables resulted in capturing > 90% of complications. Further improvement of the algorithm might require a multimodal approach also including frailty-related characteristics.

articles.title: Loss of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 activity during liquid plasma storage is associated with increased fibrinolysis in response to tissue plasminogen activator.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: In trauma, hyperfibrinolysis influences the need for massive transfusion and mortality. Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) sensitivity increases during whole blood storage despite rising plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) activity. Liquid plasma demonstrates preserved fibrinogen function in storage, but fibrinolytic regulation in stored liquid plasma remains undescribed.

**METHODS**: Liquid plasma tails (n = 28) were obtained and stored at 4 °C. Thromboelastography was challenged with 75 ng/mL exogenous tPA at three storage time points (day 1-3, 7-10, and 28) to assess resistance to fibrinolysis. PAI-1 activity was measured through a modified enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) that captures only active PAI-1 utilizing immobilized active urokinase. Statistical analysis included two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and Spearman correlation. Significance was set at p <0.05.

**RESULTS**: Aging liquid plasma units demonstrated a significant, progressive increase in fibrinolysis (LY30) in response to tPA over time (p = 0.008). Alpha angle gradually increased, and maximum amplitude remained stable with storage. PAI-1 activity decreased with storage (p < 0.001) and inversely correlated with tPA-thromboelastography LY30 (Spearman r = -0.40, p = 0.04).

**CONCLUSIONS**: Stored liquid plasma demonstrates declining PAI-1 activity, increased tPA-mediated fibrinolysis, and preserved clot strength, highlighting differences in fibrinolytic regulation compared with previously reported findings in stored whole blood. Further investigation into fibrinolytic regulation for the spectrum of blood products during storage and the implications for trauma resuscitation is warranted.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Basic Science.

articles.title: Non-operative management of penetrating abdominal trauma in a low-volume environment: a single center experience.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: High-volume trauma centers report that selective non-operative management (NOM) in patients suffering from penetrating abdominal trauma (PAT) is a safe approach. Switzerland is a low-volume environment for PAT. We hypothesize that despite the low number of PAT cases, NOM is a feasible approach with comparable outcomes to those in high incidence environments for PAT.

**METHODS**: Retrospective analysis of patients aged > 16 years who were treated for PAT between January 1, 2013, and December 31, 2023 at a Level I trauma and academic tertiary referral center in a low-volume environment for PAT. The primary endpoint was the failure rate of NOM. Successful NOM was defined as completion of NOM without the need for surgical intervention. Secondary endpoints included the rates of non-therapeutic operations, hospital length of stay and mortality.

**RESULTS**: In total, 57 patients were eligible, with 36 (63.1%) stab wounds (SW), 14 (24.6%) gunshot wounds (GSW) and seven (12.3%) impalements. Median age was 35 years (IQR 24-56) and 73.7% were male. Median ISS was 16 (IQR 4-25). In 28 patients (49.1%) NOM was attempted (23 SW, 1 GSW, 4 impalements). In these patients, median ISS was 4 (IQR 1-16.5), wound localizations were the anterior abdomen in 18 patients (64.3%), the back in 5 patients (17.9%) and the left flank in 4 patients (14.3%). A total of ten patients (35.7%) with NOM were treated as outpatients. In this small cohort there was no instance where this treatment approach had to be changed. In 29 patients (50.9%) primary operative management (POM) was performed (13 SW, 13 GSW, three impalements). Median ISS was 20 (IQR 15-32). There was one non-therapeutic laparotomy and two non-therapeutic laparoscopies. One patient died during surgery due to exsanguination caused by a high-grade liver injury with concomitant lesion of the Vena cava.

**CONCLUSION**: Selective NOM in patients suffering from PAT appears to be a feasible treatment strategy with favorable outcomes also in a low-volume environment. However, established treatment algorithms, similar to high-volume centers, are required. Possible outpatient care is resource sparing and therefore increasingly important, however, further research is required to investigate its safety and patient selection.

articles.title: Splenic artery embolization versus operative management in traumatic splenic injury: a nationwide trend analysis and hospital-level comparison from Germany, 2019-2025.
articles.abstract: The spleen is the most frequently injured solid abdominal organ in blunt trauma, and its management has evolved substantially over recent decades towards non-operative strategies. Splenic artery embolization (SAE) is recommended by current guidelines as the preferred interventional approach in hemodynamically stable patients with higher-grade splenic injury. Despite this recommendation, national data on SAE utilization in Germany are rare and temporal trends as well as the influence of hospital size on treatment choice have not been systematically described. Nationwide German inpatient data were retrospectively analyzed using the InEK DatenBrowser (datenbrowser.inek.org), covering treatment years 2019 to 2025. All inpatient cases with traumatic splenic injury as the primary diagnosis (ICD-10-GM S36.00-S36.04, S36.08) were identified. Operative management was defined by OPS codes 5-413.* and 5-419.*, SAE by a combination of six OPS codes for selective embolization (particles, coils, and liquid agents). Non-operative management (NOM) comprised all remaining cases. Hospital bed-size categories served as proxies for care level and interventional radiology (IR) infrastructure. A chi-squared test assessed the association between hospital size and SAE utilization. A total of 14,422 inpatient splenic trauma cases were identified between 2019 and 2025 (mean 2,060 per year). SAE cases increased from 50 (4.3% of interventional cases) in 2019 to 81 (6.9%) in 2025, representing a 62% relative increase. Operative case volume remained stable throughout (- 0.9%). Hospital size was a highly significant determinant of SAE utilization (p < 0.001). SAE was effectively absent in hospitals with fewer than 150 beds, reached 2.6-2.7% in regional and secondary care centers, and 14.8% in maximal care and university hospitals. SAE utilization has increased by 62% in Germany between 2019 and 2025, yet remains substantially below guideline recommendations across all hospital categories. The absolute increase in SAE rate corresponded to 1.25% points as a proportion of all splenic trauma cases (95% CI 0.2-2.3 pp). The finding that even major centers with established IR achieved an SAE rate of 14.8% of interventional splenic trauma cases points to persistent structural and process-related barriers. These data support targeted efforts to integrate SAE pathways systematically into certified trauma center care.

articles.title: When prehospital resuscitation attempts are unsuccessful: care for the relatives following termination of treatment in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Nearly 5,000 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests occur annually in Denmark. Three in four take place in the patient's home, often witnessed by relatives. In 60-70% of out-of-hospital cardiac arrests, the patient dies at the scene despite treatment. This study investigates the relatives´ perspective when resuscitation is unsuccessful, identifying their needs with a view to enhancing the quality of care provided to those left behind when resuscitation attempts are unsuccessful.

**METHOD**: Fifteen semi-structured interviews were conducted with relatives who were present during the resuscitation attempts at out-of-hospital cardiac arrests where the patient was declared dead at the scene. The interviews were recorded and transcribed. Data were analysed using Systematic Text Condensation.

**RESULTS**: Three phases were identified, each with distinct needs of the relatives. Initially, the guidance from the Emergency Medical Dispatch Centre was highly valued. Once community first responders or prehospital staff arrived, two main and contrasting responses emerged: a need to withdraw from the event or a desire to personally assist in the treatment. After unsuccessful resuscitation, compassionate and unhurried communication was considered crucial.

**CONCLUSION**: The study highlights how relatives' needs shift across the phases of unsuccessful prehospital resuscitation. Community first responders fulfil an important emotional support role beyond providing basic life support. Individually tailored and transparent communication with the relatives during and after resuscitation can ease the psychological impact of the shift from the resuscitation phase, where the relatives may have hope, to the phase of termination of resuscitation attempts and the subsequent pronouncement of death of their relative.
articles.journal: Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med

articles.title: Prehospital whole blood warming and trauma-induced coagulopathy in combat casualties: A retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: Trauma-induced coagulopathy (TIC) causes significant morbidity and mortality in severely injured casualties. While low-titer group O whole blood (LTOWB) is increasingly used for prehospital resuscitation, the clinical value of active prehospital blood warming remains uncertain. We evaluated whether warmed LTOWB reduced TIC on emergency department (ED) arrival.

**METHODS**: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of combat casualties receiving prehospital LTOWB between October 27, 2023, and January 19, 2025 using linked data from the Israel Defense Forces Medical Corps Prehospital Trauma Registry and the Israeli National Trauma Registry. Patients were categorized by LTOWB administration method: active warming versus cold blood. The primary outcome was TIC on ED arrival (international normalized ratio ≥ 1.2). Multivariable logistic regression evaluated the association between warmed LTOWB and TIC, adjusting for prehospital shock, injury severity, severe head injury, transfusion volume, and acidosis on ED arrival.

**RESULTS**: Of 275 casualties receiving prehospital LTOWB, 209 were included: 61 received warmed and 148 cold LTOWB. The median age was 23 years, and most patients sustained severe or critical injuries. TIC occurred in 54 patients (25.8%), including 13 (21.3%) receiving warmed and 41 (27.7%) receiving cold LTOWB. After adjustment, warmed LTOWB was not associated with lower odds of TIC (aOR 1.07; 95% CI, 0.45-2.49). Warming was also not associated with reduced massive transfusion or improved 24-h or 30-day survival.

**CONCLUSION**: Among combat casualties receiving prehospital LTOWB, active blood warming was not associated with reduced TIC on ED arrival. Larger studies are needed to clarify its clinical role.

articles.title: Injuries among in-school adolescents in Africa, the Caribbean, and Pacific Nations: Cross-regional findings from the global school-based student health survey.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Serious adolescent injuries, defined as injuries requiring medical treatment or causing ≥ 1 day of missed activities, remain a major global concern. However, few studies compare culturally diverse world regions. Africa, the Caribbean, and Pacific Nations (PNs) were selected to capture variation in social-ecological contexts and violence exposure.

**METHODS**: Global School-based Student Health Survey (GSHS) 2017 data from school-attending adolescents aged 11-18 in Africa (n = 5756), the Caribbean (n = 5536), and PNs (n = 5288) were analyzed. Multivariable logistic regression estimated associations between serious injuries and demographic, psychological, behavioral, and environmental factors.

**RESULTS**: Suicide attempts, being physically attacked, and involvement in fights were the most consistent correlates across regions. Marginal effects showed that violence-related exposures increased injury probability by 8-19%, while suicide attempts increased risk by 7-8%. Other associations differed by region: age (Africa, Caribbean), sex and alcohol use (Caribbean, PNs), and bullying and food insecurity (Africa, PNs).

**IMPLICATIONS**: Findings underscore the need for culturally relevant, region-specific school-based interventions addressing violence, mental health, and social determinants such as food insecurity.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Serious injuries are common across all three regions and tightly linked to psychosocial distress and violence. Targeted global and regional strategies are urgently needed to reduce injury burden and promote adolescent health equity.

articles.title: Treatment of unstable intertrochanteric fractures in elderly patients using anterior compression augmented tension-band wiring combined with primary hemiarthroplasty.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: This study investigated the efficacy of anterior-compression augmented tension-band wiring combined with primary hemiarthroplasty (aTBW+PHA) for unstable intertrochanteric fractures in elderly fragility-fracture patients. While intramedullary nailing and dynamic hip screw fixation constitute the standard-of-care for most intertrochanteric fractures, high complication rates including trochanteric fragment displacement, non-union, and re-operation remain a concern in severely unstable, osteoporotic fractures. For this high-risk elderly subgroup, aTBW + PHA aims to achieve robust greater-trochanter fragment fixation and facilitate early postoperative functional recovery.

**METHODS**: This retrospective study enrolled 105 consecutive eligible patients treated between January 2015 and May 2022 with minimum postoperative follow-up of 24 months. According to the location and displacement direction of greater-trochanter fracture lines, individualized steel-wire winding strategies of aTBW were applied. Perioperative outcomes including operative time, intraoperative blood loss, hospital stay, time to initial partial weight-bearing, fracture-healing status and implant-related complications were recorded. Hip function was assessed using the Harris Hip Score (HHS).

**RESULTS**: Mean follow-up was 28.6 ± 5.8 months (range, 24-38 months). Mean operative time was 65.74 ± 10.80 min (range, 55-95 min); mean intraoperative blood loss was 238.42 ± 25.01 mL (range, 150-380 mL). Mean hospital stay was 9.50 ± 1.64 days (range: 6-11 days). Patients commenced walker-assisted partial weight-bearing at a mean of 2.9 days postoperatively (range, 1-5 days). Four postoperative complications occurred: one deep-vein thrombosis, one greater-trochanter non-union, one prosthetic dislocation, and one steel-wire breakage (3.8% overall complication rate). The HHS improved significantly from preoperative 30.2 ± 6.2 points to 90.5 ± 8.7 points at final follow-up.

**CONCLUSIONS**: aTBW + PHA achieves favourable clinical outcomes in elderly patients with fragility-related unstable intertrochanteric fractures. Individualized anterior-compression augmented tension-band wiring, tailored to greater-trochanter fracture-line morphology, provides reliable fixation of trochanteric fragments. Further comparative clinical studies are warranted.

articles.title: Reported mortality benefit of early surgery not reproduced in hip fracture with myocardial injury.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: A post hoc substudy of the HIP ATTACK trial reported a large mortality benefit for accelerated surgery in patients with hip fracture and myocardial injury. We aimed to determine whether that benefit is reproduced at scale.

**PATIENTS AND METHODS**: Retrospective cohort study in a federated network of 112 United States health care organisations, with index events from 25 March 2006-25 March 2026. Patients had a proximal femoral fracture with same-date acute myocardial infarction or troponin I of 0.04 µg/L or greater, and underwent surgery. Windows of 0-1, > 1-2, > 2-3, and > 3 days were compared pairwise for all-cause mortality after 1:1 propensity score matching and, separately, stratified by procedure.

**RESULTS**: Across cohorts totalling 25,707 patients, no comparison at any time point showed a significant advantage for earlier surgery, with or without procedure stratification. At 3 months, confidence intervals excluded an early advantage above 1.7 percentage points; the reported benefit was 12. In 8184 matched pairs one day apart, 3-month mortality was identical (risk difference, 0.0%; 95% confidence interval, -1.2-1.2). More than 68% had death, infarction, stroke, or heart failure by 12 months. Survival appeared better beyond 3 days, but procedure stratification removed 22-45% of it, and those patients had survived an interval containing 30% of deaths among never-operated patients.

**CONCLUSIONS**: The mortality benefit reported for early surgery in patients with troponin elevation was not reproduced at scale: earlier surgery within the first 3 days conferred no survival advantage. Better survival beyond 3 days reflects procedure mix and survival to surgery, not a benefit of waiting. Clinicians should consider cardiac assessment and optimisation before surgery when it can be completed within the first 3 days.

articles.title: Late-presenting lateral humeral condyle fractures (LHC) in children: A treatment algorithm and clinical outcomes.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Lateral humeral condyle (LHC) fractures in children are commonly misdiagnosed or insufficiently treated. Management remains controversial for fractures presenting more than 3 weeks after injury.

**MATERIALS AND METHODS**: This prospective case series included 30 children with LHC fractures presenting more than 3 weeks after injury (21 boys and 9 girls; mean age at diagnosis, 8.6 years). Treatments included nonoperative management (4 patients), "in-situ" fixation (2 patients), open reduction and internal fixation (11 patients), corrective osteotomy (11 patients) and excision of bony spur (2 patients). Final radiographs were investigated for bone healing, avascular necrosis, elbow deformities and growth disturbances. Outcome analysis included standard clinical assessment and functional scoring (Dhillon score and Mayo Elbow Performance Score), in addition to plain radiographs. The management plan was revised at the end of the study.

**RESULTS**: The mean time from injury to presentation was 21.72 months. The mean follow-up was 25.06 months (range: 12-75). Complications were observed in 2 patients (6.6%). One patient had a recurrent cubitus varus deformity after previous correction, and another had a limitation of range of motion. At the latest follow-up, pain and functional scores improved in 29 of 30 patients (96.6%) compared with the baseline. ROM arc increased on average by 20 ° (p = 0.01). Pronation and supination were normal in all patients. MEPS increased on average from 60 points at baseline to 95 points at the latest follow-up visit (p < 0.001), while Dhillon score improved on average from 4.79 to 7.27 points (p < 0.001).

**CONCLUSION**: Management of late-presenting LHC fractures should focus on fragment viability, ‎displacement, and stability, not just chronicity. ORIF remains viable for extremely late cases. ‎Rigid fixation supports early rehabilitation. Further multicenter studies are needed to refine ‎guidelines.‎.

articles.title: Evaluation of the ACS Trauma Quality Improvement Program benchmark for intracranial pressure monitoring across trauma centers.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: In severe traumatic brain injury (sTBI), intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring detects and directs management for intracranial hypertension. ICP monitoring is recommended for sTBI patients and is included as a benchmarked quality metric by the American College of Surgeons Trauma Quality Improvement Programs (ACS-TQIP), which reports annual ICP monitor usage across all participating trauma centers. We evaluated whether greater institutional ICP utilization was associated with lower center-level mortality.

**METHODS**: For this retrospective observational study, adult patients aged 18 years and older meeting the ACS-TQIP definition of sTBI admitted to Level I or II trauma centers from 2013 to 2023 were identified. Patient data were aggregated by trauma center and calendar year to mirror the ACS-TQIP benchmarking framework. Annual institutional ICP monitor utilization and in-hospital mortality rates were calculated for each center-year combination. Multivariable generalized linear mixed-effects models evaluated whether centers with higher ICP monitor utilization had lower mortality after adjusting for patient demographics, injury severity, neurological status, operative intervention, injury mechanism, and hospital length of stay.

**RESULTS**: Among 191,686 sTBI patients, 29,224 (15.2%) underwent ICP monitoring. ICP monitor utilization ranged from 11% to 21% during the study period with a notable increase in 2017, whereas overall mortality remained largely unchanged. Year-specific analyses demonstrated a protective association between greater ICP monitor utilization and mortality in 2015 and an association with increased mortality in 2023. After adjustment for differences in patient and institutional characteristics, higher institutional ICP monitor utilization was not associated with lower center-level mortality (odds ratio=0.99, 95% CI=0.97-1.00; P=0.128).

**CONCLUSIONS**: Using over a decade of TQIP data, greater institutional ICP monitor utilization was not associated with lower mortality across ACS-TQIP centers. These findings suggest that greater institutional adoption of ICP monitoring alone may not improve center-level outcomes and support periodic reassessment of ICP monitoring as a benchmarked ACS-TQIP quality metric.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Level IV, prognostic & epidemiological.

articles.title: Walking Wounded Blood Bank: A new donor pool or a prioritization strategy?
Secondary traumatic stress: A threat to surgeons and the patients they serve.
articles.abstract: Secondary traumatic stress (STS) can present with symptoms nearly identical to post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). However, instead of resulting from direct exposure to trauma as the victim, STS develops after repeated indirect exposure to severe injury, death, and human suffering. This can cause significant psychological distress and ultimately contribute to PTSD-like symptoms and burnout. Evidence suggests that STS is common among trauma surgeons, although its prevalence remains poorly characterized. STS should be considered an occupational hazard of trauma surgery rather than a failure of individual determination or resilience and may have important consequences for the surgical workforce and, ultimately, patient care. We argue that institutions should consider a framework that incorporates monitoring of measurable workload and trauma-related risk factors at the individual surgeon level. These factors could prompt preventive measures such as protected recovery time and confidential screening using validated tools. When psychological injury is identified, surgeons should be afforded rapid access to mental health resources and formal peer support. Existing institutional programs demonstrate that these interventions can be operationalized, but their effectiveness in preventing, identifying, and treating STS requires further study. Addressing STS must be taken seriously as an institutional responsibility if we are to protect the trauma surgery workforce while supporting the quality and sustainability of patient care.

articles.title: Is the H-index an adequate measure of trauma surgeon research productivity?
articles.abstract: The H-index is a widely used objective metric by academia to make critical decisions such as grant funding, hiring, promotion, and retention. The H-index is defined as the largest number (h) of publications that have received at least h citations. Unfortunately, the H-index presents many limitations including its inherent cumulative nature, incompatibility among specialties, its potential opaqueness to landmark research, and gender disparity among other potential threats to its validity. Alternatives to H-index that potentially address some of its core weaknesses are the relative citation ratio (RCR), fractional H-index, and the altmetric-index. The altmetric-index measures social and internet engagement rather than citations but has the advantage over H-index in providing more immediate feedback on a paper potential impact, especially among the general public. Trauma surgeons rank in the mid-to-low median H-index, driven primarily by low H-index among young faculty. H-index has value as an objective measure of research productivity, but stakeholders must understand its limitations, and it should only be used as one component of the total holistic assessment of an individual contribution to an academic surgical department.

articles.title: Infectious complications are preceded by specific longitudinal neutrophil cell surface patterns after polytrauma: Preliminary results of a prospective analysis.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Alterations in neutrophil receptors provide valuable insights into the immune response after polytrauma. Point-of-care (POC) technologies enable rapid on-site analysis of neutrophils. Previous studies demonstrated individual neutrophil surface patterns after trauma, depending on injury severity and metabolic status. We hypothesized that infectious complications after polytrauma are preceded by specific neutrophil cell surface receptor alterations.

**METHODS**: A POC neutrophil analysis system (AQUIOS® Flow Cytometer) was implemented at a Level 1 trauma center. Polytrauma patients with an Injury Severity Score (ISS)≥25 were prospectively included. Neutrophil cell surface expression of CD10, CD11b, CD64, CD62L, and CD16 was analyzed immediately after admission and after 8 hours, 24 hours, 48 hours, and 5 days. Patients were grouped according to the occurrence or absence of infectious complications.

**RESULTS**: Thirty-two polytrauma patients with a median ISS of 34.5 were included in this study. Trauma sequelae included spine fractures, long bone fractures, and traumatic brain injury. During hospitalization, 13 out of 32 patients developed infectious complications. Patients who subsequently developed infectious complications showed significantly higher CD64 expression throughout the observation period, and CD62L demonstrated a trend toward higher expression. In addition, CD11b expression was elevated 8 hours after trauma.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Longitudinal assessment of multiple selected neutrophil markers draws an individual neutrophil surface profile, with specific patterns associated with the development of infectious complications. This offers a promising tool for early risk stratification and identification of trauma patients vulnerable to post-traumatic infectious complications and allows for future immune-protective trauma surgery.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Prognostic and Epidemiological; Level III.

articles.title: Hospital volume and outcomes in after-hours emergency general surgery: a nationwide retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: High-volume hospitals are associated with better outcomes in some surgical fields, including emergency general surgery (EGS). However, the association of hospital volume with outcomes in after-hours EGS remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the association between hospital-year volume of after-hours EGS and in-hospital mortality and total healthcare costs.

**METHODS**: We conducted a nationwide retrospective cohort study using the Japanese Diagnosis Procedure Combination database. We included patients aged ≥16 years who were directly admitted from outpatient settings and underwent after-hours EGS on or the day after admission between April 2014 and March 2023. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality; the secondary outcome was total healthcare costs during hospitalization. Associations were evaluated using mixed-effects models. Hospital-year volume was analyzed continuously using natural cubic splines and categorically (1-19, 20-49, 50-99, and ≥100 cases/year).

**RESULTS**: Overall, 235,465 patients were included. In the mixed-effects logistic regression model, each 10-case increase in hospital-year volume was associated with lower in-hospital mortality (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.97; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.96-0.98; p<0.001). Spline analyses showed that the adjusted odds of in-hospital mortality generally decreased with increasing hospital-year volume, although this decline became less pronounced at higher-volume levels. Adjusted healthcare costs decreased across most of the volume range before increasing slightly at the highest levels. Compared with 1 to 19 cases/year, the aORs for in-hospital mortality were 0.77 (95% CI, 0.71-0.83), 0.72 (95% CI, 0.66-0.78), and 0.66 (95% CI, 0.59-0.74) for 20-49, 50-99, and ≥100 cases/year, respectively (all p<0.001). The corresponding adjusted relative costs were 0.99 (95% CI, 0.99-1.00; p=0.205), 0.98 (95% CI, 0.97-0.99; p=0.001), and 0.97 (95% CI, 0.96-0.99; p<0.001).

**CONCLUSIONS**: Higher hospital-year after-hours EGS volume was associated with lower in-hospital mortality and modestly lower healthcare costs. These associations varied across the volume range.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Prognostic/epidemiological; Level III.

articles.title: Identifying At-Risk Subgroups for Suboptimal Computed Tomography Imaging in Older Patients With Blunt Trauma.
articles.abstract:
**IMPORTANCE**: Without standardized imaging algorithms for older trauma patients, there is high heterogeneity in the diagnosis of injuries in this vulnerable population.

**OBJECTIVE**: To identify clinically distinct subgroups of older patients with blunt trauma and examine if any groups have a high likelihood of suboptimal computed tomography (CT) imaging.

**DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS**: This cohort study was a secondary analysis of the multicenter Scanning the Aged trial (November 2020 to December 2021), which included 5496 patients with blunt trauma 65 years or older from 18 trauma centers. Latent class analysis identified patient subgroups using 10 categorized indicators: origin of injury, age, Charlson Comorbidity Index, functional status, Glasgow Coma Scale score, intoxication, antiplatelet or anticoagulant use, emergency department intervention, time since injury, and Injury Severity Score. Data analysis was performed from August 2025 to February 2026.

**EXPOSURE**: Latent class membership.

**MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES**: Suboptimal imaging (a mismatch between injuries and initial diagnostic CT performed), pan-scan utilization, and in-hospital mortality.

**RESULTS**: Among 5496 patients with blunt trauma, 2990 (54.4%) were female and 2506 (45.6%) male; the median (IQR) age was 79 (71-86) years. The 4-class model was selected as the optimal solution based on a comparison of model fit indices and interpretability across competing latent class models. Class 1 (scene arrival and moderate injury, n = 417; 33.1%) comprised younger patients with preserved function. Class 2 (frail with fall, n = 519; 41.3%) included older adults (median [IQR] age, 84 [78-89] years) with functional dependence. Class 3 (transfer, n = 219; 17.4%) was defined by transfer status. Class 4 (critical trauma, n = 103; 8.2%) represented severely injured patients. Suboptimal imaging rates varied significantly across classes (from 2.5% to 11.0%), with class 3 showing nearly 4-fold higher odds (odds ratio [OR], 3.85; 95% CI, 1.67-8.90; P = .002). Class 4 had 45.6% mortality (47/103) with 16-fold higher adjusted odds of death (adjusted OR, 16.40; 95% CI, 5.40-49.81; P < .001). Pan-scan utilization ranged from 49.8% (109/219) to 70.9% (73/103) across classes, with adjusted odds not differing between all classes.

**CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE**: This study identified 4 distinct phenotypes of older patients with blunt trauma and varying imaging needs. Patients transferred from nontrauma centers to trauma centers demonstrated the highest risk for suboptimal imaging, highlighting care coordination gaps. Critical trauma patients had markedly elevated mortality, with a 16-fold higher adjusted odds of death. These findings may support developing targeted imaging protocols based on patient phenotype, with particular attention to patients with the highest risk of diagnostic gaps.

articles.title: Localised geographic and socioeconomic inequalities in prehospital trauma care access for road traffic collisions in England: a spatial autocorrelation analysis.
articles.abstract:
**PURPOSE**: We examined national and local associations between socioeconomic deprivation and modelled access to major-trauma resources in England.

**METHODS**: All 33,755 English Lower-layer Super Output Areas (LSOAs) were analysed. Drive-times to the nearest adult Major Trauma Centre (MTC) and from the nearest listed Helicopter Emergency Medical Service (HEMS) base were computed; flight-time from the nearest HEMS base was estimated. Police-reported killed-or-seriously-injured (KSI) collision rates (2022-2024) and Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) decile were assessed using global and local spatial autocorrelation. KSI collisions involved at least one killed or seriously injured casualty.

**RESULTS**: Population-based KSI collision rates were spatially clustered (Global Moran's I = 0.207, p = 0.001), while national associations between deprivation and access were weak (bivariate Moran's I = 0.117, 0.023 and - 0.016 for MTC drive-time, HEMS-base road time and flight-time). National median times were 16.4, 20.9 and 4.9 min, respectively. Local analysis identified 1,101 LSOAs (3.4% of 32,747 with valid IMD data) simultaneously more deprived and access-poor across all three measures. Their median own-area times were 56.8, 42.2 and 10.4 min. This subgroup had a higher population-based KSI collision rate than the remainder of the valid-IMD sample (Welch's t = 8.1, p < 0.001), persisting in a rural-only analysis.

**CONCLUSION**: England showed no national deprivation gradient in access to major-trauma resources. Local analysis identified areas where greater deprivation, slower modelled access and higher KSI collision rates coincided, providing candidates for investigation and service planning.

articles.title: Hidden in plain sight: a comprehensive analysis of missed rib fractures across five anatomic sectors of the chest wall.
articles.abstract:
**PURPOSE**: Missed rib fractures on initial chest CT are common and under-reported. We quantified the number, location and severity of rib fractures missed on initial radiologist review compared with a trauma surgeon's systematic secondary review.

**METHODS**: This retrospective study included patients with rib fractures at three affiliated trauma centers (2023-2024). Trauma surgeons re-reviewed initial chest CT scans using the Sucher-Lim Taxonomy for Acute Rib Fractures (SL-TARF) and compared findings with the original radiologist report. Patients younger than 18 years, with non-acute fractures, not admitted, without CT imaging for review, or without an SL-TARF map recorded by the time of data collection were excluded.

**RESULTS**: Among 943 patients (mean age 63 ± 19 years; 37.4% ground-level falls), 415 (44%) had at least one missed rib fracture. Of 5,588 fractures on secondary review (4,215 reported initially), 1,373 (24.6%) were missed. By sector, missed fractures were costochondral (25.7%), anterior (21.9%), lateral (20.4%), posterior (17.9%) and paravertebral (14.1%). Most were Type 1 (incomplete; 69.1%), then Type 2 (19.2%) and Type 3 (11.7%). Patients with a missed fracture more often had ≥ 7 fractures on the initial report (26.0% vs. 19.1%, p = .011) and flail chest on secondary review (20.0% vs. 6.3%, p < .001).

**CONCLUSIONS**: Missed rib fractures occur throughout the rib cage rather than in a single region. Trauma surgeon secondary review of chest CT identifies missed fractures at rates comparable to prior post-mortem or repeat-imaging studies. These findings do not, by themselves, justify a change in practice; larger studies are under way.

articles.title: Failure of intramedullary nailing in pertrochanteric femur fractures - A retrospective analysis of 383 patients over a 5.5-year period.
articles.abstract:
**PURPOSE**: Pertrochanteric femoral fractures are a rising health and economic burden in ageing societies. Intramedullary nailing is standard treatment, yet implant failure remains a serious complication. This study evaluated patient, fracture and surgical factors associated with implant failure.

**METHODS**: This single-centre retrospective cohort study included adults who underwent primary intramedullary nailing for AO/OTA 31A1.2, 31A1.3, 31A2.2 and 31A2.3 pertrochanteric fractures at Evangelisches Krankenhaus Oldenburg, a Level I trauma centre in Oldenburg, Germany, between 1 January 2019 and 31 July 2024. Demographic, clinical and radiographic data were extracted from electronic records and imaging archives. Variables included age, sex, documented osteoporosis, AO/OTA classification, reduction quality and tip-apex distance. Implant failure, including cut-out, migration or loosening was the primary endpoint. Associations were tested using Chi-square and multivariable logistic regression.

**RESULTS**: A total of 383 patients (mean age 80.3 years; 70% women) met inclusion criteria. Osteoporosis was documented in 59%. Implant failure occurred in 4.4% (n = 17), pseudarthrosis in 1.0% (n = 4) and revision surgery in 5.5% (n = 21). In the bivariate Chi-square analysis, fracture morphology was the only parameter significantly associated with implant failure (p < 0.001). In multivariable logistic regression, the model was significant (p = 0.012; Nagelkerke R² = 0.202). Female sex (OR 5.82, p = 0.038) and fracture morphology (p = 0.026) were independent predictors.

**CONCLUSION**: Fracture morphology described by the AO/OTA classification emerged as the strongest predictor of implant failure after intramedullary nailing of pertrochanteric fractures. Unstable subtypes require careful preoperative planning and follow-up. Female sex was also independently associated with implant failure.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Level III, retrospective cohort study (Oxford 2011).

**TRIAL REGISTRATION**: German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS), DRKS00024627, retrospectively registered on 29 March 2021.

articles.title: Fragility-associated nonunion represents a distinct biological phenotype compared with trauma-associated nonunion: a retrospective cohort study of 213 consecutive cases.
articles.abstract:
**PURPOSE**: Long bone nonunion is conventionally treated as a uniform disease entity. We hypothesized that nonunion arises through distinct biological pathways, with a fragility-associated phenotype driven by systemic biological vulnerability differing fundamentally from a trauma-associated phenotype driven by local soft tissue compromise and infection.

**METHODS**: Retrospective cohort study of 213 consecutive long bone nonunions treated at a Level 1 trauma center (2007-2018). Patients were classified as fragility-associated (age ≥ 65 years and/or documented osteoporosis; n = 51, 23.9%) or non-fragility/trauma-associated (n = 162, 76.1%). Groups were compared regarding demographics, comorbidity profiles, fracture characteristics, infection rates, operative burden, laboratory parameters, and treatment strategies. Multivariate logistic regression was performed to evaluate independent predictors of septic nonunion and high revision burden.

**RESULTS**: The fragility phenotype was characterized by significantly higher comorbidity burden (3.2 ± 1.6 vs. 1.8 ± 1.6; p < 0.001), cardiovascular disease (90.2% vs. 41.4%; p < 0.001), renal insufficiency (25.5% vs. 3.7%; p < 0.001), elevated CRP (median 11.5 vs. 4.0 mg/L; p = 0.012), and higher ASA classification (ASA ≥ III: 39.2% vs. 19.1%; p = 0.006). The trauma-associated phenotype showed higher rates of open fractures (25.3% vs. 13.7%), polytrauma (27.8% vs. 9.8%; p = 0.014), and nicotine use (47.5% vs. 11.8%; p < 0.001). On multivariate analysis, fragility was not an independent predictor of septic nonunion (OR 1.07, 95% CI 0.44-2.61; p = 0.886) or high revision burden (OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.28-2.75; p = 0.829), while open fracture (OR 3.34, 95% CI 1.40-7.99; p = 0.007) and septic nonunion (OR 25.17, 95% CI 9.14-69.29; p < 0.001) were the dominant risk factors.

**CONCLUSION**: Fragility-associated and trauma-associated nonunions represent distinct clinical phenotypes. The fragility phenotype is driven by systemic biological vulnerability but does not confer increased infection or reconstructive burden. These findings support phenotype-specific approaches to nonunion prevention and treatment.

articles.title: Staged Brachialis to Anterior Interosseous Nerve Transfer With Graft for Recovery of Grasp in the Tetraplegic Patient: A Case Series.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES**: Cervical spinal cord injury often results in loss of hand function, a top functional priority in this population. Nerve transfers have become a reliable intervention for restoring hand function. Limited nerve donors in the forearm have led to the use of the brachialis (BRA) branch of the musculocutaneous nerve to reinnervate the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) to recover finger flexion. Relatively poor outcomes have been previously reported, potentially due to axon loss from proximal interconnecting fascicles. Our objective was to review a case series of single-surgeon outcomes using 2 variations of the BRA-AIN transfer that address this limitation.

**METHODS**: A single-center retrospective case series of BRA-AIN transfer was performed through either (1) a direct coaptation performed in elbow flexion followed by progressive extension or (2) an indirect, 2-stage, interpositional graft. Candidate screening consisted of physical examination and electrodiagnostics to determine the absence of volitional finger flexion and preserved BRA innervation. Manual muscle testing using Medical Research Council grading was the primary outcome.

**RESULTS**: Twenty patients (ages 18-72 years) with a C5/6 motor level underwent BRA-AIN on 28 limbs with a minimum 12-month follow-up. The median time from injury to surgery was 20.5 months. The primary outcome was Medical Research Council strength for flexor digitorum profundus of the second digit (FDP2) or flexor pollicis longus (FPL). M3 strength was achieved in 22 patients (79%) for FDP2 and 20 (71%) for FPL. Most patients (79%) underwent an indirect transfer, and FDP2 and flexor digitorum profundus of the third digit achieved functional strength (M ≥ 3) in 18 patients (82%) of this group compared with 4 (67%) of direct repairs. FPL achieved functional strength in 15 patients (68%) of the indirect repairs compared with 5 (83%) of direct.

**CONCLUSION**: These variations of the BRA-AIN nerve transfer provide improved outcomes by circumventing interconnecting fascicles to deliver more axons to the intended targets.

articles.title: Diagnostic accuracy, characteristics and survival of children with trauma in HEMS: a retrospective multi-centre observational study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Trauma is a leading cause of death in children. Paediatric patients comprise only a small fraction of HEMS missions. Little is known about the diagnostic accuracy of prehospital and in-hospital diagnoses in a large physician-staffed HEMS.

**METHODS**: This observational multicentre study included paediatric trauma patients ≤ 16 years treated by the Swiss Air-Rescue between 28/10/2021 and 20/08/2024. We included all primary missions with a National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA) score of ≥ 3 (i.e. moderate to severe trauma) transported to three paediatric trauma centres or declared dead on-scene. Data were obtained from the HEMS database and the hospital discharge report. The primary outcome was diagnostic accuracy between the prehospital and in-hospital diagnoses, measured with Cohen's kappa. Secondary outcomes included patient characteristics, interventions, and survival.

**RESULTS**: We screened 1,531 eligible missions, of which 282 met inclusion criteria. Median age was 8.3 [IQR 3.5-12.1] years, and 163 (57.8%) were male. Most missions had a NACA score of 3 [IQR 3-4] and were during the daytime (90.4%). Ten patients were declared dead on-scene. Tracheal intubation was performed in 7.5% of the patients. Cohen's kappa of the diagnostic accuracy between prehospital and in-hospital diagnoses was 0.64 (95%CI 0.58-0.70). Polytrauma was underdiagnosed; in contrast, injuries to the extremity, pelvis and traumatic brain injury were overdiagnosed. Overall survival to hospital discharge and at 1 year after trauma was 92.2%.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Paediatric trauma in this cohort was characterised by a high incidence of high-velocity injuries. The prehospital diagnosis correlated substantially with the in-hospital diagnosis, supporting the clinical value of HEMS physicians to correctly triage paediatric patients. Documentation of vital signs was heterogeneous. Hospital survival and 1-year survival were high in this cohort. However, polytrauma remained underdiagnosed and should be targeted to improve prehospital care for paediatric trauma.

**TRIAL REGISTRATION**: N/A.
articles.journal: Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med

articles.title: Severity ranking of immunocompromise conditions for patients undergoing emergency surgery: an outcomes-based reassessment of the 2021 consensus classification system published in the World Journal of Emergency Surgery.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: In 2021, the World Journal of Emergency Surgery published consensus guidelines classifying immunocompromised patients with acute abdomen into "mild-moderate" and "severe" immune deficiency categories to standardize perioperative risk assessment and guide surgical decision-making. We assessed whether published mortality and complication data are consistent with this classification.

**METHODS**: We conducted a structured literature review of PubMed and MEDLINE (2000-2025) for studies reporting mortality and complications in adult immunocompromised patients undergoing emergency colectomy, cholecystectomy, appendectomy, or small bowel resection, with a non-immunocompromised control group. Of the fifteen immunocompromising conditions in the classification, three were excluded for confounding or insufficient data (burns, trauma, post-splenectomy) and two pairs combined (symptomatic HIV/AIDS with CD4 < 200 cells/mm

**RESULTS**: The guidelines classified five conditions as severe (neutropenia, steroid use, HIV < 200 cells/mm

**CONCLUSION**: Observed procedure-specific mortality and complication data do not consistently support the 2021 consensus severity ranking: four of the ten conditions were discordant with their assigned classification. This analysis suggests reconsidering uremia and advanced age as severe, and malignancy and transplant as mild-moderate. Because immunocompromise severity may influence whether and when patients undergo surgery, these findings highlight a priority for evidence-based refinement of severity ranking in emergency general surgery.

articles.title: Micromobility crashes: A review of the demographics, risk factors, injury patterns, and preventative strategies.
articles.abstract: Micromobility device use has rapidly expanded since the last several decades, largely driven by their flexibility and utility for short-distance travel. This growth has been accompanied by a corresponding rise in the rate of micromobility-related injuries and fatalities, yet the demographic patterns, risk factors, and injury characteristics associated with these incidents remain incompletely characterized. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on micromobility user demographics, injury patterns, and modifiable risk factors and evaluates proposed strategies for improving rider and pedestrian safety. Injured riders are predominantly young and male, with alcohol use, helmet non-use, excessive speed, and nighttime riding as the most consistently identified risk factors. These behaviors frequently co-occur and may have compounding effects on injury severity. Falls represent the most common injury mechanism, though collisions with motor vehicles are associated with disproportionately severe outcomes, including traumatic brain injury. Injury rates and patterns vary meaningfully by device type, though comparisons across studies are complicated by inconsistent exposure measurements and the lack of a universally standardized definition of micromobility devices. Existing legislation on impaired riding, helmet use, and sidewalk riding varies widely across jurisdictions. Emerging evidence from cities that have implemented targeted regulatory interventions, including speed and nighttime restrictions, suggests that policy measures can meaningfully reduce injury incidence. Reducing the burden of micromobility-related injuries will require a coordinated, multifaceted approach integrating improved injury surveillance, appropriate infrastructure, rider and public education, and evidence-based policy implementation.

articles.title: Higher Quality Temperature Control Is Associated With Improved Outcomes Following Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Multicenter Validation Study.
articles.abstract:
**STUDY OBJECTIVE**: Hypothermic temperature control has not consistently demonstrated a neuroprotective effect, resulting in heterogeneity of use in clinical practice. We evaluated temperature control quality across 4 institutions and its association with clinical outcomes.

**METHODS**: Retrospective analysis of institutional registry data collected between 2021 and 2024 in survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) with Glasgow Coma Scale Motor score less than 6 from 4 academic centers with established cardiac arrest programs. Eligible patients included those 18 years of age or older, treated with hypothermic temperature control (33-36°C) using a feedback-controlled device, and admitted to an intensive care unit (ICU). A temperature control quality score (0-6) was assigned for each patient. The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge. The secondary outcome was good neurologic outcome at hospital discharge, defined as a Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) score of 1-2. Univariable and multivariable logistic regressions quantified the relationship between quality of temperature control, as an ordinal variable, and outcomes.

**RESULTS**: Among 356 included patients, most were male (N=224, 62.9%) with mean (standard deviation [SD]) age 58.1 (15.2) years. Most suffered a nonshockable arrest (N=262, 73.6%) and did not receive layperson CPR (N=225, 63.2%). Median [IQR] Pittsburgh Cardiac Arrest Category score was 4 [3,4], mean (SD) lactate 9.1 (4.1) mmol/L, and pH 7.09 (0.17). Median [IQR] preinduction time was 2.3 [1.5 to 3.5] hours and 150 (42.1%) were treated with early neuromuscular blockade. Adjusting for confounders in the multivariable model, an increase of one-point in the temperature control quality score was associated with improved survival at hospital discharge (odds ratio [OR] 1.32; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.07 to 1.64). A one-point increase in the quality score also resulted in a shift towards lower (improved) CPC score (OR 1.28; 95% CI, 0.05 to 1.55). The direction of effect was consistent across all centers.

**CONCLUSION**: In unresponsive survivors of OHCA, an increase in temperature control quality was associated with improved survival and better neurologic outcome; however, confounding by site, injury severity, or perceived prognosis is possible. Lack of temperature control parameter standardization may influence efficacy and practice variability within pragmatic-design clinical trials possibly contributed to neutral trial results. Prospective trials evaluating the importance of temperature control quality and the population most likely to benefit from hypothermic temperature control are essential.

articles.title: Prehospital Antibiotics for Patients With Suspected Sepsis: Research Summary.
Prehospital Fluid Resuscitation for Patients With Suspected Sepsis: The PITSTOP-Fluids Factorial Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract:
**IMPORTANCE**: Early resuscitation with intravenous fluids is recommended for patients with sepsis.

**OBJECTIVE**: To determine the effect of liberal vs more conservative fluid resuscitation strategies in the ambulance on mortality among patients with suspected sepsis.

**DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS**: Multicenter, 2 × 2 factorial randomized clinical trial conducted by 4 paramedic services and their destination hospitals in Ontario, Canada. Participants were adults with suspected sepsis, defined as suspected infection, fever (≥38.0 °C), and hypotension (systolic blood pressure [SBP] <100 mm Hg), and obtainable intravenous access. Patients were enrolled between March 23, 2020, and August 20, 2025, with last follow-up in December 2025.

**INTERVENTION**: Patients were randomized to receive liberal fluids (up to 2 L of normal saline regardless of subsequent SBP) or usual care (fluids only when SBP <90 mm Hg and stopped when SBP ≥100 mm Hg) during prehospital care and until transfer of care in the emergency department. (Patients were additionally randomized to receive ceftriaxone vs placebo; analysis of which is reported separately.).

**MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES**: The primary outcome was hospital mortality, defined as death prior to hospital discharge up to day 90. There were 17 secondary outcomes, including all-cause mortality at 90 days, hospitalization, intensive care unit admission, mechanical ventilation, vasopressor therapy, dialysis, and total fluids infused within 24 hours of hospital arrival.

**RESULTS**: Among 1686 randomized patients, 1669 were eligible and 1646 were included in the primary outcome analysis (830 in the liberal fluids group and 816 in the usual fluids group). The median age of patients was 76 (IQR, 63-85) years and 938 (57.0%) were male. Most patients in both groups received a fluid bolus (826/848 [97.4%] in the liberal fluids group; 700/821 [85.3%] in the usual fluids group) during transport, but patients in the liberal fluids group received a larger volume (median, 1500 mL [IQR, 1000-2000 mL]) vs 500 mL [IQR, 175-800 mL] in the usual fluids group; difference, 910.1 mL [95% CI, 857.3-962.9 mL]). Hospital mortality was 149/830 (18.0%) in the liberal fluids group and 149/816 (18.3%) in the usual fluids group (risk ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.80-1.20]; unadjusted risk difference, -0.3 [95% CI, -4.0 to 3.4]; P = .82). Among the 17 secondary outcomes, all were similar between groups. Adverse events, including pulmonary edema during transport, were infrequent in both groups.

**CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE**: A more liberal fluid resuscitation strategy for the prehospital management of patients with suspected sepsis did not reduce mortality compared with more restrictive usual care.

**TRIAL REGISTRATION**: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03068741.

articles.title: Prehospital Fluid Resuscitation for Patients With Suspected Sepsis: Research Summary.
Prehospital Antibiotics for Patients With Suspected Sepsis: The PITSTOP-Antibiotics Factorial Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract:
**IMPORTANCE**: Early treatment with antibiotics is considered an important intervention to reduce mortality for patients with sepsis.

**OBJECTIVE**: To determine the effect of earlier treatment with antibiotics in the ambulance on 90-day mortality compared with usual treatment in the emergency department.

**DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS**: This multicenter, 2 × 2 factorial randomized, placebo-controlled trial was conducted among 4 paramedic services and their destination hospitals in Ontario, Canada. Participants were adults with suspected sepsis, defined as suspected infection, fever (≥38.0 °C), and hypotension (systolic blood pressure <100 mm Hg). Patients were enrolled between March 23, 2020, and August 20, 2025, with final follow-up in December 2025.

**INTERVENTIONS**: Patients were randomized to receive 1 g of intramuscular ceftriaxone or placebo (and to receive liberal fluids vs usual fluids; reported separately) during prehospital care in the ambulance. All patients could receive open-label antibiotics in the emergency department.

**MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES**: The primary outcome was hospital mortality, defined as death prior to hospital discharge to day 90. There were 17 secondary outcomes, including all-cause mortality at 90 days, hospitalization, intensive care unit admission, use of mechanical ventilation, use of dialysis, positive culture results, and antibiotics within 24 hours of hospital arrival.

**RESULTS**: Among 2091 randomized patients, 2048 were eligible for the primary analysis, with 1026 randomized to receive ceftriaxone and 1022 randomized to receive placebo. The median (IQR) age of patients was 75 (62-85) years and 1162 (56.7%) were males. The mean (SD) time from paramedic arrival at patient to administration of study drug was 37 (36) minutes in the ceftriaxone group and 39 (55) minutes in the placebo group. Most patients (735 of 795 [92.5%] in the ceftriaxone group and 730 of 792 [92.2%] in placebo group) were treated with antibiotics in the hospital after a mean (SD) of 247.3 (207.7) minutes after paramedic arrival among patients in the ceftriaxone group and 252.8 (218.0) minutes among the placebo group. The rate of hospital mortality was 182 of 1009 (18.0%) in the ceftriaxone group and 186 of 1011 (18.4%) in the placebo group (risk ratio, 0.97 [95% CI, 0.81-1.17]; P = .77). Of 17 secondary outcomes, all were similar between the groups.

**CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE**: Among patients with suspected sepsis on evaluation by paramedics, earlier treatment with antibiotics in the ambulance did not reduce mortality compared with usual care provided in the emergency department.

**TRIAL REGISTRATION**: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03068741.

articles.title: Effect of the calming anxiety and relaxation emergency (Abdominal) surgery (CARES) program on patients' pre- and postoperative anxiety management and outcomes: a prospective quasi-experimental study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Patients undergoing emergency abdominal surgery often have limited time to prepare. This may lead to anxiety, which can adversely affect postoperative recovery. A structured intervention, Calming Anxiety and Relaxation for Emergency (Abdominal) Surgery (CARES) program, was developed to address this concern.

**METHODS**: In this prospective quasi-experimental study, the effects of the CARES program on pre- and postoperative anxiety were evaluated among adult patients undergoing emergency abdominal surgery at a regional hospital in Hong Kong. Participants were allocated to either the intervention group (IG) or the control group (CG) based on bed availability. The IG received the CARES program (pre- and postoperative counseling sessions plus daily self-practiced body-mind exercises for five consecutive days) in addition to usual care, while the CG received usual care alone. Pre- and postoperative anxiety and postoperative pain were measured using a visual analog scale and analyzed over time using a generalized estimating equation model. Postoperative analgesic consumption, time to first flatus, and length of hospital stay were compared between the groups using independent t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests. All analyses adhered to the intention-to-treat principle.

**RESULTS**: A total of 120 participants were enrolled and allocated equally to the IG and CG (n = 60 per group). The overall discontinuation rate was 3.33%. Compared with the CG, the IG demonstrated significantly lower anxiety immediately before transfer to the operating theatre (β = -1.67; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -2.18 to - 1.15; p < .01) and on postoperative days one (β = -1.29; 95% CI: -2.30 to - 0.27; p = .01) and three (β = -1.47; 95% CI: -2.58 to - 0.35; p = .01). Additionally, the IG demonstrated a significantly shorter time to first postoperative flatus (p = .01) and length of hospital stay (p = .02). No significant between-group differences were observed in postoperative pain reduction or analgesic consumption.

**CONCLUSION**: The CARES program was found to be feasible for clinical implementation and significantly reduced pre- and postoperative anxiety, time to first postoperative flatus, and length of hospital stay in patients undergoing emergency abdominal surgery.

**TRIAL REGISTRATION**: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (NO. ChiCTR2300076274) on September 28, 2023.

articles.title: An evaluation of the variability in the number of high-level trauma centers per million people in major metropolitan areas in the United States.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: The number of High-Level Trauma Centers (HLTCs) (Level I or II) per million people in major metropolitan areas is variable. The purpose of this study was to describe that variability and to determine if it was correlated with certain metropolitan area characteristics.

**METHODS**: A cross-sectional study of metropolitan areas with populations ≥ 2 million was performed using United States census data. The number of HLTCs per million people was calculated. The correlation between the number of HLTCs per million and the following variables was evaluated for: population density, race, land area, median household income, employment rate, uninsured rate, poverty rate, and public health insurance coverage rate. The association between State Certificate of Need (CON) laws for new trauma center development and HLTC per million, proportion of for-profit hospitals, and proportion of teaching hospitals was also evaluated.

**RESULTS**: There were 35 metropolitan areas identified with a population of 2000,000 or more. The median number of HLTCs per million people was 1.51 (IQR 1.06-1.79) and ranged from 0.43 in Cincinnati to 3.93 in Chicago. The median ratio of level 1 to level 2 trauma centers located in each metropolitan area was 1.0 (IQR 0.5-1.7) and ranged from 0.25 to 5.0. Areas in states with a CON (n = 22), compared to those without a CON (n = 13), had a higher median percentile of teaching hospitals (100% vs. 76.9%, p = 0.01) and no observed difference in the median number of HLTCs per million (1.4 vs. 1.6, p = 0.5) or median percentile of for-profit HLTCs (0.0% vs. 10.0%, p = 0.65). The number of HLTCs per million was found to be negatively correlated with uninsured rates (R -0.33, p = 0.04) and was not correlated with population density, land area, race, median household income, employment rate, poverty rate, or the public health insurance coverage rate (p > 0.05).

**CONCLUSIONS**: The number of HLTCs per million across major metropolitan areas varied widely. Metropolitan areas in states with a CON had a higher proportion of teaching hospitals.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Cross-sectional study, Level IV.

articles.title: Molecular, histopathological, and biomechanical evaluation of cutaneous wound healing following topical application of xenogenic leukocyte- and platelet-rich plasma (L-PRP) in a rat excisional model.
articles.abstract: This study evaluated the effects of topical application of a xenogenic leukocyte- and platelet-rich fibrin (L-PRF) membrane on cutaneous wound healing in a rat excisional wound model. Forty-five adult male Sprague-Dawley rats were randomly assigned to L-PRF-treated, positive control (Mupirocin Ointment), and negative control groups. Full-thickness dorsal skin wounds were created, and treatments were applied for seven consecutive days. Wound healing was assessed through hydroxyproline content, expression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and platelet-derived growth factor-B (PDGF-B), histopathology, and biomechanical testing. The L-PRF-treated group showed significantly higher hydroxyproline levels on days 7 and 14 compared with both control groups (p < 0.05). VEGF and PDGF-B expression was significantly upregulated, particularly during the early healing phase.
