Histopathological examination demonstrated improved granulation tissue formation, neovascularization, collagen maturation, and re-epithelialization by day 14 (p < 0.05). Biomechanical analysis revealed significantly greater yield point and ultimate tensile strength in L-PRF-treated wounds compared with controls (p < 0.05). Topical application of xenogenic L-PRF enhanced cutaneous wound healing by promoting angiogenesis, collagen synthesis, tissue remodeling, and mechanical strength. These findings support the potential of L-PRF as a regenerative biomaterial for improving wound repair.

articles.title: Motorcycle gas-tank associated pelvic trauma: A scoping review of reported injury patterns, management and outcomes.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Motorcycle gas-tank contact has been implicated in pelvic ring injury, often as part of a broader polytrauma presentation. This scoping review mapped reported injury morphology, associated injuries, management and outcomes according to the strength of tank-contact evidence.

**METHODS**: This scoping review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidance. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science databases were searched from inception to 20 September 2026. English-language clinical and forensic reports linking gas-tank contact to individually extractable pelvic ring injuries were included. Aggregate studies provided separate contextual evidence. Four contact-evidence tiers were grouped into higher-certainty and lower-certainty or inferred contact. Findings were synthesised descriptively using assessable denominators.

**RESULTS**: Twenty studies reported 27 patients: 10 with higher-certainty and 17 with lower-certainty evidence of gas tank contact. Posterior-ring involvement was documented in 92% (22/24) of assessable patients while combined anterior-posterior injury occurred in 75% (18/24) assessable patients. Urinary, genital or perineal/scrotal/groin injury was documented in all patients in each group. Definitive pelvic fixation was reported in 15 patients with status unreported in 9 patients. Three deaths were reported. Follow-up was reported in 52% (14/27) of patients; mean follow-up was 8.3 months.

**CONCLUSION**: Published gas tank-associated cases show recurring combined anterior-posterior pelvic ring disruption with adjacent genital or perineal trauma. Although selective reporting and uncertain contact attribution prevent confirmation of a gas tank-specific mechanism, these findings highlight the extent of pelvic ring involvement and associated soft-tissue injury. These findings provide an anatomical basis for future studies linking injury morphology with independently documented road traffic collision mechanisms.

articles.title: Presentation and treatment differences between upper extremity and lower extremity fracture-related infections.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: Fracture-related infection (FRI) presents a significant challenge with high rates of treatment failure and subsequent complication rates. To develop more effective and specific therapies for FRI, the purpose of this study is to analyze presentation, treatment, and outcomes of upper vs. lower extremity FRI, which were hypothesized to have distinct clinical profiles.

**METHODS**: Retrospective cohort at a Level 1 Trauma Center. Adult patients with operatively managed FRI from 2013 to 2020 with at least 6 months follow-up were included. Total operations, operations to clear infection, implant exchange, retention, and removal were compared between upper and lower extremity FRIs.

**RESULTS**: One hundred forty-six patients were included. Forty-six had upper extremity FRI; 100 had lower extremity FRI. Mean follow-up was 2.7 years (SD 3.2). Lower extremity FRIs were significantly more likely to present with higher-grade soft tissue impairments (I) (p = 0.010). Implant failure at presentation was more common in upper extremity FRI compared to lower extremity FRI (41.3% vs. 15.0%, p = 0.001). Upper extremity FRI were more likely to be infected with C. acnes (17% vs. 0%, p < 0.001). Patients with upper extremity FRI had a lower median number of reoperations until FRI resolution (2 (1-3) vs. 3 (2-4), p = 0.006). Debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention, removal, and exchange were performed similarly in upper vs. lower extremity FRI.

**CONCLUSION**: Causative bacteria, presentation characteristics and operative interventions required were different between upper and lower extremity FRIs. Upper and lower extremity FRIs exhibit distinct clinical profiles and prospective studies may be useful to compare extremity-specific treatment protocols.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: III.

articles.title: The national diagnostic landscape of acute pelvic and lower abdominal pain in reproductive-age women presenting to U.S. emergency departments.
articles.abstract:
**STUDY OBJECTIVE**: To characterize the national distribution of emergency department (ED) diagnoses among reproductive-age women presenting with pelvic or lower abdominal pain and describe the frequency of selected time-sensitive diagnoses and ED disposition.

**METHODS**: We conducted a retrospective, cross-sectional analysis of the National Hospital Ambulatory Medical Care Survey (NHAMCS) ED public-use files from 2018 through 2022. We included female patients aged 18 to 49 years whose first-listed reason for visit was pelvic pain (reason-for-visit code 17751) or lower-abdominal pain (15452), excluding trauma-related visits. The primary outcome was the distribution of the first-listed ED diagnosis. Secondary outcomes included selected time-sensitive diagnoses, disposition, and documented diagnostic evaluation and treatment. Analyses incorporated NHAMCS survey weights, strata, and primary sampling units to generate nationally representative estimates.

**RESULTS**: Among 86,864 sampled ED visits, 411 met the primary cohort definition, representing an estimated 637,594 visits annually (95% CI, 536,466-738,723). A nonspecific abdominal or pelvic pain diagnosis was the most common first-listed diagnosis (42.5%; 95% CI, 36.4%-48.9%), followed by urinary tract infection (11.1%) and ovarian cyst (8.5%). Most other individual time-sensitive diagnoses were statistically unreliable because of small sampled counts. Overall, 91.3% of visits resulted in discharge and 6.9% in admission. Diagnostic services were ordered or provided in 97.9% of visits. Visits receiving a nonspecific diagnosis had a similar mean number of diagnostic services as visits receiving another coded diagnosis (5.7 vs 5.7; P = .89) and were more likely to include imaging (78.6% vs 62.1%; difference, 16.5 percentage points; 95% CI, 4.2-28.8; P = .009). In a sensitivity cohort in which pelvic or lower-abdominal pain appeared in any reason-for-visit field (n = 740), the principal pattern persisted, with nonspecific diagnoses accounting for 31.4% of visits.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Among reproductive-age women presenting to U.S. EDs with pelvic or lower abdominal pain, nonspecific abdominal or pelvic pain was the most common final diagnosis, while individual time-sensitive diagnoses were uncommon and most patients were discharged. The frequent use of documented diagnostic services among visits ending in a nonspecific diagnosis suggests that diagnostic uncertainty often persists despite substantial ED evaluation. These national estimates provide epidemiologic context for a diagnostically challenging ED presentation and may inform future research in diagnostic reasoning, imaging, and clinical decision support.

articles.title: Antithrombin III outperforms fresh frozen plasma and improves memory recovery after severe isolated traumatic brain injury.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) administered after severe isolated traumatic brain injury (TBI) has been shown to affect subsequent neurological recovery. One component of FFP, antithrombin III (AT3), demonstrates anti-inflammatory effects on the injured brain and may be a key FFP element that supports post-TBI recovery. We hypothesized that AT3 better improves cognition following severe, isolated TBI when compared with FFP.

**METHODS**: Male CD1 mice (n=29) underwent sham craniectomy (S) or craniectomy followed by severe TBI via controlled cortical impact. Mice received saline (placebo, P), FFP (10 mL/kg), or AT3 (250 IU/kg) 30 minutes after injury. Morris water maze exercises on days 6 to 14 characterized cued/spatial learning and memory. Decreased latency/distance and increased frequency/duration across four zones [zone 5 (escape platform), zone 6/zone 7 (concentric circular areas surrounding zone 5)], and zone 1 (quadrant containing zone 5) indicated superior learning and memory. The Garcia Neurological Test (GNT) allowed scoring of global animal neurological function following surgery on days 1 to 14.

**RESULTS**: Mice treated with FFP or AT3 had consistent improvements in GNT scores back to sham levels across all the post-TBI experimental period from day 1 through 14 (p<0.01). Cued learning was unaffected by FFP or AT3. Spatial learning was consistently worsened by FFP but not by AT3, which, in comparison, demonstrated reduced latency to zones 5, 6, and 7 (p<0.01). FFP had no effect on memory, but AT3 consistently improved memory, decreasing latency to zones 1, 5, 6, and 7 (p<0.01) and increasing frequency into zones 1, 6, and 7 (p<0.01). There were no differences in brain or lung edema between groups.

**CONCLUSION**: FFP after severe TBI improves global neurological recovery but appears to worsen spatial learning. Instead, AT3 confers better neurological recuperation, particularly through improved memory recovery. Further inquiry is warranted to identify beneficial and deleterious components of commonly transfused FFP to enhance recovery after severe blunt TBI.

articles.title: Bending the learning curve: Achieving faster proficiency with intrathoracic surgical stabilization of rib fractures.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Surgical stabilization of rib fractures (SSRF) is a technique for repairing the chest wall after trauma. Two primary SSRF techniques exist-intrathoracic and extrathoracic plating. This study compares our institution's proficiency acquisition and operative reference times for both techniques.

**METHODS**: A retrospective, single-institution cohort study was conducted at a level 1 trauma center to analyze the learning curves of SSRF among 12 attending surgeons who performed the extrathoracic technique and 9 who performed the intrathoracic technique from May 2015 to September 2025. Four hundred fifty-three cases were assessed, and operative times were averaged across each surgeon's cases. Plating time and exposure/closure times were reported. Cumulative sum (CUSUM) analyses with Savitzky-Golay filtering were performed to find proficiency points and operative reference times. Statistical significance was determined using parametric or nonparametric tests and multivariable linear regression.

**RESULTS**: Surgeons demonstrated faster proficiency acquisition with the intrathoracic technique. When no co-surgeon was present, plating proficiency occurred after 7 cases for the intrathoracic approach and 17 cases for the extrathoracic approach. The reference time per plate was achieved at 17:03 min/plate for the intrathoracic technique and 16:56 min/plate for the extrathoracic technique. For exposure/closure times, proficiency occurred after 35 cases for the intrathoracic approach and 68 cases for the extrathoracic approach. Reference exposure/closure times were 78:57 min for the intrathoracic approach and 80:13 min for the extrathoracic approach.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Intrathoracic SSRF demonstrated more rapid proficiency in both rib plating and exposure. Once proficiency has been attained, operative times are expected to align with reference times, and continued improvement towards mastery is anticipated afterwards. These findings can help establish a framework for setting expectations when onboarding new surgeons using these techniques. (J Trauma Acute Care Surg. 2026;00: 000-000. Copyright © 2026 Wolters Kluwer Health, LLC. All rights reserved.).

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Retrospective Comparative Study; Level III.

articles.title: Simultaneous clavicle and rib fracture fixation in patients with severe chest wall injuries is associated with improved outcomes: A pilot study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Simultaneous clavicle open reduction and internal fixation (Clavicle-ORIF) with surgical stabilization of rib fractures (SSRFs) is an understudied but potentially beneficial strategy. We compared outcomes between patients undergoing simultaneous Clavicle-ORIF with SSRF (Clavicle-ORIF+SSRF) and those undergoing SSRF alone (SSRF-Alone) for severe chest wall injury in a pilot study to determine if there is a benefit for further research on this approach.

**METHODS**: A prospective, 2016-2025 IRB-approved database of adults undergoing SSRF at a Chest Wall Injury Collaborative Center was queried for patients with displaced clavicle fractures. Patients undergoing Clavicle-ORIF simultaneously with SSRF were compared with patients with displaced clavicle fractures for a retrospective cohort. Outcomes were daily morphine milligram equivalents, mechanical ventilation, intensive care unit days, and hospital length of stay.

**RESULTS**: Of 60 consecutive patients with displaced clavicle fractures, 52 (86.7%) had complete data, of whom 17.3% underwent simultaneous Clavicle-ORIF+SSRF. The groups were similar in age (52 vs. 57 y) and injury severity (New Injury Severity Score 22 vs. 27; RibScore 4 vs. 3). Mortality was low, with 2 deaths, both in SSRF-Alone. Clavicle-ORIF+SSRF was associated with significantly fewer intensive care unit days (2 [1-3] vs. 5 [3-11], p=0.005) and less mechanical ventilation requirement (0% vs. 42%, p=0.02). Median and maximum daily morphine milligram equivalents were lower but not statistically different for Clavicle-ORIF+SSRF (38 [30-59] vs. 62 [30-83], p=0.25; and 67 [45-155] vs. 112 [61-140], p=0.61).

**CONCLUSIONS**: This pilot study demonstrated that in patients with combined rib and clavicle fractures undergoing SSRF, simultaneous clavicle fixation has the potential to improve outcomes. The study was limited by a small sample size, but it justifies further research on the benefits of simultaneous clavicle fixation with SSRF. (J Trauma Acute Care Surg. 2026;00: 000-000 Copyright © 2026 Wolters Kluwer Health, LLC. All rights reserved.).

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Pilot Retrospective Cohort; Level III.

articles.title: Comparative validation of five early trauma scores for 24-hour in-hospital mortality in traumatic brain injury.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Early risk stratification after traumatic brain injury (TBI) is crucial to guide monitoring, escalation of care, and interfacility transfer within the first hours. Bedside scores, including the "Revised Trauma Score (RTS)," "Glasgow Coma Scale, Age, and Systolic Blood Pressure score (GAP)," "modified Rapid Emergency Medicine Score (mREMS)," "Mechanism, Glasgow Coma Scale, Age, and Arterial Pressure score (MGAP)," and "Modified Early Warning Score (MEWS)," are simple and widely available. Prior studies often use mixed trauma cohorts, later endpoints, and provide limited evaluation of calibration or threshold-level clinical utility. TBI-specific head-to-head evidence is therefore needed. The five scores summarize different clinical domains. RTS incorporates the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), systolic blood pressure (SBP), and respiratory rate; GAP incorporates GCS, age, and SBP; mREMS incorporates age, heart rate, respiratory rate, SBP, peripheral oxygen saturation, and GCS; MGAP incorporates injury mechanism, GCS, age, and arterial pressure; and MEWS incorporates routinely measured physiologic and neurologic variables, including blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature, and level of consciousness. Diastolic blood pressure is not a component of any of the five scores evaluated in this study. The component structure and clinical domains of each score are summarized in Supplementary Table S1.

**METHODS**: This study analyzed consecutive traumatic brain injury admissions in 2024 at a tertiary medical center in Nantong, China (n = 2,287; 24-hour mortality 7.3%). The five bedside scores were recalibrated with a single logistic equation. Performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), the Brier score, and calibration intercept and slope, while clinical utility was evaluated as net benefit per 100 patients at 10% and 20% thresholds. All estimates were reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) from 1,000 bootstrap resamples, and precision-recall curves were referenced to the cohort prevalence.

**RESULTS**: RTS and GAP showed the strongest discrimination, with mREMS close.

**AUROC**: RTS 0.874 (95% CI 0.841-0.903), GAP 0.863 (0.831-0.898), mREMS 0.856 (0.826-0.883); MGAP and MEWS were lower (0.632, 0.606). AUPRCs were 0.465 (0.381-0.531) for RTS, 0.382 (0.308-0.453) for GAP, and 0.370 (0.280-0.424) for mREMS (MGAP 0.154 (0.112-0.199); MEWS 0.129 (0.098-0.159)). Brier scores were 0.050, 0.053, and 0.055 for RTS, GAP, and mREMS, respectively. After simple logistic recalibration, calibration intercepts were near 0 and slopes near 1, with observed-vs-predicted curves close to the 45° line across deciles. At 10% and 20% thresholds, RTS and GAP achieved the highest net benefit and more favorable trade-offs per 100 patients; mREMS was intermediate.

**CONCLUSION**: RTS and GAP showed the best balance of discrimination, calibration, and net benefit at 10% and 20% thresholds; mREMS was comparable after simple recalibration. These findings support prioritizing RTS and GAP for early TBI risk stratification.

articles.title: Pathogen-reduced platelets for the prevention of bleeding.
articles.abstract:
**RATIONALE**: Platelet transfusions are used to prevent and treat bleeding in people who are thrombocytopenic (they have a low blood platelet count). Despite improvements in donor screening and laboratory testing, a small risk of viral, bacterial, or protozoal contamination of platelets remains. There is also an ongoing risk from newly emerging blood transfusion-transmitted infections (TTIs), for which laboratory tests may not be available at the initial outbreak. The risk of blood TTIs from platelet transfusion may be reduced by photochemical pathogen reduction. Pathogens are either inactivated or significantly depleted in number, thereby reducing the chance of transmission. Although current pathogen-reduction technologies have been proven to reduce pathogen load in platelet concentrates, some published clinical studies have raised concerns about the effectiveness of pathogen-reduced platelets for post-transfusion platelet count recovery and the prevention of bleeding compared with standard platelets. This is an update of a Cochrane review first published in 2013 and updated in 2017.

**OBJECTIVES**: To assess the benefits and harms of pathogen-reduced platelets for the prevention of bleeding in people of any age requiring platelet transfusions.

**SEARCH METHODS**: We searched for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) in CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, the Transfusion Evidence Library, and ongoing trial databases. The latest search date was 14 January 2025.

**ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA**: We included RCTs that compared the transfusion of pathogen-reduced platelets (PRP) with standard platelets, or that compared different types of PRP.

**OUTCOMES**: Our outcomes were post-transfusion bleeding, mortality, serious adverse events, platelet refractoriness and mean number of transfusions required per participant.

**RISK OF BIAS**: We used the Cochrane Risk of bias tool (ROB 1) to assess RCTs.

**SYNTHESIS METHODS**: We performed meta-analyses using the Mantel-Haenszel method with the fixed-effect model to avoid over-weighting small studies, and assessed the certainty of the evidence using GRADE.

**INCLUDED STUDIES**: We identified four new trials in this update, with a total of 18 trials eligible for inclusion (one is awaiting classification, and one study of two people was terminated early and not included in our analyses). We included 16 RCTs with 2964 participants in the meta-analyses comparing PRP to standard platelets stored in either plasma (or unknown solution) or platelet additive solution (PAS). Twelve of the 16 completed trials were included in the previous review. Methods of pathogen reduction assessed included Intercept (11 RCTs), Mirasol (5 RCTs), and Theraflex (1 RCT). One study assessed both Intercept and Mirasol, though they did not directly compare the methods (instead, each was randomised with their own control group). No RCTs compared the transfusion of one type of PRP with another.

**SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS**: We grouped the data into two comparisons based on the storage solution of the untreated platelets. Two studies included more than one control group: one control stored in plasma, and one control stored in PAS. Comparison 1. PRP versus standard (untreated) platelets stored in plasma (or unknown solution) (11 RCTs) There is an increased risk of developing platelet refractoriness (risk ratio (RR) 2.04, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.74 to 2.39; 8 RCTs, 1937 participants, high-certainty evidence) as a result of using PRP compared to standard platelets. There is probably an increase in clinically significant bleeding (WHO grade 2+) (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.18; 7 RCTs, 2272 participants, moderate-certainty evidence), and the mean number of platelet transfusions required per participant (mean difference (MD) 1.09, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.50; 7 RCTs, 2079 participants, moderate-certainty evidence). There may be an increase in any bleeding (WHO grade 1+) (RR 1.09, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.14, 8 RCTs, 2122 participants, low-certainty evidence). There is probably no difference in serious adverse events (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.17, 8 RCTs, 1956 participants, moderate-certainty evidence), and may be no difference in all-cause mortality (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.20, 8 RCTs, 2381 participants, low-certainty evidence). Comparison 2. PRP versus standard (untreated) platelets stored in PAS (7 RCTs) There is probably an increased risk of developing platelet refractoriness (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.28 to 1.70; 4 RCTs, 1288 participants, moderate-certainty evidence), and an increased mean number of platelet transfusions required per participant (MD 0.94, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.33; 4 RCTs, 1302 participants, moderate-certainty evidence), as a result of using PRP compared to standard platelets. There may also be an increased risk of clinically significant bleeding (WHO grade 2+) (RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.38; 5 RCTs, 1348 participants, low-certainty evidence) and any bleeding (WHO grade 1+) (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.21; 4 RCTs, 938 participants, low-certainty evidence). There may be no difference in all-cause mortality (Peto odds ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.47; 7 RCTs, 1548 participants, low-certainty evidence). We are uncertain about the impact on serious adverse events. There were no credible subgroup differences for any of our outcomes, in either comparison, between methods of pathogen-reduction (Theraflex, Intercept, Mirasol). The most common source of bias was trial funding, with some trials directly funded by the PRP technology being assessed. Blinding of personnel (performance bias) was often not reported, or was described as open-label, though this would not have impacted objective measures such as mortality and laboratory tests. Small sample sizes impacted the width of the confidence intervals, leading to lower certainty for imprecision. None of the studies reported quality of life. We did not evaluate any economic outcomes.

**AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS**: Findings from this review were based on 16 trials of 2964 participants; only 44 participants (1 RCT) did not have a haematological or oncological diagnosis. In people with haematological or oncological disorders who are thrombocytopenic due to their disease or its treatment, we found high-certainty evidence that PRP transfusions increase the risk of platelet refractoriness and the platelet transfusion requirement, moderate-certainty evidence of increased risk of clinically significant bleeding (WHO 2+), and low-certainty evidence that it increases the risk of any bleeding (WHO 1+). There was insufficient evidence for people with other diagnoses.

**FUNDING**: This review had no dedicated funding.

**REGISTRATION**: Protocol and previous versions available at DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD009072.

articles.title: Population-based implementation of a mobile emergency medical service platform in Hiroshima, Japan.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: In Japan, despite high emergency medical services (EMS) demand (exceeding 7.6 million ambulance dispatches in 2023), reliance on paper-based operations and phone communication continues to delay hospital coordination. Digitizing and standardizing prehospital data collection is an important step toward improving EMS efficiency. This study describes the implementation of a mobile application to streamline EMS operations in Hiroshima Prefecture, Japan, and characterizes the population-based prehospital data it captures.

**METHODS**: This population-based, descriptive study analyzed EMS transport cases, including interhospital transfers, in Hiroshima Prefecture from October 2023 to December 2024. Our mobile app was used by EMS personnel to collect structured data, including demographics, chief complaints, past medical histories, medications, vital signs, and prehospital interventions. The app featured a dedicated data entry mode for cardiac arrest cases; these data were aggregated and analyzed separately. Data entry was facilitated by features such as optical character recognition (OCR), voice input, and automatic coding standardization (e.g., ICD-10).

**RESULTS**: During the 15-month study period, 147,213 EMS transport cases were eligible for analysis. 131,843 (90%) were emergency transports, including 129,855 standard emergency transport cases and 1,988 cardiac arrest mode cases, and 15,370 (10%) were interhospital transfers. Of the standard emergency transport patients, the median age was 75 years (< 18 years, 7%, 65-84, 39%, > 84, 26%), and 50% were male. Common chief complaints were fatigue/weakness (8%), abdominal pain (8%), and shortness of breath (7%). Hypertension (24%) and diabetes (14%) were the most prevalent comorbidities. The median on-scene time was 19 min, and the median transport time was 11 min. Hospital acceptance was achieved on the first request in 66% of cases, with a median negotiation time of 5.2 min. The OCR feature was used in 74% of cases, and voice input in 5%. A total of 1,988 cases of cardiac arrest or suspected cardiac arrest were recorded, providing detailed data on prehospital settings.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Our mobile app was used to achieve standardized and real-time data collection for 147,213 cases in Hiroshima Prefecture. Future research may explore the potential impact of the app on clinical outcomes and examine possibilities for integration with hospital electronic records.
articles.journal: Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med

articles.title: The Björck classification of the open abdomen revisited: clarifying concepts for modern complex abdomen management.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: The open abdomen (OA) has become an integral component of modern acute care, trauma, and vascular surgery. Since 2009, the Björck classification, amended in 2016, has provided a common language for describing the status and progression of the OA and remains the most widely used system worldwide. More than fifteen years of international experience, together with advances in temporary abdominal closure, negative pressure wound therapy, mesh-mediated fascial traction, critical care, more timely effective septic source control and abdominal wall reconstruction, have broadened the spectrum of patients encountered and altered the natural history of the OA. In this setting, certain concepts within the classification-particularly developing fixation and the frozen abdomen-are interpreted inconsistently among surgeons and institutions.

**MATERIALS AND METHODS**: In this narrative review, we revisit the contemporary application of the Björck classification and argue that its principal current challenge is one of interpretive consistency rather than validity.

**CONCLUSION**: We distinguish OA from complex abdomen, clarify the practical meaning of each grade, and emphasise that anatomical grade describes a current state rather than an inevitable trajectory. The aim is to preserve the simplicity and structure of the original framework while improving communication, research comparability, and clinical decision-making in the management of patients with complex OA conditions. To this end we propose that interpretation is enhanced by considering two complementary domains: a contamination domain, already embedded in the amended system, and a surgical accessibility domain that describes the progressive loss of operative access from free access through developing fixation to loss of lateral access (the frozen abdomen).

articles.title: History of operative pelvic ring fixation is associated with increased risk of cesarean delivery: A matched retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Pelvic ring injuries requiring surgical fixation are uncommon among women of childbearing age, and evidence to guide delivery in subsequent pregnancies is limited. Cesarean delivery (CD) is vital when indicated, but carries risk of complications, such as pulmonary and infectious complications in the child and an increased risk of infection, hysterectomy, and cardiac arrest in the mother. The purpose of this study was to compare the likelihood of CD in women with a history of pelvic fixation (HPF) and those with no history of pelvic injury (NPI) who were matched on factors related to CD.

**METHODS**: We conducted a retrospective review of live deliveries among military beneficiaries in Birth and Infant Health Research program data between 2002 and 2021. All patients with HPF prior to delivery were selected. A cohort of patients with NPI were randomly selected in a 10:1 ratio, matched on age, year of delivery, number of prior births, and history of CD. The primary outcome of interest was CD. The secondary outcome of interest was indication for CD among the HPF cohort.

**RESULTS**: There were 79 patients with HPF who had a subsequent pregnancy that resulted in a live birth and 790 controls were selected based on the matching criteria, for a total of 869 patients. The average age at delivery was 26.8 years, 85% had no prior births, and 10% had a prior CD. Patients with HPF had higher prevalence of CD compared to those with NPI (54.4% vs 25.7%; risk ratio: 2.12; 95% confidence interval: 1.52-2.94). History of orthopedic fixation was the most common indication for CD in patients with HPF.

**CONCLUSION**: HPF increased risk of CD, even when controlling for a history of CD. Women with HPF had approximately twice the prevalence of CD compared with matched women with NPI. Still, nearly half of women with HPF delivered vaginally, suggesting that prior pelvic fixation does not necessarily preclude vaginal delivery. Given that orthopedic fixation itself was frequently documented as an indication for CD, these findings highlight the need for individualized obstetric assessment and further evidence to guide delivery planning after pelvic fixation.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Prognostic Level III.

articles.title: Additional FiberTape-Cerclage® augmentation or "Bumper-plate" osteosynthesis for symphyseal arthrodesis - A biomechanical study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Chronic anterior pelvic instability may require symphyseal arthrodesis when conservative treatment and isolated plating fail. Therefore, dual plating has been clinically used to improve stability. As a novel augmentation FiberTape® cerclage may provide and alternative stabilization method with comparable mechanical stability, providing radiolucency for improved analysis of bone healing. Therefore, we conducted a biomechanical study to compare the effects of dual plating to a plate/ FiberTape® cerclage construct.

**METHODS**: Twenty-four synthetic pelvic models (n = 8 per group) were stabilized using symphyseal plating, dual plating, or plate-cerclage constructs. Cyclic axial loading (50-400 N) was applied in a unilateral stance and bilateral-leg stance biomechanical model.

**RESULTS**: The plate-cerclage resulted in significantly higher compression force (131.5 ± 31.7 N) compared to plate-only fixation (88.2 ± 20.9 N; p = 0.019), corresponding to a 49% increase. Dual plating reduced contact area (p ≤ 0.049). No significant differences were observed in one-leg stance.

**CONCLUSION**: Fiber-Tape cerclage augmentation significantly enhances distraction resistance and preserves contact area compared to dual plating. Furthermore, this technique will potentially allow improved radiological visualization of the area of interest in the pubic symphysis after arthrodesis to analyze bone healing and osteointegration.

articles.title: Optimizing success in scalp replantation for total scalp avulsion injuries: A systematic review and case series.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Total scalp avulsion is a rare injury often caused by hair entrapment in rotary machinery. The avulsed tissue can include the eyebrows, eyelids, auricles, and rarely deeper facial structures. Microsurgical replantation is the gold-standard for management. This report provides an up-to-date systematic review of total scalp revascularization in adults and outlines principles to optimize outcomes in this challenging reconstruction.

**METHODS**: We reviewed 162 cases from 70 studies published between January 1976 (the first successful total scalp microsurgical replantation) and January 2025. Inclusion criteria were patients aged ≥ 16 years with total, near-total, or ≥ 70% scalp avulsion injuries.

**RESULTS**: Mean patient age was 31.4 years (range 17-64). Most patients were female (88.8%, n = 127). The average number of arterial and venous anastomoses was 1.8 and 2.5, respectively. The superficial temporal vessels were the most frequently utilized vessels for anastomosis and remain our preferred choice given their accessibility and suitability for reliable vascular reconstruction. Among articles reporting vein graft use, the average number was 1.7. Complete scalp survival (≥90%) was achieved in 64.2% of cases. Two patient cases from our trauma center are presented, along with technical recommendations.

**DISCUSSION**: Total scalp avulsion requires urgent microsurgical replantation for optimal outcomes. Our review underscores the importance of prioritizing superficial temporal vessels and performing multiple venous anastomoses to establish adequate venous drainage, although an optimal anastomotic ratio has not been established. Minimizing vein grafts may shorten operative time and decrease complications. Despite inherent challenges, over 60% of cases achieve excellent scalp survival. Close postoperative monitoring, anticoagulation, and psychiatric support are critical to managing physical and psychological sequelae. These findings support the need for specialized microsurgical expertise and multidisciplinary care to improve outcomes in this rare but severe injury.

articles.title: Traumaplasty for acetabular fractures: Factors associated with additional fracture fixation.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Acute hip arthroplasty with additional fracture fixation, termed fix and replace (FAR), is an established option for selected acetabular fractures. The factors associated with adding fixation remain incompletely defined. We examined treatment selection in a mixed adult acetabular fracture cohort.

**METHODS**: This retrospective single-centre study included 29 adults undergoing hip arthroplasty for acetabular fractures, including periprosthetic or peri-implant injuries. Sixteen received FAR and 13 received arthroplasty without separate fracture fixation, termed fracture joint replacement (FJR). Preoperative computed tomography was used to measure fracture displacement. An exploratory logistic regression included maximum fracture displacement and Paprosky grade, with 26 complete cases. A sensitivity model additionally included articular displacement.

**RESULTS**: Mean age was 72.8 ± 13.3 years (range 36-94); 20 patients were male and 10 had periprosthetic or peri-implant fractures. Mean maximum fracture displacement was 19.95 ± 10.00 mm in FAR and 6.66 ± 5.84 mm in FJR. In the two-predictor model, greater displacement was associated with FAR (odds ratio [OR] 1.22 per mm, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.03-1.46; p = 0.021). The Paprosky grade 3 estimate was imprecise (OR 4.41, 95% CI 0.47-41.85; p = 0.196). The model's 50% probability point was 9.7 mm when Paprosky grade was held at its cohort mean. Adding articular displacement attenuated the statistical evidence for the fracture-displacement association (p = 0.128).

**CONCLUSIONS**: Greater fracture displacement was associated with additional fixation in an exploratory two-predictor model. The small, heterogeneous cohort and model sensitivity preclude a validated displacement threshold or a conclusion that fixation can safely be omitted. These findings require prospective validation.

articles.title: Methamphetamine use and homelessness are risk factors for recurrent trauma and premature mortality in survivors of violent injury.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Methamphetamine use and homelessness have markedly increased nationally, and this trend is especially evident among those experiencing violent trauma. However, no study to date has examined the long-term outcomes of recurrent injury and death associated with methamphetamine use and homelessness in survivors of violent trauma.

**METHODS**: In this retrospective single-institution study, the electronic medical records of patients who presented between 2015 and 2023 with violent injuries were reviewed for toxicology results, housing status, and recurrent injury. The coroner's database was queried to identify unnatural postdischarge deaths. Cox proportional hazards regression models were used in a time-to-event analysis, with recurrent traumatic injury and death as the events of interest, to analyze HRs associated with the risk factors of methamphetamine use and homelessness whereas adjusting for covariates.

**RESULTS**: Among the 2,468 patients meeting our inclusion criteria, 1,039 (42.4%) tested positive for methamphetamine, and 800 (32.4%) were experiencing homelessness. There were 181 (7.3%) who returned at least once to the emergency department (ED) with a new traumatic injury and 106 (4.3%) who died postdischarge after a median of 4.3 years of follow-up. Methamphetamine-positive patients returned to the ED with a new traumatic injury at a rate two-thirds higher than methamphetamine-negative patients (HR, 1.67; 95% CI 1.18 to 2.36), and unhoused patients returned at twice the rate of housed patients (HR, 2.16; 95% CI 1.54 to 3.04). When compared with their counterparts, methamphetamine-positive patients had similar rates of postdischarge death (HR, 1.10; 95% CI 0.73 to 1.66), and unhoused patients had a threefold higher rate (HR, 3.19; 95% CI 2.11 to 4.83).

**CONCLUSION**: Methamphetamine use and homelessness significantly increase the risk of recurrent traumatic injury in survivors of violent trauma. Homelessness is also a significant risk factor for unnatural death after discharge. It is imperative that trauma care includes screening for substance use and housing insecurity.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Level III, Prognostic/Epidemiological.

articles.title: Does CT seatbelt sign, traumatic abdominal wall hernia or body habitus predict injuries and patient outcomes following a restrained motor vehicle collision? A New Zealand cohort study.
articles.abstract:
**AIMS**: to assess for associations between CT seatbelt sign (CTSBS), traumatic abdominal wall hernia and central adiposity with the severity of injury and subsequent management following a restrained motor vehicle collision.

**METHODS**: Included patients were all major trauma patients (with an injury severity score ≥12), who were involved in a motor vehicle collision (MVC) and were restrained by a seatbelt, presenting to Christchurch Hospital between July 1st, 2018, and June 30th, 2023. Clinical data was collected prospectively by the Trauma team nursing staff at the time of injury and throughout the patient's admission. Original trauma CT imaging either performed at Christchurch hospital or the presenting hospitals were re-reviewed by a trauma specialist radiologist, as well as a post part 2 FRANZCR final year radiology trainee. The presence of a seatbelt sign, injuries and central adiposity were calculated from these images. Both univariable and multivariable analyses were performed.

**RESULTS**: After exclusions 316 patients were included in the study. For CTSBS, there was Statistically higher incidence and grade of organ injury in both the thoracic and abdominal compartments except for large thoracic and abdominal vascular injuries, spinal injuries and pelvic injuries. Multivariable analysis demonstrated 10.41 times higher rates of death when CTSBS is present albeit with just 11 deaths. Outcomes were also worse when CTSBS was present; Injury severity score (13% higher), number of operating sessions (15% higher), length of ICU stay (64% higher) and hospital stay (32% higher). Regarding traumatic abdominal wall hernias, there was a higher incidence of any intra-abdominal organ injury (p = 0.042), as well as a higher incidence of GI tract (p < 0.001) and mesenteric injuries (p < 0.001). Regarding central adiposity, there was no significant difference of any of the measured outcomes when looking at different central adiposity groups except for number of operating sessions (p = 0.012).

**CONCLUSION**: The presence of a CTSBS or traumatic abdominal wall hernias are associated with a higher rate of organ injury and worse outcomes. Radiologists should include these signs in their reports. Differences in central adiposity have no significant associations with outcomes as the result of a restrained MVC.

articles.title: When drowning surveillance misses the mechanism.

Total gastric and intragastric air volumes in immediate post-resuscitation whole-body computed tomography after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: Association with airway management, aspiration, diaphragmatic position and initial blood gas analysis.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Gastric distension (GD) may occur during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), but quantitative human data after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remain limited. We quantified gastric volumes after OHCA and explored associations with prehospital airway strategy, CT-defined aspiration, diaphragmatic position, and initial blood gases.

**METHODS**: This retrospective single-center study included OHCA patients undergoing post-resuscitation whole-body computed tomography (CT) within 180 minutes of emergency department (ED) admission between January 1, 2020, and March 31, 2025. Total gastric volume (TGV) and intragastric air volume (GAV) were quantified by CT volumetry.

**RESULTS**: Of 255 identified patients, 120 underwent CT within 180 minutes. Median TGV was 594 mL and correlated strongly with GAV (p < 0.001). Among patients with an advanced airway at ED arrival, neither TGV (p = 0.20) nor GAV (p = 0.24) differed significantly between the tracheal airway (TA; n = 87) and supraglottic airway (SGA; n = 28) groups. CT-defined aspiration was numerically more frequent with SGA than TA (78.6% vs. 57.5%; OR 2.7; p = 0.071), whereas neither TGV nor GAV was associated with CT-defined aspiration. Weak positive correlations were observed between initial pCO

**CONCLUSION**: Gastric volumes were high in this selected post-OHCA immediate CT (< 180 minutes) cohort. No significant differences were detected according to recorded prehospital airway strategy, and gastric volume was not associated with CT-defined aspiration. Mechanisms and clinical consequences remain uncertain and require prospective studies before preventive/ therapeutic implications can be established.

articles.title: Frequency of On-Scene Goal-Directed Field Interventions for Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in a Regional System of Care.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: Early on-scene resuscitation improves outcomes from pediatric non-traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA); however, for pediatric patients, the early evacuation strategy remains commonplace. We sought to determine the frequency of goal-directed interventions initiated by paramedics prior to transport for pediatric patients with OHCA in a regional emergency medical services (EMS) system.

**METHODS**: In this retrospective observational study and cross-sectional analysis, we analyzed the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival (CARES) and linked electronic patient care reports (ePCR) data for patients aged <15 years treated by EMS for nontraumatic OHCA in Los Angeles (LA) County from January 2021 to December 2022. The primary outcome was the frequency of goal-directed therapies administered on scene prior to transport, which we defined as defibrillation for shockable rhythms and administration of epinephrine and fluid resuscitation for non-shockable rhythms. We also tabulated descriptive statistics regarding arrest characteristics, scene times, frequency of other prehospital treatments, and patient outcomes.

**RESULTS**: Among 176 eligible pediatric OHCA cases analyzed in CARES, 112 (64%) were male, the median age was 10 months (IQR 3-51), and 162 (92%) had an initial non-shockable rhythm. Of these, 156 patients were successfully linked to electronic patient care report (ePCR) records for analyses of prehospital interventions. Among 143 patients with non-shockable rhythms, EMS administered epinephrine before transport in 58 (41%) and fluids in 12 (8%). Among 13 patients with shockable rhythms, EMS delivered defibrillation before transport in 11 (85%). Bag-valve-mask (BVM) use was documented in 80 (51%) patients, although its timing relative to scene departure could not be determined. Median on-scene time was 10 minutes (IQR 5-18). Ten patients (6%) survived to hospital discharge, including 6 (3%) with a favorable neurologic outcome.

**CONCLUSIONS**: In this regional EMS system, fewer than half of patients with non-shockable rhythms received a dose of epinephrine and fewer than one in ten received intravenous fluids prior to transport, whereas most patients with shockable rhythms were defibrillated on scene. Further work is needed to identify barriers to timely delivery of on-scene resuscitative interventions.

articles.title: Prevention of fireworks-related injuries: a systematic review and practice management guideline from the Eastern Association for the Surgery of Trauma.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Fireworks-related injuries (FRIs) are an increasingly common and preventable problem worldwide. Fireworks have highly variable regulation, and yet there are no evidence-based guidelines for injury prevention.

**METHODS**: A priori Population(s), Intervention(s), Comparison(s), and Outcomes (PICO) questions were created. PICO 1 asked, "For children (age<18), should their interaction with fireworks be restricted to professional fireworks displays as compared to private fireworks use to reduce incidence of any FRI, rates of amputation, mortality, vision loss, and burns, and increase return to school or work after injury?" PICO 2 asked, "For both adults and children, should restrictive fireworks-related legislation, as opposed to more lenient legislation, be enacted to decrease the same outcomes?" A systematic search and review of the literature was performed, and the quality of evidence was graded per the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology. Final evidence-based recommendations were developed with working group consensus.

**RESULTS**: No studies were included to answer the question related to professional versus private firework displays due to the lack of direct comparisons. Ten studies were identified to analyze the impact of fireworks-related legislation. Eight studies had positive results, suggesting that more stringent legislation of fireworks sale and use is associated with a lower incidence of FRI, and two studies showed no difference. Quality was deemed to be very low.

**CONCLUSION**: Although of very low quality, available data are consistent in showing that more stringent legislation is associated with a lower incidence of FRI. We therefore conditionally recommend restrictive legislation to limit the sale and use of Class C fireworks by non-professionals to reduce FRI. We cannot make any recommendations regarding private fireworks use because of limited available data, but it is important to note that very few reported injuries occurred at professional displays.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Guideline; Systematic review, level IV.

articles.title: Feasibility of a prehospital point-of-care bioassay in patients with mild traumatic brain injury (GFAP-TBI): a pilot simulation study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Rapid prehospital identification of intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) after traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a challenge. Point-of-care (POC) bioassays of biomarkers of ICH, glial fibrillary acidic protein, and ubiquitin carboxyl-terminal hydrolase L1 offer promise for early detection of intracranial injury and improved triage and prehospital treatment decisions.

**METHODS**: We conducted a prospective pilot feasibility simulation study to evaluate operational implementation of a prehospital whole blood POC device (i-STAT Alinity, Abbott) performed by paramedics in Maryland. Emergency medical services (EMS) clinicians were trained to interact with physicians using a mobile communication platform, Pulsara, during a simulated prehospital encounter involving patients with mild TBI, Glasgow Coma Scale Score of 15, who would be eligible for a research protocol using the POC testing. Saline from a simulated IV was used in place of a blood draw. Time metrics were recorded, and participants completed postsimulation surveys assessing usability and workflow integration.

**RESULTS**: Twenty-four paramedics completed simulations. Median time for teleconsent was 2 (IQR 2-2.5) minutes, device data entry 1 (1-2) minutes, and blood transfer to assay 1 (1-2) minutes. Median total workflow time from consent initiation to assay completion was 6.5 (5-7) minutes. Survey responses demonstrated high usability, with over 90% of participants reporting that training was sufficient. The device was easy to operate, and the workflow could be integrated into routine EMS care. All participants indicated willingness to adopt the device in clinical practice.

**CONCLUSIONS**: In this pilot simulation study, prehospital teleconsent and implementation of a whole blood POC bioassay by paramedics were feasible within simulated EMS workflows and could be completed within typical transport intervals. These findings support further clinical investigation of biomarker-based triage strategies for patients with suspected TBI.

articles.title: Gram stain results provide reliable guidance for antibiotic decisions in a surgical trauma intensive care unit.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: The frequent use of broad-spectrum antibiotics and rising antimicrobial resistance in the intensive care unit (ICU) makes antimicrobial stewardship essential. Gram stain results have been used to guide initial therapy, but their role in de-escalation is less defined. This study evaluated the reliability of Gram stain results for early antibiotic de-escalation, hypothesizing that blood culture Gram stains are highly predictive compared with other specimen types.

**METHODS**: We conducted a retrospective diagnostic accuracy study of cultures from patients admitted to a surgical/trauma ICU during a 1-year period. Gram stain results were compared with final culture results to assess concordance. Specimen types with fewer than 20 samples were excluded from secondary analysis.

**RESULTS**: Of 319 patients, 109 (34%) had cultures collected (n=378). Blood (42%), lung (28%), and urine (21%) were most common. Overall, Gram stain results demonstrated 73% positive predictive value (PPV), 87% negative predictive value (NPV), and 84% accuracy. Blood cultures (n=157) had 100% PPV and NPV with 100% accuracy. Urine cultures were highly reliable for identifying infection (PPV 100%) but less so for ruling out infection (NPV 93%, accuracy 94%). Lung cultures showed poor predictability (PPV 44%, NPV 70%, accuracy 63%).

**CONCLUSION**: Gram stain results can support early antibiotic de-escalation in the ICU. Blood culture Gram stains are highly reliable, urine moderately so, while lung specimens are less predictive. These findings may inform antimicrobial stewardship strategies in critical care settings.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Diagnostic tests-level III.

articles.title: Bedside electromagnetic neuronavigation for cranial access procedures in neurotrauma and neurocritical care.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Bedside cranial access devices (external ventricular drain (EVD), subdural evacuation port system (SEPS), parenchymal intracranial pressure (ICP) monitor) are foundational to neurotrauma and neurocritical care. Craniometric-based techniques are limited by aberrant anatomy, clot-filled ventricles, and complex extra-axial collections. Bedside electromagnetic (EM) neuronavigation registered to computed tomography (CT) imaging may enable precise targeting without requiring transport to the operating room, general anesthesia, or rigid cranial fixation.

**METHODS**: We retrospectively reviewed patients undergoing bedside cranial procedures with EM-neuronavigation (Medtronic StealthStation) from November 1, 2025 to July 21, 2026 at our Level I trauma center neurocritical care unit for distorted anatomy, atypical targets, and/or high consequences of imprecision. Outcomes included device function, post-procedure neuroimaging confirmation of device placement, and navigation-related complications.

**RESULTS**: Ten patients underwent 15 EM-navigated bedside procedures (11 EVDs, 2 SEPS, 2 parenchymal ICP monitors). Clinical indications included aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, traumatic brain injury, loculated subdural hematoma, ventriculitis, ventricular trapping, obstructive hydrocephalus, and intracerebral hemorrhage. Notably, EM-navigation enabled dual-catheter placement to access non-communicating ventricular compartments and optimized SEPS placements at maximal extra-axial collection thickness while avoiding vascular membranes. All procedures achieved intended device function and intended positioning on post-procedure imaging. There were no complications or revision procedures related to EM-navigation.

**CONCLUSIONS**: In this single-center proof-of-principle series, bedside EM-navigation was feasible, safe, and readily integrated into high-risk patient care workflows in neurocritical care. Whether bedside neuronavigation improves procedural precision, supports clinician education, or reduces operative and transport needs was beyond the scope of the current study and requires well-designed prospective evaluation.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Level V, Therapeutic/Care Management.

articles.title: Accountability in emergency surgery: moving beyond blame toward high reliability: a WSES-JMESE position paper.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Emergency surgery is characterized by clinical uncertainty, time pressure, evolving information, physiological instability, and substantial variability in available resources. In this setting, adverse outcomes may occur despite timely and appropriate care and should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of professional failure. Nevertheless, surgeons may be exposed to retrospective, outcome-driven, and overly individualized attribution of blame when the complexity of the original decisional environment is insufficiently considered. A structured framework is therefore needed to support fair, proportionate, and learning-oriented accountability in emergency surgical practice.

**METHODS**: This evidence-informed position paper was developed through a structured multidisciplinary review of literature from patient-safety science, cognitive psychology, medical ethics, health-systems research, surgical professionalism, and high-reliability organization theory, complemented by iterative expert discussion within the World Society of Emergency Surgery-Journal of Medical and Surgical Errors working group. The literature was synthesized narratively to identify the principal contextual, cognitive, ethical, professional, and organizational domains relevant to fair accountability and adverse-event review in emergency surgery. The resulting statements were framed as ungraded evidence-informed Good Practice Statements according to the GRADE framework rather than clinical practice recommendations based on comparative effectiveness evidence.

**RESULTS**: The synthesis identified seven interrelated principles for fair accountability in emergency surgery: contextual proportionality; distinction between accountability and blame; mitigation of hindsight, outcome, and attribution bias; recognition of distributed responsibility across individuals, teams, and systems; protection of professional integrity; procedural fairness and institutional responsibility; and application of high-reliability principles. Particular attention is given to the dynamic and time-dependent nature of emergency surgical decision-making, the incomplete representation of clinical reasoning in contemporaneous documentation, the limitations of population-based scoring systems and benchmarks, and the influence of resource availability on feasible treatment options. These principles were integrated into a structured framework for adverse-event review aimed at supporting proportionate analysis of adverse outcomes and avoiding premature attribution of individual blame when harm reflects interacting clinical, cognitive, team-level, and system-level factors.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Accountability in emergency surgery should evaluate decisions according to the information, physiological condition, reasonable alternatives, and resources available at the time of care. Contextualization should not eliminate individual responsibility; rather, it should make responsibility attribution more accurate, proportionate, and fair. A bias-aware, procedurally fair, and high-reliability approach can protect surgeons from premature, punitive, outcome-driven blame while preserving legitimate accountability for unsafe practice, reckless conduct, or misconduct. Such a framework may strengthen patient safety, professional integrity, organizational learning, and public trust.

articles.title: Evolution of surgical indication strategies and their impact on treatment outcomes in acute superior mesenteric venous thrombosis: a single-center retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: To compare how different surgical indication strategies affect treatment patterns and outcomes in patients with acute superior mesenteric vein thrombosis (SMVT), and to identify independent risk factors for intestinal wall full-thickness necrosis and in-hospital mortality.

**METHODS**: We retrospectively analyzed 125 patients with acute intestinal ischemia secondary to SMVT from October 2014 to October 2025. Patients were divided into two chronological cohorts according to the change in surgical indication strategy implemented at our institution: the liberal surgical indication period (October 2014 - October 2023, n = 102) and the strict surgical indication period (November 2023 - October 2025, n = 23). Baseline characteristics, treatment pathways, and in-hospital outcomes were compared between the two periods. Multivariate logistic regression was used to identify independent risk factors for in-hospital mortality and for full-thickness necrosis in patients undergoing surgery.

**RESULTS**: The two periods were comparable with respect to baseline characteristics (P > 0.05). Compared with the liberal period, the strict period had significantly lower rates of early surgery (4.3% vs. 63.7%, P < 0.001) and overall surgery (26.1% vs. 80.4%, P < 0.001). Full-thickness necrosis was identified in a significantly higher proportion of surgical specimens in the strict period than in the liberal period (83.3% vs. 18.3%, P = 0.002). Patients in the strict period had a longer median hospital stay (19 days vs. 12 days, P = 0.011), a trend toward lower ICU admission (30.4% vs. 50.0%, P = 0.089), and no significant difference in mortality (13.0% vs. 7.8%, P = 0.423). Multivariate analysis showed that lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L (aOR = 7.545, 95%CI: 1.827-31.149, P = 0.005) and elevated D-dimer (aOR = 1.047, 95%CI: 1.012-1.084, P = 0.008) were independently associated with in-hospital mortality. Given the limited number of death events (n = 11), the above multivariate analysis results should be considered exploratory findings that require validation in larger prospective cohorts. In surgical patients, CT evidence of impaired bowel wall perfusion independently predicted pathologically confirmed full-thickness necrosis (aOR = 6.236, 95%CI: 1.663-23.388, P = 0.007).

**CONCLUSION**: A strict surgical indication strategy with an anticoagulation-first approach was associated with a lower rate of surgery in SMVT patients and directs surgical intervention more precisely to those with established full-thickness necrosis. CT evidence of impaired bowel wall perfusion is a key warning sign for full-thickness necrosis and warrants urgent surgical evaluation. Hyperlactatemia and elevated D-dimer independently predict in-hospital mortality and should serve as core elements for early risk assessment and dynamic monitoring.

articles.title: Plasma eMTBR-tau as a Biomarker for Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy Tau Tangle Neuropathology.
articles.abstract:
**IMPORTANCE**: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a neurodegenerative disease that cannot accurately be diagnosed during life due to the absence of in vivo biomarkers for CTE neuropathology.

**OBJECTIVE**: To evaluate plasma endogenously cleaved microtubule-binding region tau (eMTBR-tau) as a candidate biomarker for CTE tau tangle neuropathology.

**DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS**: This case series included 21 former American-style football players who completed a blood draw as part of participation in clinical research at Boston University beginning April 17, 2008, and who subsequently died, donated their brain, and had completed autopsy by October 9, 2026.

**EXPOSURES**: Plasma eMTBR-tau nucleic acid-linked immunosandwich assay single-plex immunoassay and plasma phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) (SP-X n = 20; Elecsys n = 1).

**MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES**: CTE status and stage. Cumulative neuropathologic tau burden scores ranged from 0 to 33 (higher scores indicate tau burden; 0, no tau burden).

**RESULTS**: Among 21 male brain donors (median age at blood draw, CTE positive: 68 years [IQR, 61-77]; CTE negative: 49 years [IQR, 47-56]), 18 had a neuropathologic diagnosis of CTE. Of these participants, 16 had a diagnosis of high-stage CTE (stage IV = 8, stage III = 8); and 2, of low-stage CTE (stage II = 1, stage I = 1). Five CTE-positive participants had intermediate or high Alzheimer disease neuropathologic change (ADNC). Plasma eMTBR-tau concentration was significantly higher in CTE-positive participants (median, 0.019 pg/mL [IQR, 0.004-0.030]) compared with CTE-negative participants (0.001 pg/mL [IQR, 0.001-0.001]; β = 1.61 [95% CI, 0.51-2.70]). Plasma eMTBR-tau concentrations were highest among CTE-positive participants with comorbid ADNC (0.082 pg/mL [IQR, 0.059-0.131]) and intermediate among those with high-stage CTE without ADNC (n = 11; median, 0.009 pg/mL [IQR, 0.004-0.021]). Plasma eMTBR-tau concentration was significantly higher in high-stage CTE (median, 0.021 pg/mL [IQR, 0.006-0.038]) compared with low-stage CTE (median, 0.001 pg/mL [IQR, 0.001-0.002]; β = 1.79 [95% CI, 0.45-3.13]) or no CTE (median, 0.001 pg/mL [IQR, 0.001-0.001]; β = 1.78 [95% CI, 0.85-2.71]). Differences remained significant after exclusion of 5 cases with comorbid ADNC. Plasma eMTBR-tau concentration was associated with higher cumulative neuropathologic tau burden score across 11 brain regions (β = 0.71 [95% CI, 0.38-1.05]). Plasma p-tau217 concentration was positively associated with eMTBR-tau (β = 0.68 [95% CI, 0.32-1.04]) but was not associated with CTE. P-tau217 concentrations were in the negative range (n = 11) or intermediate range (n = 5) for participants without ADNC copathology. Four participants with ADNC had p-tau217 concentrations in the positive range; and 1, in the intermediate range.

**CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE**: Participants with high-stage CTE had higher concentrations of plasma eMTBR-tau than those with low-stage or no CTE; concentrations were highest among those with CTE and comorbid ADNC. Plasma eMTBR-tau may represent a feasible biomarker candidate for high-stage CTE tau tangle neuropathology. Larger autopsy and clinical validation studies are needed to establish overall diagnostic accuracy and specificity of plasma eMTBR-tau for CTE neuropathology, in addition to the associated prognostic and clinical implications.

articles.title: What's Blood Got to Do with It? Identifying MPDS® Dispatch Codes Most Commonly Associated with Prehospital Blood Administration.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: This study aimed to identify Medical Priority Dispatch System (MPDS®) codes most frequently associated with prehospital blood utilization.

**METHODS**: We examined Delaware's prehospital blood database to determine dispatch codes where low titer group O positive whole blood (LTOWB) was administered. We calculated the number of blood units under each dispatch code within the study period (May 2023- February 2026). Using this data, we identified the MPDS® codes associated with the highest number of blood units, including the top five codes overall, top medical codes, and as well as blood utilization rates for penetrating versus blunt traumas.

**RESULTS**: The most frequent blood utilization came from the following dispatch codes: 29D02 (traffic collision, high mechanism) 32 patients, 27D04G (penetrating trauma with central wounds) 32 patients, 29D02M (auto versus pedestrian) 28 patients, 29D05 (traffic collision with entrapment) 24 patients, and 29D02L (auto versus bicycle/motorcycle) 20 patients. These five dispatch codes accounted for 29% of all prehospital LTOWB utilized within the 33-month study period. Analyzing blood utilization for non-traumatic dispatch codes revealed: 21D04/21D04M (dangerous hemorrhage, medical) 18 patients, 21D03/21D03M (hemorrhage, not alert, medical) 13 patients, 9E01/M9E01/M9E02 (cardiac or respiratory arrest/death, not breathing) 13 patients, and 21D05/21D05M (hemorrhage, abnormal breathing, medical) 7 patients. These four dispatch codes accounted for 11% (51 patients) of LTOWB utilization. When performing odds ratio analysis to determine odds of blood administration, we found 27D04G, 29D02M, and 29D02L to be statistically significant with 95% confidence intervals of [0.35- 0.87], [2.42- 5.72], [1.47- 3.91], and odds ratios of 0.55, 3.72, and 2.40, respectively. Additionally, our analysis demonstrated that patients with MPDS® coding for penetrating trauma with a delta level priority (27D) have higher likelihood of prehospital blood administration than delta priority high mechanism traffic incidents (29D). This comparison showed an OR of 10.40 that blood would be given to the penetrating trauma patient with a 95% confidence interval of [7.93- 13.66].

**CONCLUSIONS**: Specific MPDS® codes are strongly associated with prehospital blood utilization. Identifying these patterns offers a unique opportunity for emergency medical services systems to implement automatic blood dispatch protocols based on dispatch code.

articles.title: Prolonged Onboard Storage of Red Blood Cells in Ground Ambulances for Prehospital Transfusion: A Real-World Study.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: Permanent onboard storage of red blood cells (RBC) units could facilitate timely prehospital transfusion but may expose blood products to cumulative transport-related mechanical stress. We evaluated the quality of RBC units stored continuously in operational ground ambulances under real-world emergency medical service conditions.

**METHODS**: In this randomized controlled experimental study of RBC units, leukoreduced RBC units were randomly assigned to continuous onboard ambulance storage from day 7 to day 42 (

**RESULTS**: All RBC units remained below the European regulatory hemolysis threshold of 0.8% at day 42. Hemolysis was higher in ambulance-stored units at day 28 (Hodges-Lehmann difference, +0.043 percentage points; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.010-0.076; 

**CONCLUSIONS**: Continuous onboard RBC storage in operational ground ambulances maintained all units within regulatory hemolysis limits through day 42. However, higher hemolysis and late divergence in SME accumulation suggest that prolonged ambulance exposure may influence RBC storage quality. These findings provide preliminary support for the feasibility of continuous onboard RBC storage, particularly earlier in the storage period, but do not establish equivalence with conventional blood bank storage.

articles.title: Early arthroplasty versus conversion arthroplasty after failed PFNA in elderly patients with unstable intertrochanteric fractures: a multicenter matched cohort study.
articles.abstract:
**PURPOSE**: In our study, the clinical and functional outcomes of early arthroplasty versus late conversion arthroplasty approaches were compared in individuals over 75 years of age who underwent PFNA for complex intertrochanteric fractures but whose treatment failed.

**METHODS**: This multicenter, retrospective cohort study analyzed data from 136 patients treated between January 2023 and March 2025. The cohort consisted of 62 patients who underwent conversion arthroplasty after failed PFNA fixation and 74 patients who received primary early arthroplasty. Demographic characteristics, surgical parameters, complications, and functional and rehabilitation outcomes were compared between groups.

**RESULTS**: Early arthroplasty was associated with significantly better six-month functional outcomes, including higher Parker mobility and Merle d'Aubigné scores. The early arthroplasty group also demonstrated shorter times to effective weight-bearing and recovery of walking distance. Perioperative transfusion requirements and systemic complication rates were higher in the PFNA conversion group. However, the time to recovery of unassisted gait did not differ significantly between groups.

**CONCLUSION**: Conclusion In elderly patients over 75 years of age with unstable intertrochanteric fractures, early arthroplasty was associated with better short-term functional outcomes, earlier effective weight-bearing and recovery of walking distance, and fewer systemic complications than conversion arthroplasty following failed PFNA. However, these findings should be interpreted in the context of the retrospective design and the functional deterioration that occurred between initial PFNA and subsequent conversion surgery. Primary arthroplasty may be a reasonable option in carefully selected patients with fracture patterns, poor bone quality, or clinical characteristics associated with a high risk of fixation failure.

articles.title: Prehospital Trauma Compendium: Prehospital Management of Pediatric Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Circulatory Arrest - A Joint Position Statement and Resource Document of NAEMSP, ACS-COT, ACEP, and AAP.
articles.abstract: In 2014 the National Association of EMS Physicians (NAEMSP), American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma (ACS-COT), American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP), and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) published the first joint position statement discussing withholding and discontinuing resuscitation attempts for pediatric traumatic out-of-hospital circulatory arrest (TOHCA). Since then, the body of literature addressing pediatric TOHCA has evolved and evidence has grown that demonstrates the nearly uniformly poor prognosis of children who suffer circulatory arrest in the prehospital setting as a result of trauma. To support emergency medical services (EMS) clinicians in their approach to these high-acuity, low-frequency, and challenging cases, this project aimed to update guidance regarding decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts for pediatric traumatic circulatory arrest. NAEMSP, ACEP, ACS-COT, and AAP recommend:EMS resuscitation of pediatric TOHCA should:Prioritize prompt identification of patients who may benefit from transport to definitive care at trauma centers when safe and appropriate. On-scene resuscitation should be balanced against the potential benefit of transfer to a proximate trauma center.Emphasize the identification of reversible causes of traumatic circulatory arrest and timely use of clinically indicated life-saving interventions (LSIs) within the EMS clinician's scope of practice. These include:External hemorrhage control with direct pressure, wound packing, and tourniquetsAirway management using the least-invasive airway interventions required to achieve and maintain airway patency, oxygenation, and adequate ventilation.Chest decompression if clinical concern for tension pneumothorax. Empiric bilateral decompression is not recommended in the absence of suspected thoracic trauma.External chest compressions and ventilations have a larger role in pediatric TOHCA resuscitation than in adult TOHCA resuscitation, with children frequently having TOHCA secondary to head injury, hypoxia and other non-hemorrhagic mechanisms. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) should be provided when the cause of circulatory arrest is unclear.Epinephrine is of lower priority than other LSIs.Consider point of care ultrasound (POCUS) to guide decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts.Resuscitation attempts may be withheld in pediatric TOHCA patients with:Injuries that are incompatible with life (e.g., decapitation, hemi-corpectomy, incineration).Evidence of prolonged circulatory arrest (e.g., rigor mortis, dependent lividity, decomposition).Advanced care planning documents that indicate Do Not Resuscitate (DNR)/ Do Not Attempt Resuscitation (DNAR)/Allow Natural Death medical orders.Resuscitation attempts may be discontinued in pediatric TOHCA patients who:Have no return of spontaneous circulation after provision of at least 15 minutes of high-quality CPR in addition to performance of other lifesaving interventions directed at treating potentially reversible causes of pediatric TOHCA. Longer durations of CPR, up to 30 minutes, may be considered for patients with positive predictors of survival such as organized rhythm, witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, or with proximate access to a trauma center.Have known predictors of very low probability of survival such as penetrating trauma without proximate access to a trauma center, asystole, unwitnessed arrest, or lack of bystander CPR.Protocols guiding decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation of pediatric TOHCA benefit from oversight by EMS physicians in collaboration with pediatric experts and local or regional trauma system stakeholders. Implementation of such protocols for pediatric patients benefits from involvement of community stakeholders including family representatives, law enforcement, medical examiner, and child fatality review committees.Considerations for protocol implementation include local resource availability, EMS clinician and public safety, psychosocial support to surviving family members and emergency responders, and dignified handling of the deceased patient.Training needs for EMS clinicians include techniques to communicate with family members regarding the death of a child and understanding the clinician's own response to this low-frequency, high-emotion experience.

articles.title: Prevalence and Characteristics of Coma in Latin American Critical Care Units: The COMA LATAM Study.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: To determine the point prevalence of coma across Latin American critical care units, characterize its etiology, and explore short-term outcomes.

**DESIGN**: Multinational, cross-sectional point prevalence study with exploratory 14-day follow-up assessment.

**SETTING**: Three hundred ninety-two hospitals across 19 Latin American countries, including ICUs, intermediate care units, neurocritical care units, cardiovascular ICUs, and trauma ICUs.

**PATIENTS**: Adult patients (≥ 18 yr) meeting the Coma Epidemiology, Evaluation, and Therapy care survey (COME-TOGETHER) criteria on May 28, 2024. Patients under deep sedation or pharmacological coma induction were excluded unless the coma state preceded pharmacological intervention.

**INTERVENTIONS**: None (observational study).

**MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS**: Among 8305 critically ill patients, 1145 met coma criteria (point prevalence 13.8%), with country-specific rates ranging from 5.1% to 36.8%. Individual patient data were available for 729 patients (63.7%). Traumatic brain injury was the leading individual cause (24.8%), followed by hypoxic-anoxic brain injury (14.6%) and intracerebral hemorrhage (13.5%). When categorized by pathophysiology, vascular causes predominated (48.6%), followed by traumatic brain injury (24.8%) and other causes (26.6%). Age-stratified analysis revealed trauma predominantly affecting younger patients, while cerebrovascular causes predominated in older groups. Among patients with 14-day follow-up data (29% of cohort), mortality was 29.2%, with 67.7% of survivors recovering from coma. Only the Charlson Comorbidity Index was independently associated with implementation of life-sustaining therapy limitations (adjusted odds ratio, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.15-1.30; p < 0.001).

**CONCLUSIONS**: Coma affects nearly one in seven ICU beds across Latin America, with substantial country variation and distinct age-dependent etiology patterns. The significant burden highlights the need for targeted prevention strategies and specialized neurocritical care resources throughout the region.

articles.title: Trauma Clinician Perspectives on Geriatric-Centered Trauma Care: A Qualitative Study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Despite national geriatric trauma guidelines, care delivery varies across trauma centers, and existing quality measures may not capture outcomes important to older injured adults. We examined clinician perspectives on geriatric-centered care structures, processes, and implementation barriers.

**STUDY DESIGN**: We conducted a descriptive, exploratory qualitative study of US trauma clinicians between September 2022 and December 2024. Semi-structured interviews explored geriatric trauma care delivery and clinician-reported outcomes.
