Current nutritional recommendations are largely extrapolated from heterogeneous intensive care populations. Available evidence suggests that AKI primarily influences energy balance rather than energy expenditure, which appears broadly comparable to that of other critically ill populations. While evidence specific to AKI is limited, protein provision of approximately 1.2-1.3 g/kg/day is generally recommended during critical illness. However, higher intakes of up to 1.7-2.5 g/kg/day may be considered in patients receiving RRT to offset extracorporeal amino acid losses and increased protein catabolism. In this setting, emerging concepts such as metabolic tolerance and biomarker-guided metabolic phenotyping may facilitate individualised nutritional strategies.

**CONCLUSIONS**: AKI, particularly when requiring RRT, is associated with profound and dynamic metabolic disturbances that substantially influence energy and protein requirements, thereby making nutrition an integral component of organ support therapies. Future research should evaluate precision nutrition strategies that tailor nutritional support to the phase of critical illness, measured energy expenditure, metabolic tolerance, and RRT-related nutrient losses and gains. Such studies should prioritise patient-centred outcomes, including physical function and recovery, in addition to nutritional and metabolic endpoints.

articles.title: Task-specific gait biomechanics following unilateral iliosacral screw fixation for posterior pelvic ring injury.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Patients treated with unilateral iliosacral screw fixation for posterior pelvic ring injury may experience residual functional limitations. It remains unclear how these limitations manifest during tasks with different biomechanical demands. This exploratory study compared task-specific gait biomechanics between patients after fixation and healthy controls.

**METHODS**: In this prospective cross-sectional observational study, 11 patients after unilateral iliosacral screw fixation (mean age 68.73 ± 9.89 years; 10 women) were compared with 21 healthy controls (52.48 ± 20.36 years; 11 women). Participants performed level walking, stair climbing, and step crossing using an Xsens MVN inertial motion capture system. Pelvic kinematics and model-estimated muscle activation and joint contact forces were evaluated using Computed MyoGraphy. Repeated trials were analyzed using participant-level random-intercept mixed models adjusted for age and sex. Pelvic rotation during stair climbing was the primary outcome; other outcomes were secondary or exploratory.

**RESULTS**: Pelvic rotation during stair climbing was lower in patients (adjusted difference -5.45°, 95% CI -7.98 to -2.92°; within-family FDR-adjusted q = 0.0003). Contralateral pelvic tilt during step crossing was greater (adjusted difference 1.44°, 95% CI 0.46-2.41°; q = 0.011). No statistically significant group differences were detected in the analyzed level-walking parameters, thoracic counter-rotation, lower-limb muscle activation, or hip joint contact-force asymmetry. Model-estimated peak L5-S1 joint contact force during stair climbing was lower in patients (adjusted difference -0.70 × body weight; q = 0.001).

**CONCLUSIONS**: Patients after posterior pelvic ring injury treated with unilateral iliosacral screw fixation showed task-specific differences in pelvic movement during demanding locomotor activities. The findings support including stair and step tasks in functional assessment, but do not establish that fixation caused the observed differences. Small sample size, demographic imbalance, and the absence of patient-reported outcomes limit clinical interpretation.

articles.title: Whole blood transfusion in adult patients with traumatic brain injury: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Whole blood (WB) transfusion may improve outcomes in trauma patients compared with component therapy, but evidence in traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains limited. We evaluated the clinical effectiveness of WB transfusion in adults with TBI requiring transfusion.

**METHODS**: We searched PubMed, Cochrane CENTRAL, CINAHL, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP for studies published from January 2006 through August 31, 2026. Eligible studies included randomized trials and observational studies using propensity score matching or inverse probability of treatment weighting. Random-effects meta-analysis with Hartung-Knapp adjustment was performed for mortality. Component-specific transfusion requirements were summarized qualitatively.

**RESULTS**: Five studies were included in the systematic review, and four studies were included in the mortality meta-analysis. WB transfusion was not clearly associated with lower mortality (RR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.62-1.16; P = 0.19; I

**CONCLUSIONS**: Current evidence is insufficient to determine whether WB transfusion reduces mortality after TBI because of the limited number of studies, clinical and methodological heterogeneity, risk of bias, and imprecision. Further randomized trials in clearly defined TBI populations are needed.

articles.title: Effect of airway assistant training on intubation time during simulated prehospital airway management: A pilot study.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: Challenging airways are common in the out-of-hospital setting, where delays or failure to secure the airway can result in significant morbidity and mortality. Therefore, this pilot study aimed to determine whether training paramedics in the role of airway assistant improves intubation time during a simulated regurgitating airway using suction-assisted laryngoscopy and airway decontamination (SALAD).

**METHODS**: Twelve qualified paramedics were randomly allocated to one of two groups (n = 6) and paired with intensive care paramedics (ICPs). Airway assistants in Group 1 completed a one-hour airway assistant training program, whereas airway assistants in Group 2 received no training. Participants completed a standardized, timed simulation using a continuously regurgitating mannequin designed to replicate the challenges of out-of-hospital intubation. The primary outcome was time to successful intubation, defined as passage of the endotracheal tube through the vocal cords with cuff inflation.

**RESULTS**: Airway assistant training significantly reduced intubation time. The untrained group recorded a median intubation time of 102.5 seconds (IQR 36), compared with 53 seconds (IQR 19) in the trained group. Group comparisons demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in intubation time (

**CONCLUSIONS**: In this pilot study, training paramedics to perform the airway assistant role significantly reduced intubation time in a simulated regurgitating airway. These preliminary findings suggest that incorporating structured airway assistant training into prehospital education programs may improve airway management performance in challenging environments. Given the small sample size and simulated setting, larger studies are required to confirm these findings and determine whether the observed benefits translate to clinical practice.

articles.title: Intraoperative visualization with 3D fluoroscopy for posterior pelvic fixation is associated with lower cumulative imaging-related radiation exposure.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: Achieving optimal screw positioning in posterior pelvic ring (PR) fracture fixation is critical for fracture stability and safety. Formerly, our institution used intraoperative plain-film fluoroscopy followed by postoperative computed tomography (CT) to assess fracture reduction and screw placement. Introduction of the 3D mobile C-arm enables immediate volumetric intraoperative assessment, may improve intraoperative visualization, and may alter conventional imaging requirements. This study compared cumulative imaging-related radiation exposure between cases performed with intraoperative 3D fluoroscopy (3DF) against standard intraoperative plain-film fluoroscopy (2DF), including postoperative CT utilization.

**METHODS**: A retrospective review was conducted on patients treated for posterior PR fractures at a level 1 trauma center between 2014 and 2023. Utilization of 3DF or plain-film fluoroscopy, and any intraoperative screw changes were documented. Rates and details of postoperative complications and subsequent reoperations were recorded for patients with > 3 months follow-up. Radiation doses for 3DF, 2DF, and postoperative CT were extracted from radiology reports.

**RESULTS**: Among 245 patients (mean age 47.2, 52.2% male) undergoing fixation for posterior PR fractures, 89 (36.3%) had 3DF intraoperatively, while 156 (63.7%) had 2DF. 27 patients (8 3DF, 19 2DF, p = 0.443) had screws changed intraoperatively, primarily to modify screw path (n = 16, 59.3%), to achieve better purchase/reduction (n = 5, 18.5%), to modify screw size (n = 3, 11.1%), to change screw type (n = 2, 7.4%), and failure to advance screw (n = 1, 3.7%). Mean radiation dose for the 3DF group was significantly lower (179.2 mGy vs 526.1 mGy, p < 0.001). When excluding postoperative CT dose (n = 194), intraoperative-only radiation remained lower with 3DF (median 79.1 (IQR 51.5-148.7) vs 318.0 (IQR 71.6-751.5) mGy; p < 0.001). Among 119 patients with > 3 months follow-up, reoperation was less frequent with 3DF (9.5% vs 31.2%, p = 0.012), predominantly for symptomatic implant removal.

**DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION**: Intraoperative 3DF was associated with lower cumulative radiation exposure compared to traditional fluoroscopy with routine postoperative CT, and intraoperative dose alone was also lower. Reoperation was less frequent in the 3DF group, but most reoperations were implant removals for symptomatic or planned indications. These findings highlight the potential of 3DF as a practical radiation efficient quality assurance tool in posterior pelvic fixation.

articles.title: Effect modification by arterial pH on the association between extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation and neurological outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with shockable rhythm: A multicenter registry study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Arterial pH on emergency department (ED) arrival predicts outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but its effect on the association between extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) and neurological outcomes is unclear. We evaluated this association in patients with an initial shockable rhythm and assessed whether pH modified it.

**METHODS**: We retrospectively analyzed the Korean Cardiac Arrest Research Consortium registry. Adults with presumed cardiac-origin OHCA, an initial shockable rhythm, ED cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and arterial blood gas data measured after ED arrival were included. Exposure was ECPR initiated in the ED; the primary outcome was favorable neurological outcome at discharge (Cerebral Performance Category 1-2). Arterial pH was categorized as low (≤6.85), medium (>6.85 and <7.05), or high (≥7.05). Multivariable logistic regression assessed ECPR-by-pH interaction, with optimal 1:2 propensity score matching as a sensitivity analysis.

**RESULTS**: Of 2183 patients, 213 (9.8%) received ECPR and 154 (7.1%) had a favorable neurological outcome. The association between ECPR and favorable outcome differed across pH categories (p for interaction = 0.004): adjusted odds ratio (aOR) 7.34 (95% confidence interval [CI], 2.84-18.98) in the low-pH group, 2.07 (95% CI, 1.06-4.03) in the medium-pH group, and 0.85 (95% CI, 0.37-1.94) in the high-pH group. The propensity score-matched analysis showed a similar pattern (p for interaction = 0.036).

**CONCLUSIONS**: Initial arterial pH modified the association between ECPR and neurological outcome after OHCA with an initial shockable rhythm. The association was strongest at low pH and not observed at high pH. Arterial pH may inform ECPR evaluation but should not determine treatment thresholds.

articles.title: Defining organized cardiac motion and cardiac standstill in cardiac arrest using point of care ultrasound: A Delphi study.
articles.abstract:
**AIM**: There are no widely accepted definitions of organized cardiac motion (OCM) and cardiac standstill (CS) using point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) during cardiac arrest. We aimed to define these terms and provide guidance on the clinical application of these findings.

**METHODS**: Statements defining OCM and CS were developed by a steering committee of experts after a comprehensive literature review aided by a librarian. A diverse panel of 20 experts was convened. Using Delphi methodology, the panel came to a consensus on definitions of OCM and CS after three rounds of voting.

**RESULTS**: The panelists voted on 64 total statements pertaining to OCM and CS in cardiac arrest: 29 defining OCM, 23 defining cardiac standstill, and 12 examining clinical implications of OCM and CS. We defined OCM as coordinated contraction with change in left ventricular chamber size. Coordinated contraction with any change of the right ventricle may also be used if visualization of the left ventricle was not possible. Ventricular fibrillation, agonal motion, and isolated valvular movement were deemed not consistent with OCM. Cardiac standstill was defined as including the absence of all cardiac motion or the presence of isolated valvular movement alone. The panel recommended that POCUS can guide cardiac arrest resuscitation, and that these definitions are applicable to pediatric patients and the prehospital setting.

**CONCLUSION**: The expert panelists established consensus definitions of OCM and CS during cardiac arrest. These definitions can guide further research into POCUS use during cardiac arrest and aid ongoing efforts to standardize its use.

articles.title: Prehospital Advanced Airway Management in Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Cohort Study Using Time-Dependent Propensity Score Sequential Matching.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: Traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (TCA) has extremely poor outcomes, and the benefit of prehospital advanced airway management (AAM) remains uncertain, partly because previous observational studies may have been affected by resuscitation time bias. We examined the association between prehospital AAM and clinical outcomes in adults with TCA using a time-dependent analytic approach.

**METHODS**: We conducted a nationwide retrospective observational cohort study using the All-Japan Utstein Registry linked with emergency medical services transport records from 2021 to 2023. Adults (≥18 years) with TCA were included. The exposure was successful prehospital AAM, including supraglottic airway placement or endotracheal intubation. The primary outcome was 30-day survival, and the secondary outcome was favorable neurological outcome (Cerebral Performance Category 1-2) at 30 days. We applied time-dependent propensity score sequential matching and estimated corrected risk differences (RDs) using generalized estimating equations with inverse-frequency weighting.

**RESULTS**: Among 7,217 patients, 2,653 (36.8%) received prehospital AAM, of whom 2,637 were successfully matched within the analytic cohort. Thirty-day survival was 1.8% in the AAM group and 1.4% among matched controls (corrected RD, 0.6%; 95% confidence interval (CI), -0.1 to 1.2). Favorable neurological outcome occurred in 0.2% and 0.4%, respectively (corrected RD, -0.2%; 95% CI, -0.6 to 0.1). No significant timing-dependent association or prespecified subgroup heterogeneity was observed.

**CONCLUSIONS**: In this nationwide cohort study using time-dependent propensity score sequential matching, prehospital AAM was not significantly associated with improved outcomes in adults with TCA.

articles.title: Resuscitation using fresh-frozen plasma is associated with improved contextual fear memory in a non-TBI mouse model of trauma and hemorrhagic shock.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Cognitive dysfunction is a consequence of traumatic injury with lasting impacts. Even without direct brain injury, trauma and hemorrhagic shock (T/HS) can cause malperfusion, inflammation, and neuronal injury. Disruption of the endothelial glycocalyx (eGC), a key regulator of vascular homeostasis, contributes to trauma-induced endotheliopathy and may influence secondary neurologic injury. Prior work demonstrated that fresh-frozen plasma (FFP) resuscitation preserves eGC expression and reduces maladaptive vascular repair in a murine T/HS model. This study evaluates post-injury cognition and FFP protection against cognitive impairment compared with lactated Ringer's (LR).

**METHODS**: Male C57BL/6 mice were randomized to sham procedure or T/HS followed by a volume-driven LR or pressure-directed FFP resuscitation approach. T/HS mice underwent laparotomy, femoral artery cannulation, hemorrhagic shock, pseudofractures via bone homogenate injection, and hindlimb muscle crush injuries. Sham mice received laparotomy and femoral artery cutdown. Four days postsurgery, open field testing assessed locomotion, followed by fear conditioning on days 7 to 8 to assess cognition. Brains were collected to analyze hippocampal glycosaminoglycans hyaluronan, heparan sulfate (HS), and chondroitin sulfate (CS).

**RESULTS**: Open field testing showed intact locomotion at post-injury day 4 in all groups. On day 8, mice resuscitated with FFP had significantly greater contextual freezing compared with mice resuscitated with LR, consistent with improved hippocampal-dependent contextual memory. Cued fear conditioning did not differ between groups. LR and FFP resuscitation strategies resulted in distinct hippocampal hyaluronan and HS staining patterns, without synthesis gene expression differences. T/HS+LR brains showed increased 4-O-sulfated CS (CS-4S), a neurologically detrimental sulfation pattern, whereas FFP decreased CS-4S and increased CS-6S.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Goal-directed plasma resuscitation is associated with improved spatial memory and distinct eGC structural remodeling compared with volume-driven crystalloid resuscitation following T/HS. These findings highlight the potential for resuscitation strategy after hemorrhagic shock to influence neurological recovery, even in the absence of direct brain injury.

articles.title: Treatment of Acute Ischemic Stroke: A Review.
articles.abstract:
**IMPORTANCE**: Acute ischemic stroke, caused by thrombotic or embolic occlusion of a cervical or cerebral artery, leads to neurologic injury due to sudden disruption of blood flow to the brain. Ischemic stroke is a leading cause of disability and death and accounts for about 85% of strokes in the US.

**OBSERVATIONS**: Symptoms of acute ischemic stroke vary based on the area of the affected brain. Common presentations include sudden arm or leg weakness, aphasia or slurred speech, sudden loss of balance or coordination, sudden visual difficulties, and/or facial drooping. Patients with suspected stroke should be transported to the nearest emergency department for urgent brain imaging, typically noncontrast computed tomography (CT). Based on 2026 American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (AHA/ASA) guidelines, first-line therapy for patients with acute ischemic stroke presenting within 4.5 hours from symptom onset with disabling symptoms (eg, affecting the ability to perform activities of daily living) is intravenous thrombolysis (tenecteplase or alteplase) in those without intracranial hemorrhage or other contraindications to thrombolysis. The treatment window can be extended to 9 hours-and up to 24 hours in patients with large vessel occlusion (eg, involving the internal carotid artery or proximal middle cerebral artery [M1 segment]) who are unable to receive thrombectomy-based on identification of salvageable tissue using perfusion imaging with CT perfusion or magnetic resonance imaging. In appropriately selected patients with acute ischemic stroke, pooled randomized trial data show an approximately 10% absolute increase in the probability of a better functional outcome with intravenous thrombolysis. Based on 2026 AHA/ASA guidelines, endovascular thrombectomy, which involves clot removal with an intra-arterial mechanical device, is recommended for patients with large vessel occlusion within 6 hours of stroke onset (class 1 recommendation) and is recommended in selected patients with large vessel occlusion within 24 hours of last known well (class 1 recommendation). Endovascular therapy should be performed after intravenous thrombolysis unless patients have contraindications to thrombolytic therapy. Compared with medical management, which includes intravenous thrombolysis when indicated, endovascular thrombectomy produces an approximately 20% absolute increase in functional independence.

**CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE**: Acute ischemic stroke causes substantial disability and mortality. First-line therapy for patients with disabling acute stroke symptoms is intravenous thrombolysis (if no contraindications) within 4.5 hours of stroke onset and up to 24 hours in carefully selected patients not receiving mechanical thrombectomy; for large vessel occlusions, mechanical thrombectomy may be performed up to 24 hours after stroke onset in eligible patients.

articles.title: Traumatic renal injuries: the prevalence, management and outcome of renal vascular injury.
articles.abstract:
**PURPOSE**: To assess the prevalence, management and outcome of renal vascular injuries (RVIs; active bleeding and contained vascular injuries) seen on admission CT. Also, we wanted to find out the prevalence and survival of patients with concomitant injury to liver, spleen, and kidney seen on admission CT.

**METHODS**: We conducted a retrospective, single-center, longitudinal cohort study with nine-year data (2013-2021) of all ≥ 15-year-old patients with renal injury identified in a trauma registry. Admission CT and angiographic examinations were reviewed to assess RVIs, including active bleeding, arterial dissection, segmental infarct, pseudoaneurysm or AV-fistulae. Medical records were reviewed for treatment, hospital length of stay and 30-day survival rate.

**RESULTS**: Out of 2805 patients with abdominal trauma, 243 (8.7%) had a renal injury, of whom 182 (74.9%) underwent CT on admission. RVI was found in 56 patients (30.8%). Among these 56 patients, 42 (75%) had active bleeding, eight (14.3%) segmental infarct, six (10.7%) pseudoaneurysm, and three (5.4%) arterial dissection. Of these, ten patients (17.9%) underwent angioembolization, and three (5.4%) underwent laparotomy. Patients with RVI were slightly older than those without RVI (43.6 vs. 37.8 years, p = 0.0409) and had more often a penetrating trauma (OR 2.836; 95% CI 1.127-7.136, p = 0.0416). Hospital length of stay (14.7 vs. 14.9 days, p = 0.9520) and 30-day survival (95.2% vs. 92.6%, p = 0.3165) did not differ significantly between patients without and with RVI. Among patients with available CT, fourteen (14/182; 7.7%) had concomitant injuries to the liver, spleen and kidney, with no statistically significant difference in 30-day survival compared with patients without such concomitant injuries (92.9% vs. 94.6%; p = 0.5237).

**CONCLUSION**: RVI was not uncommon in our study cohort, occurring in 30.8% of patients with renal injury who underwent CT on admission. Of these, 17.9% were treated with angioembolization. Patients with RVI were slightly older and were more likely to have a penetrating injury than patients without RVI. No statistically significant difference in hospital length of stay or 30-day survival was found between patients without and with RVI.

articles.title: The Impact of Hospital Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Volume and Its Distribution Across ICUs on Adult Patients' Outcomes: An Analysis of the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization Registry.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: Research from a prior era of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) found that higher hospital ECMO volume was associated with higher survival rates, but it did not examine whether distributing ECMO volume across multiple ICUs affected this relationship.

**DESIGN**: Retrospective analysis of the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) registry.

**SETTING**: ECMO centers contributing to the registry.

**PATIENTS**: Adult patients required ECMO support from 2012 to 2023.

**INTERVENTIONS**: None.

**MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS**: We analyzed adult patients from the ELSO registry (2012-2023), adjusting for hospital factors and case mix using multivariable hierarchical logistic regression. The main outcome was in-hospital mortality. Hospital experience was measured by the annual number of adult ECMO cases and total ECMO hours. Volume-outcome associations were modeled for all centers and by total adult ICUs per center. We included 115,849 adults on ECMO across 495 hospitals. Model estimates showed small decreases in mortality odds with higher annual case counts (odds ratio [OR], 0.98; 95% CI, 0.97-0.99 per 10-case increase) and ECMO hours (OR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.99-1.00 per 1000 hr increase). Hospitals with one ICU had a median of 10 cases (interquartile interval [IQI], 3-25 cases), while those with four or more ICUs had a median of 50 (IQI, 28-91). Adjusted mortality was higher in centers delivering ECMO across four+ ICUs compared with one ICU (OR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.06-1.31), the annual case model (OR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.06-1.26), and the annual ECMO hours model. Higher volume was associated with a reduction in the odds of mortality for hospitals with four+ ICUs compared with those with one ICU (OR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.96-1.00 per 10 cases and OR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.99-1.00 per 1000 hr).

**CONCLUSIONS**: Higher hospital ECMO volume is associated with reduced mortality. Hospitals with more adult ICUs that perform ECMO may experience higher mortality, which may be explained by increased patient complexity and is offset by the higher center volume. More research is needed to better understand the optimum design of ECMO centers.

articles.title: Airway management during missions of a neurologist-staffed mobile stroke unit: a retrospective registry study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Following their endorsement by international guidelines, mobile stroke units (MSUs) are increasingly being integrated into emergency medical services worldwide. In real-world use, physician-staffed MSUs can be dispatched beyond their intended indication, exposing on-board neurologists to non-stroke emergencies. This raises important clinical and regulatory questions about the competencies MSU physicians need. Advanced airway management is one of the most critical prehospital interventions. Yet, its frequency, indications, procedural characteristics and success rates have not been investigated in neurologist-staffed MSU services.

**METHODS**: We retrospectively analysed a prospective registry of mission documentation from a neurologist-staffed MSU service in Berlin, Germany from 31 August 2024 to 15 March 2026. Dispatches of the MSU were classified as stroke or non-stroke dispatches using the recorded activation code. The primary outcome was the dispatch-based frequency of endotracheal intubation (ETI), defined as a documented intubation attempt. All ETIs were performed by the on-board neurologist. Secondary outcomes included supraglottic airway (SGA) use, first-pass success rate, procedural characteristics and self-reported post-mission National Aeronautics and Space Administration Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) workload. Proportions are reported with 95% Wilson confidence intervals (CI).

**RESULTS**: We analysed 3,887 dispatches. ETI occurred in a total of 49 dispatches (1.26%; 95% CI 0.95-1.66) with 2 in 1,755 stroke- (0.11%; 95% CI 0.03-0.41) and 47 in 2,132 non-stroke dispatches (2.20%; 95% CI 1.66-2.92). SGA use occurred in 22 dispatches (0.57%; 95% CI 0.37-0.86). All 49 intubation attempts were successful (100.0%; 95% CI 92.7-100.0). First-pass success was achieved in 43/49 (87.8%; 95% CI 75.8-94.3) with no ETI requiring more than two attempts. Videolaryngoscopy was used in all ETIs and capnographic confirmation of tube position in 48/49 (98%). Non-traumatic cardiac arrest was the most frequent indication (30/49). In the exploratory workload analysis, the median NASA-TLX score was 59.8 [IQR 50.0-68.7] in 49 dispatches with ETI and 27.0 [15.5-41.7] in 2,700 dispatches without ETI.

**CONCLUSIONS**: ETI was infrequent overall and particularly rare during stroke dispatches, yet first-pass success was high. Prospective studies are needed to define airway management requirements and training standards for MSU physicians.
articles.journal: Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med

articles.title: Implementation of a low-cost trauma intake form with real-time clinical decision support: Mixed-methods findings from a stepped-wedge clinical trial in Ghana.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Most injured patients in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) receive care from non-specialist providers at smaller hospitals lacking trauma experience and standardized protocols. A trauma intake form (TIF) with real-time clinical decision support prompts was developed to address this gap. This study examined key implementation outcomes, including adoption, usability, acceptability, appropriateness, feasibility, and sustainability.

**METHODS**: This study was conducted at six district and two regional hospitals in Ghana as part of a hybrid effectiveness-implementation stepped-wedge clinical trial. Direct observation of 4077 injured patients over 17.5 months was combined with a structured questionnaire administered to all 241 participating clinicians, alongside thematic analysis of open-ended responses.

**RESULTS**: Overall observed TIF uptake was 85.6%, with five of eight hospitals classified as adopters. Implementation outcomes were consistently positive across qualitative and quantitative measures, with high levels of acceptability, appropriateness, feasibility, and usability reported across both adopting and non-adopting facilities. Barriers included time constraints, a lack of pre-existing documentation culture, and a perception among some clinicians that patients were too sick to prioritize use of the form.

**CONCLUSION**: The TIF achieved high adoption among non-specialist providers in a resource-limited setting, demonstrating that low-cost, contextually developed tools can bridge the gap between clinical effectiveness and implementation success. Sustained scale-up will require structural solutions to address time and documentation barriers, targeted training to correct the misperception that the tool is unsuitable for the most severely injured patients, and embedded feedback mechanisms to maintain clinician engagement.

articles.title: Predictors and clinical outcomes of extubation failure in patients with cervical spinal cord injury.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: Respiratory compromise is common in cervical spinal cord injury (SCI) and poses a challenge in deciding whether to extubate or perform a tracheostomy. This study evaluated the characteristics of failed extubations and hypothesized that those with unsuccessful extubation attempts would have a higher trauma burden and worse weaning parameters.

**METHODS**: This was a retrospective review of intubated cervical SCI at a Level 1 trauma center from 2018 to 2024. Demographics, injury, surgical and airway management data were collected. Location of intubation and extubation, weaning parameters, and time to airway event or failure were tabulated. Statistical analysis was completed using Stata with p < 0.05 as significant.

**RESULTS**: Seventy patients with SCI were analyzed with a mean age of 54 years (range 18-89) and 62 (89%) males. Twenty successful extubations (SE) were compared to 36 failed extubations (FE), excluding the direct to tracheostomy (10) or terminally extubated (4) patients. Frequency of TBI (5% FE vs 14% SE, p = 0.3), blunt cerebrovascular injury (25% vs. 32%, p = 0.63) and ISS (30 vs 23, p = 0.13) were not statistically different. Documented weaning parameters - rapid shallow breathing index and negative inspiratory force were similar, although more FE patients were extubated in the OR/PACU. FE patients had significantly fewer hospital and ICU-free days; however, mortality differences did not reach statistical significance.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Failed extubation in SCI is associated with longer length of stay. Trauma burden and weaning parameters were not correlated with FE; however, extubation outside of the ICU may increase the risk of failure.

articles.title: Fracture-related infection after operative fixation of acetabular fractures: Incidence and factors independently associated with infection.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: The purpose of this study was to determine the incidence of fracture-related infection following acetabular fracture fixation and to identify factors independently associated with its occurrence.

**METHODS**: A retrospective single-center cohort study was conducted at a Level I trauma center. Patients aged ≥ 18 years who underwent operative fixation of an acetabular fracture between January 2021 and July 2025 were included. Fracture-related infection was defined according to the AO/EBJIS consensus definition. Patients were followed for a minimum of 12 months. Multivariable analysis was performed using Firth penalized logistic regression.

**RESULTS**: Of 359 patients, 27 (7.5%) developed fracture-related infection. All 27 met at least 1 confirmatory criterion. The median time to diagnosis was 9 days (IQR, 7-14), with 20 infections (74.1%) diagnosed within 14 days of fixation. Sixteen infections (59.3%) were culture-positive, with gram-negative organisms more common than Staphylococcus aureus. Eleven infections (40.7%) were culture-negative, including 6 patients who had received empirical linezolid before tissue sampling. All infected patients underwent infection-related reoperation; 23 (85.2%) were managed with debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention, and 4 (14.8%) underwent implant removal. On Firth penalized multivariable analysis, higher body mass index (adjusted OR, 1.33; 95% CI, 1.15-1.55), longer operative duration (1.63; 1.11-2.36), diabetes mellitus (2.55; 1.09-6.05), and a longer admission-to-surgery interval (1.08; 1.00-1.16) were independently associated with infection. Polytrauma was not independently associated with infection (2.10; 0.89-5.09). At final follow-up, fracture union was achieved in 20 patients (74.1%).

**CONCLUSIONS**: Fracture-related infection after acetabular fracture fixation appears to reflect a combination of patient-related and operative factors. Recognizing these factors may help identify patients at higher risk and allow closer postoperative surveillance.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Prognostic Level III.

articles.title: Preoperative CT-derived psoas attenuation and correction loss after traumatic thoracolumbar fracture fixation: A construct-dependent association.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Postoperative correction loss remains a concern after posterior fixation of traumatic thoracolumbar fractures. Although bone quality and construct characteristics influence mechanical stability, the role of preoperative muscle quality remains poorly defined. We examined whether CT-derived psoas attenuation was associated with correction loss and whether fracture-level screw placement modified this association.

**METHODS**: This retrospective single-center cohort included 78 adults who underwent posterior pedicle screw fixation for traumatic AO Spine A3 thoracolumbar fractures. Preoperative psoas and paravertebral attenuation and cross-sectional area were measured at L3. Correction loss was defined as the difference between final-follow-up and immediate postoperative Cobb angles measured on supine sagittal CT reconstructions. Multivariable linear regression tested the interaction between centered psoas attenuation and fracture-level screw placement, adjusting for age, sex, vertebral attenuation, instrumented levels, and follow-up duration. An extended model added vertebral height loss and canal compromise. HC3 robust variance estimation and sensitivity analyses were performed.

**RESULTS**: Mean correction loss was 4.1 ± 5.4°, and 23 patients (29.5%) experienced loss greater than 5°. The psoas attenuation-by-fracture-level screw interaction was significant (B=0.311°/HU; 95% CI, 0.091-0.530; p = .006; HC3 p = .037). Without fracture-level screws, each 10-HU increase in psoas attenuation corresponded to approximately 2.6° less correction loss (B=-0.255°/HU; 95% CI, -0.440 to -0.071; p = .007), although HC3 inference crossed the null (p = .068). No clear association was observed with fracture-level screws. The interaction persisted after adjustment for vertebral height loss and canal compromise (B=0.342°/HU; 95% CI, 0.127-0.556; p = .002; HC3 p = .016), when short- versus long-segment fixation replaced instrumented-level count, and in patients with at least 12 months of follow-up. Paravertebral attenuation showed a similar pattern, whereas muscle cross-sectional area did not.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Preoperative psoas attenuation showed a construct-dependent association with correction loss after fixation of traumatic AO Spine A3 fractures. Lower attenuation may identify mechanical vulnerability when the fractured vertebra is not incorporated into the construct. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation before CT-based muscle assessment can guide construct selection.

articles.title: Comparative mortality of pelvic ring fractures vs. hip fractures in adults ≥55 years: A propensity-matched cohort study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Hip and pelvic fragility fractures are associated with substantial mortality in older adults. While standardized care pathways are established for hip fractures, management of pelvic fragility fractures remains less defined. This study compared mortality between matched hip and pelvic ring fracture patients managed operatively or nonoperatively.

**HYPOTHESIS**: Pelvic and hip fractures would demonstrate comparable mortality within operative and nonoperative treatment groups.

**PATIENTS AND METHODS**: This retrospective cohort study used the TriNetX network to identify adults aged ≥ 55 years with hip or pelvic ring fractures. Patients were stratified by operative or nonoperative management, and cohorts were propensity score matched 1:1 based on demographic and clinical characteristics. The primary outcome was 1-year all-cause mortality; secondary outcomes were mortality at 30 days, 90 days, and 2 years. Cox proportional hazards models evaluated 1-year mortality.

**RESULTS**: After matching, 255,202 patients per cohort were included in the nonoperative subgroup and 11,448 per cohort in the operative subgroup. Among nonoperative patients, 1-year mortality was higher after hip than pelvic fracture (11.13% vs 10.68%; HR 1.123, 95% CI 1.105-1.141). Among operative patients, 1-year mortality was also higher after hip fracture (8.84% vs 5.94%; HR 1.424, 95% CI 1.314-1.545). However, 30-day mortality was higher after operative pelvic fracture (3.11% vs 2.49%; p = 0.004). Male sex, older age, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease were associated with increased mortality.

**DISCUSSION**: Hip fractures were associated with greater 1-year mortality across management strategies; however, operative pelvic fractures demonstrated greater early mortality. These findings highlight pelvic fragility fractures as high-risk injuries warranting further evaluation of standardized geriatric care pathways.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: III.

articles.title: Facial burns as functional trauma: Integrating expression, identity and long-term recovery: A narrative review.
articles.abstract: Advances in acute burn care have improved survival, shifting focus toward long-term functional recovery. Facial burns present a distinct clinical challenge due to the concentration of ocular, oral, respiratory, and expressive functions within a highly visible anatomical region. This narrative review synthesises functional and psychosocial literature to examine facial burns as trauma that disrupts dynamic facial movement, communication, and participation, and to evaluate limitations in current outcome frameworks. The face supports ocular protection, articulation, alimentation, airway patency, and non-verbal signalling. Contracture patterns, including microstomia, ectropion, nasal distortion, and midfacial contracture, may impair both mechanical function and expressive range. Recovery is typically longitudinal and iterative, addressing evolving distortion rather than restoring pre-injury dynamics. Even subtle restrictions of facial movement may alter speech clarity, eye contact, and self-recognition, with consequences extending beyond visible scarring. Existing outcome measures, including body image scales, burn-specific health instruments, and isolated physical metrics, do not adequately capture the interaction between structural repair, expressive mobility, and communicative participation. Recognition of facial burns as functional trauma supports the need for facial-specific composite outcome models and coordinated multidisciplinary care to optimise long-term recovery.

articles.title: A tale of two nails: A retrospective cohort comparison of TFNA and PFNA in proximal femoral fracture fixation.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: The aging population has transformed proximal femoral fractures into a public health crisis, resulting in an increased burden of postoperative complications and revision surgeries. While the Proximal Femoral Nail Antirotation (PFNA) has been a standard in certain countries, the Trochanteric Fixation Nail Advanced (TFNA) was introduced with engineering refinements intended to enhance fixation. This study aims to compare the two implants, specifically focusing on fixation failure rates and distinct biomechanical failure mechanisms.

**METHODS**: We conducted a retrospective cohort study at an Academic Level I trauma center involving 1006 patients treated between January 2020 and March 2025. Patients with a minimum six-month follow-up were included (681 PFNA, 325 TFNA). Radiographic assessments, including reduction quality, Tip-Apex Distance (TAD), and blade positioning, were independently performed by two senior fellowship-trained surgeons. The primary outcome was fixation failure requiring reoperation.

**RESULTS**: The fixation failure rate was 1.6% (n = 11) in the PFNA group and 3.4% (n = 11) in the TFNA group; however, this difference was not statistically significant. While radiographic parameters such as TAD and reduction quality did not differ significantly between the failure groups, a distinct shift in biomechanical failure modes was identified. PFNA failures were overwhelmingly characterized by the classic "cut-out" mechanism (91%), whereas TFNA failures frequently involved medial migration or "cut-through" (55%).

**CONCLUSION**: Although the TFNA was associated with a higher absolute rate of fixation failure, no statistically significant difference in fixation failure rates was observed between the two implants. However, the failure profile shifted toward medial "cut-through" migration with the TFNA. These findings suggest that the TFNA may possess a unique failure profile, potentially reflecting a learning curve or specific biomechanical properties. Suboptimal reduction and blade positioning were frequent among the failures and may have contributed to them; however, a considerable proportion of failures occurred after a reduction graded as good. These findings emphasize that technical precision remains the primary determinant of stability, regardless of the cephalomedullary device used.

articles.title: The Effect of Guanfacine on Delirium in Surgical and Trauma ICU Patients: A Pilot Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: To evaluate the feasibility of conducting a randomized controlled trial investigating guanfacine for ICU delirium, including assessment of recruitment, retention, protocol adherence, and data completeness, while estimating treatment effects to inform future trial design.

**DESIGN**: Single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial conducted from November 2020 to February 2023.

**SETTING**: Surgical and Trauma ICUs at the University of Alabama at Birmingham Hospital.

**PATIENTS**: One hundred critically ill adults with Confusion Assessment Method-ICU-confirmed delirium randomized 1:1 to guanfacine or placebo.

**INTERVENTIONS**: Patients received 2 mg guanfacine or matching placebo nightly for up to 14 days, or until ICU discharge or delirium resolution.

**MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS**: Primary feasibility outcomes included protocol adherence (target ≥ 90%), retention (target ≥ 80%), recruitment rate (target ≥ 2 patients/mo), and data completeness (target ≥ 95%). Most feasibility targets were achieved: protocol adherence was 100%, retention was 100%, and data completeness was 100%. Recruitment was significantly impacted by COVID-19 pandemic disruptions, achieving 0.9 patients/wk during active recruitment periods.For clinical outcomes, in unadjusted analyses, median delirium and coma-free days were higher with guanfacine than placebo (2 [interquartile range [IQR], 0-6] vs. 1 [IQR, 0-4]; p = 0.02); however, this association was not statistically significant after adjustment for prespecified baseline covariates. ICU and hospital length of stay and duration of mechanical ventilation did not differ significantly between groups. No hemodynamic differences or safety concerns were observed.

**CONCLUSIONS**: This pilot study successfully supports feasibility for a definitive trial, with excellent protocol adherence, adequate retention, and preliminary signals that warrant further evaluation. Although adjusted analyses were not statistically significant, the observed unadjusted difference in delirium and coma-free days and favorable safety profile support progression to a multicenter trial informed by these pilot estimates.

articles.title: From sirens to systems: Characterizing EMS and trauma care across America.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: State emergency medical services (EMS) and trauma systems determine prehospital triage, transport, trauma center designation, data reporting, and quality improvement, yet their contemporary organization has not been systematically characterized. We sought to describe state-level EMS and trauma system structures, policies, resources, and perceived gaps across the United States.

**METHODS**: We conducted a cross-sectional survey of EMS and trauma system leaders in all 50 states and the District of Columbia from July 2025 through March 2026. A 56-item instrument utilizing categorical, Likert-type, rank-order, and free-text items assessed oversight, prehospital triage and transport, clinical protocols, trauma center verification, registries, quality improvement, and funding. Respondents were recruited by email and phone. Multiple respondents could contribute complementary domain-level information to a single state profile. Responses were summarized descriptively.

**RESULTS**: All 51 jurisdictions participated. Most states reported a state EMS medical director (84%), statewide trauma triage protocols (84%), and mandatory participation in their state trauma registry (88%). However, operational coordination varied: only 29% had a centralized trauma communications center, only 6% of states reported a single point of contact for helicopter EMS dispatch, and 35% required a certificate of need for new helicopter services. Trauma center verification relied on American College of Surgeons (ACS) verification in 59% of states, while others used state-administered processes. More than half of states rated EMS financial resources in the two lowest adequacy categories, and 55% reported that their trauma system required at least moderate improvement. Rural populations were most frequently identified as underserved (96%) and as experiencing worse outcomes (92%).

**CONCLUSIONS**: State EMS and trauma systems share broad adoption of national clinical standards but differ substantially in governance, coordination, verification, data integration, and funding.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE AND STUDY TYPE**: Level V, Prognostic/epidemiological.

articles.title: Non-urgent emergency department utilization in adults: a systematic review of associated factors across diverse health systems.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Non-urgent emergency department (ED) visits represent a growing global challenge with significant economic and operational consequences. Despite previous reviews, important gaps remain. No review has included all commonly used terms for non-urgent ED visits, recent evidence has not been synthesised, and factors related to patients, health systems, and care contexts have rarely been examined together. This systematic review aimed to identify and categorize factors associated with non-urgent ED visits in adults.

**METHODS**: A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for articles published between January 2015 and May 2026. We included cross-sectional, cohort, and case-control studies that compared urgent and non-urgent ED visits and reported at least one associated factor. Quality assessment was performed using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) checklists. Because of substantial heterogeneity in definitions, the findings were synthesised narratively.

**RESULTS**: Thirty-two studies from 21 countries were included. The proportion of non-urgent visits ranged from 1% to 82.4%, depending on the definition and measurement approach used. Five approaches were used to define non-urgent visits. The most common were triage-based (41%) and clinical judgment-based (28%). Associated factors were classified into three main categories: (1) demographic and socioeconomic (younger age, female sex, low income, lower education, non-native nationality); (2) access and health system (self-referral, arrival on foot, weekend visits, shorter distance to ED, lack of a family physician, public insurance); and (3) clinical and perceptual (non-specific diagnosis, musculoskeletal problems, mental health conditions, prior ED visit history, and patient perception of illness severity). The strongest associations were reported for frequent previous ED visits (aOR up to 82.13) and patients who perceived their illness as non-serious (aOR up to 21.03).

**CONCLUSION**: Non-urgent ED visits are influenced by multiple individual, health system, and perceptual factors. The substantial heterogeneity in definitional approaches underscores the need for conceptual standardization. No single intervention is likely to reduce non-urgent ED visits. Effective strategies should strengthen primary care, improve insurance policies, increase public health education, and empower patients.
articles.journal: Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med

articles.title: A bedside score using arrival data to identify major hemorrhage after blunt pelvic ring fracture: Development and validation.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Early recognition of major hemorrhage after blunt pelvic ring injury could guide mobilization of transfusion and hemorrhage-control resources. We developed an arrival-based bedside score and compared its performance with shock index.

**METHODS**: We studied 239,736 adults with documented blunt pelvic ring fractures in the 2019-2024 National Trauma Data Bank. Major hemorrhage was defined as a hemorrhage-control procedure, hemorrhagic death, or transfusion of ≥ 1000 mL or ≥ 4 units of red blood cells within 4 h. Penalized logistic regression selected arrival variables for an integer score. We assessed performance in a held-out test set (n = 79,912) and at approximately matched alert volume. A model refitted on 2019-2022 admissions was evaluated in 2023-2024. Subgroup analyses were post hoc.

**RESULTS**: Major hemorrhage occurred in 26,479 patients (11.0%); 31.0% were aged ≥ 75 years, and 45.9% had fallen. In the test set, the score achieved an AUROC of 0.882 (95% CI, 0.879-0.886), exceeding shock index by 0.060 (95% CI, 0.055-0.064; P < 0.001). At approximately 15.6% of patients flagged, the score identified 678 additional major hemorrhage cases with 684 fewer false-positive alerts. The temporally validated model achieved an AUROC of 0.885 (95% CI, 0.881-0.888). Discrimination exceeded shock index for pelvic ring disruption (0.830 vs 0.778) and high-energy mechanisms (0.811 vs 0.764), but was lower after falls (0.779 vs 0.800).

**CONCLUSIONS**: In patients with documented blunt pelvic ring fractures, an arrival-based score identified major hemorrhage more accurately than shock index at a similar alert burden. Reduced performance after falls and uncertain applicability to suspected fractures warrant caution. External validation and prospective impact assessment are needed before clinical use.

articles.title: Traumatic hip dislocation: Clinical and epidemiological features, management and prognostic factors in a series of 44 cases from a tertiary centre.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: Traumatic hip dislocation is an uncommon but potentially severe injury requiring emergency management. We aimed to describe the clinical and epidemiological features and associated injuries of patients with traumatic hip dislocation treated at a tertiary centre, and to analyse the factors related to complications and to the need for salvage surgery.

**PATIENTS AND METHODS**: Retrospective observational study of 44 patients aged 15 years or older treated between 2010 and 2024. Demographic variables, injury mechanism, direction of the dislocation, associated fractures (Judet-Letournel and Pipkin classifications), management and complications were recorded. Bivariate analysis used Fisher's exact test for categorical variables and the Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables; a p value < 0.05 was considered significant.

**RESULTS**: Mean age was 37.4 years (SD 19.3) and 70.5% of patients were men. The commonest mechanism was a road traffic accident (52.3%) and the posterior direction was the most frequent (72.7%). A complex dislocation (with an associated fracture) was present in 72.7% of patients, and 36.4% occurred in the context of polytrauma. Closed reduction was performed in 88.6% of cases, with a median time to reduction of 2 h. The most frequent complication was sciatic nerve injury (20.5%). Femoral head osteonecrosis occurred in 2 patients (4.5%). Male sex was associated with more late complications (p = 0.043), and a prolonged hospital stay was associated with both early (p = 0.002) and late (p = 0.017) complications. Complex dislocations showed a consistent trend towards greater morbidity.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Traumatic hip dislocation predominantly affects young men after high-energy trauma. Prompt reduction was associated with a low rate of osteonecrosis. The presence of associated fractures and a prolonged hospital stay identify patients with a worse course.

articles.title: Does the number of debridement procedures impact risk of infection in open fractures?
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVE**: This study aimed to evaluate the relationship between the number of debridements and risk of infection, while stratifying by degree of wound contamination. It was hypothesized that patients with severe contamination, a higher number of debridements would be associated with lower risk of infection.

**METHODS**: This is a retrospective secondary analysis of prospectively collected data in the PREP-IT trial (Program of Randomized trials to Evaluate Preoperative antiseptic skin solutions in orthopaedic Trauma). The primary outcome measure was adjudicated surgical site infection. Independent variables were number of debridement procedures and time from injury to definitive wound closure. Analysis was stratified by degree of contamination and multivariable analyses were performed to control for confounders.

**RESULTS**: 3502 total open fractures corresponding to 3222 patients with a median (interquartile range, IQR) age of 42 (29-58) years (2199 [62.8%] men; median (IQR) body mass index 27.7 [24.3-32.6]) were included in this analysis. 2199 patients were included in the non/minimal contamination group, 970 in the surface contamination group, and 333 in the embedded contamination group. After controlling for patient-level characteristics there was a 27% increase in the risk of infection for each debridement performed in the overall patient cohort (OR 1.27 [1.12-1.43] p < 0.001), and a 45% increase in the embedded contamination group (OR, 1.45 [1.12-1.88] p = 0.004). There was no statistically significant difference between minimal contamination groups and the surface contamination group.

**CONCLUSION**: The results of this study indicate that increased number of debridement procedures was not associated with lower infectious rates. Patients with the highest degree of contamination demonstrated significantly increased risk of developing an infection with each additional debridement. These findings support the importance of limiting unnecessary additional debridement procedures to reduce infection risk and optimize outcomes.

articles.title: Cone-Beam CT-Guided SpineJack® vertebral augmentation: A reproducible technique for accurate pedicular access and implant deployment.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: SpineJack® vertebral augmentation requires precise bilateral transpedicular access and accurate implant deployment. This study evaluated the feasibility, safety, and technical performance of cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)-guided SpineJack augmentation.

**METHODS**: This retrospective single-institution, two-site study included consecutive CBCT-guided procedures performed between May 2021 and April 2026. Technical success required planned bilateral implantation, expansion, and cement augmentation without pedicle breach or implant malposition on final CBCT. Secondary outcomes included immediate vertebral height restoration, complications, procedure duration, radiation exposure, and treatment setting.

**RESULTS**: The analysis included 178 procedures; median age was 45 years (interquartile range [IQR], 27-59), and 158 procedures (88.8%) involved traumatic fractures. Technical success was 100% (178/178), including 64 procedures (36.0%) with pedicle-implant clearance < 0.8 mm. Median absolute vertebral body height gain was 4.1 mm (IQR, 2.7-6.1), and median restoration of baseline height loss reached 77% (IQR, 47-98). All 24 cement leaks (13.5%) were asymptomatic. No neurological, vascular, infectious, or implant-related complications occurred. Median procedure duration was 60 min (IQR, 50-90), and median dose-area product was 33.2 Gy·cm² (IQR, 19.4-53.1). One hundred procedures (56.2%) were performed on an outpatient basis.

**CONCLUSIONS**: CBCT-guided SpineJack augmentation achieved accurate bilateral implant deployment and substantial immediate vertebral height restoration without major procedure-related complications. These findings support CBCT as a reliable guidance strategy for vertebral augmentation, with demonstrated feasibility in outpatient practice.

articles.title: The MIS-Diamond fixation: A minimally invasive diamond-shaped construct for spinopelvic dissociation in polytrauma patients.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: Sacral fracture with spinopelvic dissociation (SPD) is a rare, high-energy injury associated with substantial mortality and morbidity. Surgical stabilization is technically challenging and has historically been associated with relatively high rates of construct failure. The present study describes and evaluates a novel minimally invasive spinopelvic diamond-shaped construct (The MIS-Diamond fixation), designed to improve rigid triangular stabilization while minimizing soft-tissue morbidity and facilitate the fracture reduction.

**METHODS**: A retrospective observational study was conducted including patients who underwent MIS-Diamond fixation for AO Type C3 sacral fractures at a single Level-I Trauma Center between January 2014 and December 2024, with a minimum follow-up of 12 months. Neurological status, operative parameters, perioperative complications, and radiological outcomes were systematically assessed. Fractures were classified according to the AO Spine Sacral Injury Classification System.

**RESULTS**: Thirty-two patients (mean age 39 years) were included. Surgery was performed at a median of 5 days post-injury, with a mean operative time of 115.8 min and mean estimated blood loss of 82.7 mL. No intraoperative complications occurred. One patient developed a postoperative S1 motor impairment attributed to indirect radicular injury during reduction. Implant-related complications were recorded in 4 patients (12.5%), including one late-onset surgical site infection and three cases of asymptomatic iliac screw loosening. No soft tissue or wound healing complications were observed. Implant removal was successfully completed in 28 patients (87.5%) at 12 months postoperatively.

**DISCUSSION**: MIS-Diamond fixation demonstrated a favourable safety profile while enabling early postoperative mobilization. The incorporation of a 5.5 mm transverse iliac rod converts the classical triangular construct into a rigid box-like configuration, enhancing rotational stability and preventing coronal diastasis during vertical distraction. Limiting instrumentation to L4-L5 reduces the number of immobilized motion segments compared to previously described longer constructs, potentially mitigating long-term degenerative sequelae.

**CONCLUSIONS**: The MIS-Diamond fixation represents a safe and effective minimally invasive surgical option for SPD, providing reliable multiplanar stabilization with a low complication profile. Routine implant removal at 12 months is feasible and recommended to preserve motion segment function. Prospective multicentre studies are warranted to further validate these findings.

articles.title: Pooled Prevalence of Infectious Diseases Among First Responders in the Prehospital Setting: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis by Occupation.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: First responders often work in unpredictable, uncontrolled environments, where exposure to infected patients and contaminated environments heighten the risk of communicable disease transmission. Their higher infection prevalence compared with the general population has driven the implementation of personal protective equipment, vaccination requirements, safety protocols, and infection prevention education. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to estimate the pooled prevalence of infections among first responders in the prehospital workers including paramedics, emergency medical technicians, patient transport staff, firefighters, police, and police officers.

**METHODS**: Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, and PUBMED/Medline were systematically searched. Pooled prevalence estimates were calculated using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation, with Freeman-Tukey double-arcsine transformation and back-transformation to the original prevalence scale. Heterogeneity was assessed using 

**RESULTS**: Following the initial search, 34,874 articles were identified, of which 88 were full-text screened. Of these, 22 studies representing 19,188 first responders were included in this systematic review. The pooled prevalences of hepatitis B and C were 6.2% (95% CI 4.5%-8.2%) and 1.8% (95% CI 0.9%-2.9%), respectively. Around 4% (95% CI 2.6%-5.9%) of the first responders had MRSA colonization. Current or past infection with COVID-19 among non-vaccinated first responders was 13.6% (95% CI 4.8%-25.9%), which reduced to 7.3% (95% CI 3.6%-12%) after exclusion of studies with high risk of bias. Of the known study characteristics, geographic region significantly contributed to heterogeneity, explaining 36.7% of between-study variance, 

**CONCLUSIONS**: Infectious disease prevalence varied across pathogens, occupations, and geographical settings among first responders. These findings should be interpreted in light of substantial heterogeneity and limitations in the available evidence but may help inform infection prevention, occupational health policy, vaccination strategies, and future research in first responder services.

articles.title: Prehospital Whole Blood Resuscitation in Pediatric Patients: A San Antonio Cohort Descriptive.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: The objective of this study is to describe the demographic, clinical, and prehospital care characteristics of pediatric patients receiving whole blood (WB) resuscitation by San Antonio Fire Department (SAFD).

**METHODS**: We conducted an observational retrospective cohort study to evaluate pediatric patients who received prehospital low-titer group O positive WB transfusion through the SAFD prehospital blood program between October 2018 and June 2025. The objective was to characterize patient demographics, injury patterns, resuscitative interventions, shock physiology, and outcomes among pediatric recipients in a mature civilian emergency medical services WB program.

**RESULTS**: Of 1703 WB transfusions, 73 (4.3%) were pediatric. Most patients were male (76%), age range 1-17 years old with a mode of 17 years, adolescents represented 78%. Trauma accounted for 96% of cases, firearm injury (74%); all penetrating (84%), blunt (12%), with the remainder classified as medical/unknown. Vascular access was intravenous (73%), intraosseous (26%). Tranexamic acid was co-administered in 39%; 12% received ceftriaxone. When analyzed using age-adjusted Shock Index Pediatric Age-Adjusted (SIPA) thresholds (>1.2 for 1-6 years, >1.0 for 7-12 years, and >0.9 for 13-17 years), based on the initial available prehospital heart rate and systolic blood pressure, 45% of patients had an elevated SIPA, 22% had a normal SIPA, 20% were pulseless and therefore could not undergo SIPA calculation, and 14% lacked sufficient vital-sign data for classification. Survival was 50%; died 39%, and unknown outcomes 11%. Mean delta shock index values were most negative in toddlers (1-4 years) -0.97 ± 1.29, followed by children (5-11 years) -0.76 ± 1.07 and adolescents (12-17 years) -0.16 ± 0.46, indicating a greater physiologic response to resuscitation among younger pediatric patients.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Pediatric WB recipients were predominantly adolescent males who sustained penetrating trauma and presented with moderate-to-severe shock. Younger age groups had larger descriptive decreases in shock index during the prehospital encounter; however, these findings should be interpreted cautiously given the small subgroup sizes and observational design.

articles.title: Hospital cost structures and resource utilisation across representative treatment pathways relevant to complex orthopaedic infection care: a nationwide DRG-based analysis in Germany.
articles.abstract:
**PURPOSE**: Implant-associated orthopaedic infections require prolonged inpatient treatment, repeated surgery and multidisciplinary care, yet nationwide evidence on how hospital resources are distributed across clinically distinct treatment pathways is limited. This study characterised hospital-side case costs, resource utilisation and aggregate expenditure across representative German diagnosis-related groups (DRGs) relevant to complex orthopaedic infection care.

**METHODS**: Publicly available 2024 data from the German Institute for the Hospital Remuneration System (InEK) were analysed. Twelve representative DRGs were selected a priori from official definitions and diagnostic/procedural profiles and grouped into six treatment pathways. The InEK cost matrix reflects standardised hospital-side resource costs from participating calculation hospitals and does not represent actual DRG reimbursement. National case frequencies, length of stay and mean case costs were analysed using frequency-weighted pathway estimates, while pathway-level cost composition was calculated from aggregate component expenditure.

**RESULTS**: The included DRGs represented 36,212 hospitalisations and €305.2 million in aggregate annual hospital-side expenditure represented by the selected DRGs. Mean hospital-side costs ranged from €5,859 to €22,495 per case. Ward care accounted for approximately 34-69% of pathway expenditure; operating theatre services contributed up to 39% in revision arthroplasty. Geriatric rehabilitation generated the largest aggregate expenditure (€119.0 million; 39.0%) because of high case volume, whereas complex vacuum-assisted wound care had the highest per-case cost but only 2.9% of aggregate expenditure. At the aggregated DRG level, mean length of stay was associated with mean case cost (Pearson r = 0.87, 95% CI 0.60-0.96; P < 0.001); leave-one-out correlations ranged from r = 0.79 to r = 0.96.

**CONCLUSION**: Resource requirements differ markedly across representative DRG pathways relevant to complex orthopaedic infection care. Because the selected DRGs are not infection-exclusive, the reported expenditure should not be interpreted as the national economic burden of implant-associated orthopaedic infection. The findings may inform hospital resource planning and future cost-revenue analyses.

articles.title: Violent Reinjury Trajectories Across Injury Mechanisms: A Multicenter Cohort Study.
articles.abstract:
**STUDY OBJECTIVE**: Survivors of violent injury often experience reinjury. We sought to identify demographic and clinical factors associated with violent reinjury across different injury types.

**METHODS**: We conducted an observational cohort study of individuals with violent injury (ie, blunt assaults, stabbings, and firearm injuries) across 2 adult and 2 pediatric Level I trauma centers from 2016 to 2023. Covariates included age, sex, race, hospital type, insurance status, and social vulnerability. Our primary outcome was time to reinjury. We used multivariable Cox proportional hazards models to measure associations between each covariate and time to reinjury across injury types.

**RESULTS**: There were 29,038 individuals with nonfatal violent injuries. Male sex (n=19,273; 66.4%), Black and other race (n=21,403; 73.7%), presentation to adult hospitals (n=24,200; 83.3%), public insurance (n=13,879; 47.8%), and living in an area with high social vulnerability (n=21,044; 72.5%) were associated with a greater risk of any violent reinjury, adjusting for covariates. For index firearm injuries, patients younger than18 years had greater risk of firearm reinjury than patients aged 18 to 26 years (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR]:0.65 [0.47 to 0.91]) and for those older than 26 years (aHR:0.47 [0.34 to 0.66]). Although women with firearm injury had a lower risk of firearm reinjury compared with men (aHR:0.46 [0.36 to 0.58]), they had greater risk of blunt reinjury (aHR:1.77 [1.34 to 1.24]). Patients living in areas with high social vulnerability had a higher risk of escalating reinjury mechanism (eg, blunt to firearm; aHR:1.46 [1.11 to 1.90]) versus patients in areas with low/average social vulnerability.

**CONCLUSION**: This research underscores how sequelae of violent reinjury are shaped by certain demographic and clinical characteristics, highlighting opportunities to strengthen reinjury prevention in key subgroups.

articles.title: Prospective Observational Study Assessing Patient Characteristics, Management and Early Outcomes of Major Trauma Patients With Prehospital Shock. A preliminary report of the Sydney COAST study.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVE**: Despite advances in trauma resuscitation, significant gaps remain in understanding how early physiological and biochemical derangements influence clinical outcomes. The Sydney 'Clinical Outcomes following Acute Shock in Trauma' (COAST) registry was developed by clinicians containing both prehospital and in-hospital data, allowing for the identification of risk factors that influence early mortality for major trauma patients with shock. This study reports the formation of the registry and the patient cohort enrolled over its first 12 months.

**METHODS**: A multi-centre, prospective registry of shocked adult trauma patients treated by prehospital medical teams and transported directly to a Sydney-based major trauma centre. Shock was defined as either (1) systolic blood pressure less than 100 mmHg, (2) shock index greater than one, (3) blood transfusion or (4) administration of inotropes. Descriptive statistics were used to report outcomes including injuries, pathology, transfusions, immediate intervention, mortality and length of stay.

**RESULTS**: Two hundred fifty seven patients were enrolled. The predominant shock criteria for inclusion was hypotension (90% of cases), whilst 53% received prehospital blood transfusion. Interventional haemorrhage control was required in 31% of cases, whilst 74% received in-hospital transfusion. Injury severity was high (median injury severity score of 27). Four-hour mortality was 4.7% (9% at 24-h and 21% at 30-days).

**CONCLUSIONS**: Consistent with recent observational studies, the Sydney COAST registry captured a cohort of critically ill trauma patients, not all of whom may have had haemorrhage. This will serve as an important dataset, allowing clinicians to better understand factors driving traumatic shock whilst exploring avenues for improving care in these cases.

articles.title: Supply of Fibrinogen Concentrate Across Queensland Health.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVE**: To describe fibrinogen concentrate (FC) supply across Queensland Health.

**METHODS**: Statewide FC supply from January 2016 to September 2026 was analysed by service type, geography, major trauma designation, viscoelastic haemostatic assay (VHA) availability and temporal trends.

**RESULTS**: Of 24,717 g FC supplied, 97.0% was distributed to 54 hospitals, 2.0% to retrieval services and 1.0% to ambulance services. Of hospital supply, 25.4% reached regional and 6.1% remote/very remote hospitals; 66.2% was supplied to major trauma services and 92.9% to VHA-capable hospitals. Population-adjusted FC supply increased from 8.19 to 59.2 g per 100,000 population between 2016 and 2025.

**CONCLUSION**: FC supply has increased substantially across Queensland, extending to regional, remote and prehospital services. This highlights the value of statewide patient-level utilisation data for haemovigilance.

articles.title: Synovial fluid biomarker changes after acute anterior cruciate ligament injury: comparison with primary osteoarthritis as a biological comparator.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUNDS**: Post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA) typically develops 10-20 years after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury, but reliable early biomarkers are lacking. We examined synovial fluid biomarker changes in patients with acute ACL injury (PTOA-risk group) and in patients with primary OA. The primary OA group served as a biological comparator representing established degenerative OA, not as a healthy or matched control.

**METHODS**: Our study included patients from January 1, 2021 to September 30, 2023: 51 with primary OA biological comparator and 53 with acute ACL injury (PTOA-risk group). Levels of Interleukin (IL)-1β, sulfated glycosaminoglycans (sGAG), aggrecan neoepitope fragment (ARGS-aggrecan), and cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP) were measured in synovial fluid and compared between the two groups at baseline and one year later. Patients underwent unilateral knee MRI and bilateral weight-bearing radiography at follow-up.

**RESULTS**: The findings demonstrated that synovial fluid from acute ACL injury (PTOA-risk group) and primary OA biological comparator contained inflammatory mediators, collagen markers, and aging-related indicators such as CRP. Following one year of surgical follow-up, PCT, GAG, CTxI, osteocalcin, β-aspartate, and COMP all showed significant decreases. Biomarker comparisons between groups revealed that the primary OA biological comparator had significantly lower levels of CRP, GAG, ARGS, BMP2, FGF-10, and ADAM-TS5 than the ACL-injured (PTOA-risk) group, while CTX-II showed no discernible difference. The Spearman rank correlation was used to examine synovial fluid biomarker concentrations relative to injury duration. Significant time-dependence was observed for: IL-1b (p = 0.025, Rs=-0.112), GAG (p = 0.011, Rs=-0.265), ARGS aggrecan (p = 0.032, Rs=-0.021), C1,2 C (p = 0.002, Rs=0.665), CTxI (p = 0.025, Rs=0.251), C2C (p = 0.011, Rs=0.055), CPII (p = 0.015, Rs=0.336), Osteocalcin (p = 0.029, Rs=0.114), β-aspartate (p = 0.001, Rs=-0.77), D-Asx (p = 0.0215, Rs=-0.425), MMP-3 (p = 0.0201, Rs=0.356), and WOMAC (p = 0.001, Rs=0.264). Univariate regression analysis demonstrated significant associations of IL-1β and osteocalcin with ACL-injured (PTOA-risk) group membership. Multivariate logistic regression revealed significant associations with increased levels of β-aspartate, WOMAC, GAG, IL-1β, and osteocalcin. LASSO regression analysis was employed as an exploratory feature selection method to identify the biomarker panel that best distinguished between the ACL-injured (PTOA-risk) group and primary OA biological comparators within this cohort. Among the 20 variables included in the analysis, five demonstrated non-zero coefficients in the LASSO model: WOMAC, GAG, β-aspartate, IL-1β, and osteocalcin. These findings suggest that inflammatory markers, matrix turnover products, and functional status are prominent features differentiating the acute post-injury state from chronic degenerative OA in this dataset. However, given the exploratory nature of this analysis and the lack of external validation, these results should be interpreted with caution and require confirmation in independent cohorts.

**CONCLUSION**: Our findings demonstrate that patients with acute ACL injury (PTOA-risk group) exhibit distinct synovial fluid molecular signatures compared with a primary OA biological comparator. These signatures encompass acute inflammatory responses and early matrix remodeling. However, this study cannot explain why only approximately 18.8% of ACL-injured patients later develop PTOA. Future longitudinal studies including ACL-injured non-progressors and age-, sex-, and activity-matched controls are required.

articles.title: Direct ICU admission versus floor-to-ICU upgrade in geriatric patients with multiple rib fractures and flail chest: A national analysis.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: It remains unclear whether direct ICU admission benefits geriatric patients compared with delayed floor-to-ICU upgrade. The study evaluated the association of direct ICU admission versus floor-to-ICU upgrade with clinical outcomes in geriatric trauma patients with flail chest and thoracic injury, stratified by oxygenation compromise, frailty, and rib fracture burden.

**METHODS**: This retrospective cohort study used the 2017-2024 ACS-TQIP-PUF to identify patients aged 65 years or older with blunt trauma, flail chest, at least three rib fractures, an Injury Severity Score of 9 or greater, and thoracic injury. Patients were classified as floor admission without ICU upgrade, direct ICU admission, or floor-to-ICU upgrade. The primary adjusted analysis compared direct ICU admission with floor-to-ICU upgrade, using floor-to-ICU upgrade as the reference group.

**RESULTS**: A total of 6743 patients were included.
