Mortality did not differ significantly between direct ICU admission and floor-to-ICU upgrade in the primary adjusted analysis (aOR 0.732, 95% CI 0.467-1.148, p = 0.174). Direct ICU admission was associated with lower odds of unplanned intubation (aOR 0.355, 95% CI 0.251-0.502, p < 0.001), ARDS (aOR 0.412, 95% CI 0.172-0.987, p = 0.047), sepsis (aOR 0.352, 95% CI 0.171-0.725, p = 0.005), and DVT (aOR 0.444, 95% CI 0.209-0.942, p = 0.034). Mortality was lower with direct ICU admission among patients with 3-5 documented rib fractures (aOR 0.535, 95% CI 0.296-0.969, p = 0.039), and the association with fewer unplanned intubations persisted across all subgroups. In the secondary analysis, both direct ICU admission and floor-to-ICU upgrade were associated with higher mortality, lower odds of discharge home, and fewer ventilator-free days than floor admission without ICU upgrade.

**CONCLUSION**: Direct ICU admission was associated with lower odds of unplanned intubation, ARDS, sepsis, and DVT compared with floor-to-ICU upgrade. These findings support identifying at-risk geriatric rib fracture patients for direct ICU admission before deterioration occurs.

articles.title: Predicting survival in pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: Development and internal validation of risk scores.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) in the pediatric population is associated with poor survival and neurological outcomes. We aimed to develop and internally validate risk scores to predict survival to discharge in pediatric OHCA patients.

**METHODS**: We included pediatric OHCA patients in the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival from 2013 to 2023. We used logistic regression (LR) and classification and regression trees (CART) to develop risk scores using 70% of the data and validated them using the remaining 30% of the data. We used discrimination and predictive accuracy to evaluate model performance.

**RESULTS**: We included 26,895 pediatric patients, of whom 27.8% survived to hospital admission and 11.9% survived to hospital discharge. We developed three separate risk scores for i) infants ii) preschool and school-age children, and iii) adolescents. The most important predictor variables were gender, arrest location, witness status, etiology of arrest, bystander CPR, use of prehospital AED, and first rhythm. Models developed using both LR and CART approaches had good classification accuracy (AUROCC for LR: 0.81, 0.77 and 0.82, AUROCC for CART: 0.78, 0.76, 0.82 for the three age groups) However, we found CART models to be the most useful because they are simpler to follow, classified more patients in low and high survival categories using a smaller number of predictors. The average survival probability in infants for each risk group was 3%, 13%, and 33%, for preschool and school-age children it was 4%, 11%, and 29%, whereas for adolescents it was 4%, 13%, and 48% for the low, moderate, and high survival categories.

**CONCLUSION**: Pediatric patients experiencing OHCA can be classified into low, moderate, and high survival categories using a simple risk score and easily identified prehospital variables. These risk scores can facilitate research, monitor the quality of medical services and can potentially support clinical decision-making.

articles.title: Integration of multimodal large language models into point-of-care ultrasound documentation: A pilot study.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: There are no studies evaluating the potential to deploy artificial intelligence in the interpretation of cardiac point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) documentation. Telexy Health developed an image interpretation and documentation system using multimodal model extensions with video capabilities (MLLM) and deployed it on the POCUS manager QpathE. This study evaluated the MLLM's agreement to experts in identifying cardiac POCUS views and interpreting normal and abnormal examinations.

**METHODS**: This was a retrospective pilot study using cardiac POCUS studies stored in QPathE. The MLLM was applied to POCUS examinations until 350 examinations were reached, 100 normal, and 250 with pathology. MLLM view identification and interpretation were recorded using Qualtrics, with expert image review serving as the gold standard.

**RESULTS**: The MLLM was applied to 370 examinations, with 20 failures. View identification agreed with expert review in 151 examinations (43.1%). Cohen's kappa showed fair agreement for apical four-chamber views between expert and MLLM, with moderate agreement for parasternal long axis, parasternal short axis, subxiphoid, and inferior vena cava views. The MLLM agreed with expert interpretation 86 of 100 normal examinations; the agreement varied by pathology with pericardial effusion, ejection fraction, aortic outflow tract, chamber size, and inferior vena cava having an agreement of 8%, 4%, 70%, 0%, and 12% respectively.

**CONCLUSION**: While agreement in image interpretation was poor, this vendor agnostic workflow demonstrated the ability to integrate an MLLM model into image interpretation. While it should not be incorporated into clinical practice in this state, future model improvement may enable automated POCUS interpretation and documentation.

articles.title: Emergency Response and Patient Transport in Remote Indigenous Communities: A Scoping Review.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: Prehospital and inter-facility transport, such as air medical retrieval and pre-birth evacuation, often move Indigenous patients in rural and remote settings out of their communities, where care is already shaped by fragmented funding and structural inequities; no review has mapped these pathways globally. This scoping review mapped evidence on prehospital emergency response and patient transport for this population.

**METHODS**: A librarian-assisted PubMed, Embase, and Scopus search was conducted for English-language publications on March 9, 2026. Eligible studies included an explicit rural Indigenous population with a defined prehospital pathway. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts and assessed full texts, and a third reviewer resolved disagreements. Data were charted using a standardized form and synthesized descriptively.

**RESULTS**: Across eight countries, 76 studies met the inclusion criteria, primarily from Australia (

**CONCLUSIONS**: The published evidence disproportionately described transporting patients out of their communities. Community first response and tele-support were described more often than their standing in the literature suggests; however, they were rarely evaluated, and Indigenous-led governance of the research itself was reported in 7% of publications. Low reporting frequency does not establish that these models are uncommon in application and practice. Future priorities include community-partnered evaluation of community-based capacity and telehealth-supported care, alongside the development of patient and family cultural safety.

articles.title: Navigating Uncertainty: 2026 AAST Presidential Address.
Global, Regional, and National Burden of Head Injuries and Main Causes, 1990-2021: A Systematic Analysis of the Global Burden of Disease Study With Projections to 2050.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES**: We report the global, regional, and national burden of head injuries and their principal causes from 1990 to 2021, with projections to 2050.

**METHODS**: In the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021, "head injuries" denotes the cause category "injuries to the head". We extracted age-standardized prevalence, incidence, and years lived with disability (YLDs), with absolute case counts and 95% uncertainty intervals, stratified by age, sex, year, country, and sociodemographic index; the etiological category "transport injuries" includes both motorized and nonmotorized modes. Temporal trends were assessed using the estimated annual percentage change, and projections to 2050 were generated with autoregressive integrated moving average models, with order selected by the Akaike information criterion and residual diagnostics.

**RESULTS**: In 2021, head injuries accounted globally for an estimated 37.9 million prevalent cases, 20.8 million new cases, and 5.5 million YLDs. Compared with 1990, these absolute counts had risen by 54.4%, 22.6%, and 52.7%, respectively, reflecting population growth and aging. Over the same period, age-standardized rates (ASRs) declined by 16.5% for prevalence (536.7-448.0 per 100 000), 20.2% for incidence (324.4-259.0), and 16.2% for YLDs (77.3-64.8). Transport injuries were the leading etiological contributor to YLDs (20.7%), followed by falls (9.0%). The highest age-standardized burden was observed in high-middle sociodemographic index regions and in Europe, with older adults and males disproportionately affected. Autoregressive integrated moving average projections suggest a continued decline in ASRs through 2050.

**CONCLUSION**: ASRs of head injury have declined globally between 1990 and 2021, yet absolute case numbers have continued to rise because gains in per-capita risk reduction have been outpaced by population growth and aging.

articles.title: Rapid Endovascular Hemorrhage Control in Trauma: Joint Position Statement from the American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma and the Society of Interventional Radiology.
articles.abstract: Timely hemorrhage control is a critical determinant of survival after traumatic injury, and advances in transarterial embolization have made rapid access to endovascular intervention an increasingly important component of contemporary trauma care. This joint position statement from the American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma and the Society of Interventional Radiology clarifies expectations for interventional radiology under ACS Verification, Review, and Consultation Program Standard 4.15 and provides practical guidance for integrating endovascular hemorrhage control into trauma centers. Standard 4.15 reflects a requirement for system readiness rather than a universal mandate that every vascular intervention begin within 60 minutes. Rapid intervention is expected when clinically indicated, particularly for patients with an endovascular target who are hemodynamically labile, and the relevant performance interval is the time from a shared decision by trauma surgery and interventional radiology to proceed with intervention to arterial puncture. Trauma centers should establish multidisciplinary activation pathways that enable rapid mobilization of personnel and resources while preserving clinical judgment regarding patient selection and competing priorities. Recommended strategies include standardized activation protocols, process mapping, parallel rather than sequential workflows, early patient transport when appropriate, documentation of key time points, structured debriefing, and continuous performance monitoring. Interventional radiologists should be integrated as essential members of multidisciplinary trauma teams rather than engaged late as procedural consultants. Applying the 60-minute expectation according to clinical urgency and monitoring decision-to-puncture time focuses Standard 4.15 on its intended objectives: institutional readiness, timely definitive hemorrhage control in appropriately selected high-risk patients, and continuous performance improvement.

articles.title: Prehospital Extracorporeal Life Support in Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: In patients with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) with the use of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation can be performed to establish reperfusion. Data comparing prehospital ECPR with conventional care regarding survival until hospital discharge among patients who are 50 years of age or younger with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest are limited.

**METHODS**: In a nationwide, nonrandomized study conducted in the Netherlands, we evaluated the outcomes in young adults who were attended by Helicopter Emergency Medical Services (HEMS) that were equipped to deliver prehospital ECPR (intervention group) as compared with those attended by HEMS without ECPR capability (conventional group). The primary outcome was survival until hospital discharge.

**RESULTS**: A total of 144 patients were included in the intervention group, and 87 were included in the conventional group. In the intervention group, 57 of 144 patients (40%) survived until hospital discharge, as compared with 17 of 87 patients (20%) in the conventional group (odds ratio, 2.72; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.59 to 4.66; P = 0.002). At 6 months, a favorable neurologic outcome was reported in 51 of 141 patients (36%) in the intervention group and in 11 of 85 patients (13%) in the conventional group (odds ratio, 4.22; 95% CI, 2.82 to 6.32). There were 32 adverse events in the intervention group and 11 in the conventional group.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Among patients who were 50 years of age or younger with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, incorporating ECPR into HEMS was associated with improved survival until hospital discharge, as compared with conventional care. (Funded by the Dutch Ministry of Health; OnScene ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04620070.).

articles.title: Laparoscopic approach for emergency colon resection: a retrospective propensity score-matched study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Despite its routine use in elective procedures, the role of laparoscopy in emergency colorectal surgery remains debated due to limited evidence. This study compared laparoscopic and open surgery regarding complications, mortality, and hospital stay following emergency colon operations.

**METHODS**: This retrospective study included adult patients treated at Päijät-Häme Central Hospital between 2010 and 2020 who underwent emergency colon resection. Propensity score matching was used to adjust for comorbidities, prior ICU admission, surgical indication, and contamination between laparoscopic and open surgery groups.

**RESULTS**: All together 484 patients had an emergency colorectal resection of which 85 (17.6%) were carried out laparoscopically, 31 (6.4%) were converted and 377 (76.0%) were open. In the whole cohort, Comprehensive complication index was lower among laparoscopy patients than open surgery patients if intraoperative conversion to open surgery was avoided (25.8 vs. 34.9, p = 0.012). The subgroup analysis also showed lower CCI after laparoscopic resection for patients presented with obstruction (21.3 vs. 29.7, p = 0.046) or colorectal cancer (21.1 vs. 29.4, p = 0.020) A multivariable regression analysis also showed that starting the procedure laparoscopically predicted lower complication rates. Patients who had a laparoscopic resection also had shorter hospital stay (9.0 vs. 12.9 days, p < 0.001). Patients with open surgery had significantly more wound complications (10.3% vs. 1.2%, p = 0.010). Open surgery was also an independent risk factor for higher CCI (p = 0.008) and the need for intensive care (p = 0.027). Mortality was similar regardless of the approach in short term (30 days, p = 0.810; 90 days, p = 0.354) and in long-term survival (p = 0.466).

**CONCLUSIONS**: The laparoscopic technique in colorectal emergencies may offer similar benefits as in elective surgery, with a lower burden of total complications, less wound complications and shorter hospital stay. Laparoscopy was not associated with any unexpected harmful events.

articles.title: Association of tranexamic acid with early death or massive transfusion after severe pelvic ring fractures: A nationwide registry-based cohort study.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: Evidence for tranexamic acid during emergency treatment of severe pelvic ring fractures is limited. We examined its association with early death or massive transfusion.

**METHODS**: We studied adults in the Japan Trauma Data Bank from 2019 to 2023 with blunt pelvic ring fractures of Abbreviated Injury Scale severity 3 or higher. Exposure was any in-hospital tranexamic acid. The primary outcome was death within 24 h after arrival or transfusion of at least 20 Japanese red blood cell units within 24 h after injury. We used multiple imputation, propensity-score overlap weighting, and hospital-clustered standard errors.

**RESULTS**: Among 5288 patients, 1985 (37.5%) received tranexamic acid. The weighted primary-outcome risks were 13.0% with tranexamic acid and 18.1% without it (risk ratio 0.72, 95% confidence interval 0.60-0.87). The association was driven by 24-hour mortality (risk ratio 0.62, 95% confidence interval 0.48-0.80); massive transfusion alone (risk ratio 0.94, 95% confidence interval 0.73-1.21) and mean red blood cell use did not differ. Any red blood cell transfusion was more frequent with tranexamic acid (risk ratio 1.20, 95% confidence interval 1.11-1.30). The primary-outcome risk ratio was 0.76 (0.62-0.93) after excluding deaths within 2 h and 0.81 (0.65-1.00) when both components were assessed within 24 h after injury.

**CONCLUSION**: The mortality association was not accompanied by lower transfusion requirements and weakened when outcome time origins were aligned. Because treatment timing was unavailable, these findings do not establish an independent survival benefit and provide no corroborating transfusion evidence of a pelvic-specific hemostatic benefit.

articles.title: Survival From Traumatic Cardiac Arrest After Sequential Decompression of Dual-Tension Thoracic Physiology Without Chest Compressions.
articles.abstract: Traumatic pulseless electrical activity arrest from simultaneous dual-tension thoracic physiology-bilateral tension pneumothorax and tension pneumomediastinum-with concurrent oropharyngeal hematoma causing airway obstruction has not been described as a unified presentation in the published literature. We report a 28-year-old male who sustained penetrating machete injuries producing this presentation and arrested in pulseless electrical activity on arrival. A sequential surgical resuscitation was performed without external chest compressions: hemostasis and evacuation of an oropharyngeal hematoma restored ventilation, with return of peripheral photoplethysmographic signal consistent with pseudo-pulseless electrical activity physiology; bilateral finger thoracostomies achieved pleural decompression; digital exploration through the manubrial wound vented tension pneumomediastinum, producing an audible air rush, immediate resolution of jugular venous distension, and confirmed return of spontaneous circulation. The patient ambulated independently within hours of arrest and was discharged neurologically intact on day 7. This case illustrates that mechanically mediated pulseless electrical activity arrest from dual thoracic obstructive physiology may be reversible by sequential surgical decompression, and that persistent jugular venous distension following pleural decompression may signal residual mediastinal tension warranting urgent decompression.

articles.title: Administered opioids and benzodiazepines and the interpretation of positive trauma urine drug screens.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Urine drug screening (UDS) is routine in trauma care, and results populate trauma registries, quality review, and research. Trauma patients receive opioids and benzodiazepines before urine is collected, so a positive class-matched screen may reflect administered drug rather than pre-injury use. We estimated the magnitude of this effect by drug class and its impact on reported prevalence.

**METHODS**: Retrospective cohort of all trauma patients at a Level II center, 2023-2024 (n = 2538), of whom 1420 (55.9%) underwent UDS. Medication administration was matched to the corresponding immunoassay channel, with fentanyl analyzed against its dedicated assay and opiate-assay-matched opioid against the opiate assay. Logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, Injury Severity Score, activation, intubation, and substance use disorder. Treatment-associated positives were estimated by g-computation with bootstrap confidence intervals; cannabinoids, amphetamines, and cocaine were negative controls.

**RESULTS**: Class-matched positivity greatly exceeded unexposed positivity: 70.0% versus 12.5% for the fentanyl assay (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 15.3, 95% CI 11.5-20.4), 59.0% versus 19.0% for the opiate assay given an opiate-assay-matched opioid (aOR 5.9), and 51.6% versus 8.9% for benzodiazepines (aOR 6.1). Restricting exposure to pre-hospital administration, which necessarily precedes collection, preserved the effect (fentanyl aOR 19.9). Negative controls showed minimal association (amphetamine aOR 1.1). By g-computation, an estimated 62.8% (56.9-68.6) of fentanyl-assay positives, 33.7% of opiate positives, and 29.3% of benzodiazepine positives were associated with administered drug. Any-positive prevalence was 64.4% overall and 37.3% among patients given neither class.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Administered fentanyl was associated with a model-estimated majority of positive fentanyl-assay screens; administered opiates and benzodiazepines were associated with smaller shares of their corresponding positive screens. Class-matched results should be interpreted alongside the medication record. These findings do not establish the source or analytical validity of an individual positive result.

articles.title: Does greater orthoplastic integration reduce deep infection after open tibial fracture? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVE**: Combined orthoplastic management of open tibial fractures is widely recommended, but existing evidence has not quantified whether the degree of care-pathway integration, beyond a binary orthoplastic-versus-orthopaedic distinction, is associated with a graded difference in outcome. This systematic review and meta-analysis quantified deep infection and secondary outcome rates across four care-pathway models of increasing team continuity.

**METHODS**: MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and grey literature were searched in collaboration with a specialist medical librarian. Studies were classified into four care-pathway groups: Group 1, single-setting simultaneous fixation and soft tissue coverage; Group 2, staged care with continuous orthoplastic team involvement; Group 3, discontinuous or delayed plastic surgical involvement; Group 4, purely orthopaedic management. Random-effects meta-analysis pooled deep infection, limb salvage, reoperation, and non-union rates per group. Comparative meta-analyses used genuine within-study comparator arms. Confounding was assessed via meta-regression and subgroup analysis. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I and certainty of evidence was rated using GRADE.

**RESULTS**: Fifty-eight studies (81 classified arms) were included. Pooled deep infection rates rose progressively with decreasing care-pathway integration: 8% (95% CI 5-12%) in Group 1, 16% (9-24%) in Group 2, 28% (11-49%) in Group 3, and 37% (25-50%) in Group 4. A similar gradient was observed for non-union (4-26% across groups). Limb salvage was near-universal (94-99%) and did not discriminate between pathways. Leave-one-out and sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness for Groups 1, 2, and 4; Group 3's estimate was substantially influenced by a single Critical-risk-of-bias study, with deep infection rates attenuating from 28% to 23% on exclusion. No significant publication bias was detected. Certainty of evidence, per GRADE, was Very Low for majority of the pooled estimates, reflecting serious risk of bias and inconsistency, and Low where heterogeneity was minimal.

**CONCLUSION**: Progressive care-pathway integration is associated with a consistent, graded reduction in deep infection and non-union risk following open tibial fracture, independent of injury mechanism. These findings support continued investment in combined orthoplastic care, including partial integration models where single-setting surgery is not achievable.

articles.title: Osteoporosis treatment gaps and risk of recurrent hip fracture following initial fragility fracture: Insights from over one million cases.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: Patients who sustain a hip fracture are at high risk of a second hip fracture, yet most do not receive osteoporosis pharmacotherapy. We evaluated the association between bone-health medication initiation after a first hip fracture and the risk of a second hip fracture.

**METHODS**: This retrospective cohort study used Epic Cosmos, a de-identified multi-institutional electronic health record database. Adults who underwent surgery for a first femoral neck, intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric hip fracture were classified as having no bone-health medication, as baseline users (medication documented at admission), or as initiators within six months of the index fracture. Second hip fracture was assessed over fixed 1-, 2- and 5-year horizons. We estimated absolute risks, cumulative incidence accounting for death as a competing risk, and multivariable cause-specific Cox proportional hazards models.

**RESULTS**: Overall, 1,051,020 patients were eligible for the 5-year analysis: 705,059 (67.1%) had no medication, 83,452 (7.9%) were baseline users and 262,509 (25.0%) initiated medication within six months. Five-year cumulative incidence of second hip fracture was 17.2% (95% confidence interval [CI] 17.1-17.3) with no medication, 14.1% (95% CI 13.8-14.4) among baseline users and 8.9% (95% CI 8.8-9.1) among initiators. In adjusted models, the hazard of second hip fracture was lower among baseline users (hazard ratio [HR] 0.71, 95% CI 0.69-0.73) and initiators (HR 0.38, 95% CI 0.37-0.39) than among patients with no medication.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Initiation of bone-health medication within six months of a first hip fracture was associated with a lower risk of a second hip fracture. Baseline users had intermediate risk, which may reflect confounding by indication, agent selection or adherence. These findings support early, coordinated post-fracture osteoporosis treatment; the observational design precludes causal inference.

articles.title: Aspirin is safe and effective for prevention of deep vein thrombosis following acetabular fracture surgery.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Patients with acetabular fractures are at significant risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE), yet the optimal chemoprophylactic agent remains undefined. Emerging evidence from elective arthroplasty and general orthopaedic trauma populations suggests that aspirin (ASA) may be a safe and effective alternative to traditional anticoagulants. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of ASA compared to other anticoagulants for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prevention following acetabular fracture surgery.

**METHODS**: A retrospective cohort analysis was performed using a global, web-based health research network that provides on-demand access to de-identified, real-world data from electronic health records and claims. Adult patients (≥18 years) who underwent surgical treatment for acetabular fractures between January 2014 and December 2025 and received VTE prophylaxis within 14 days of surgery were identified. Patients were stratified into ASA (n = 1189) and other anticoagulant (n = 5478) cohorts. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed to balance baseline characteristics, yielding 1174 patients per cohort. Rates and odds of DVT, emergency department (ED) visits, deep infection, stroke, and readmission were assessed at 14-, 30-, and 90-day postoperative intervals. Temporal trends in VTE prophylaxis utilization were also analyzed.

**RESULTS**: Compared to other anticoagulants, ASA was associated with significantly lower odds of DVT at 14 days (1.11% vs. 2.22%; odds ratio [OR]: 0.494; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.253-0.967; P = 0.036), 30 days (1.45% vs. 2.73%; OR: 0.524; 95% CI: 0.290-0.950; P = 0.030), and 90 days (2.56% vs. 4.34%; OR: 0.577; 95% CI: 0.365-0.913; P = 0.018). ASA was also associated with significantly lower odds of ED visits at 90 days (OR: 0.741; 95% CI: 0.570-0.963; P = 0.024). There were no significant differences in deep infection, stroke, or readmission rates. ASA utilization increased from 7.2% in 2014-39.5% in 2025.

**CONCLUSIONS**: ASA is safe and effective for DVT prevention following acetabular fracture surgery and is associated with fewer ED visits compared to other anticoagulants. These findings support the growing adoption of ASA as a VTE prophylactic agent in the acetabular fracture population.

articles.title: Surgical anatomy of the Over-the-Rectus Extrapelvic (OREX) approach defines safe zones for W-plate fixation of the anterior pelvic ring.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: To define the procedure-specific surgical anatomy of the pre-symphyseal region relevant to W-plate fixation by characterizing the soft-tissue layers, identifying critical neurovascular structures, and defining quantitative safe zones for dissection and plate placement.

**METHODS**: Fresh-frozen adult cadavers underwent standardized low Pfannenstiel dissections reproducing the Over-the-Rectus Extrapelvic (OREX) exposure required for W-plate fixation. Pre-symphyseal soft-tissue layers were sequentially dissected from the skin to the anterior pubic symphysis. The locations of critical neurovascular structures relative to the pubic midline and pubic tubercles were recorded, together with anatomical layers, dimensions of the prepubic ligamentous-aponeurotic complex, soft-tissue thickness, sex-related anatomical differences, and surgical safe zones.

**RESULTS**: Three reproducible anatomical layers were identified in ten specimens. The superficial layer contained the pre-symphyseal fat pad and superficial epigastric vessels. The intermediate layer contained the spermatic cord or round ligament, ilioinguinal and genitofemoral nerves, and suprapubic artery, with these critical structures located at a mean distance of approximately 3.2 cm from the midline. The deep layer was consistently formed by the Pyramidalis-anterior pubic Ligament-Adductor longus Complex (PLAC), which covered the anterior pubic symphysis and measured a mean of 4.6 × 3.1 cm. No critical neurovascular structure crossed the central trajectory corresponding to W-plate placement. Female specimens demonstrated greater preperitoneal soft-tissue thickness, whereas lateral surgical safe zones were narrower in male specimens.

**CONCLUSION**: The pre-symphyseal region demonstrated a reproducible three-layer surgical anatomy with a predictable distribution of critical neurovascular structures. Quantitative anatomic mapping defined procedure-specific safe zones for extrapelvic W-plate fixation and provided practical guidancefor surgical exposure, implant positioning, and avoidance of iatrogenic injury.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Level IV, therapeutic study.

articles.title: Common acetabular fracture patterns in patients with femoroacetabular impingement.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: The incidence of acetabular fractures is rising, affecting both younger and elderly patient populations. Developmental abnormalities such as femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) and hip dysplasia alter hip biomechanics, potentially predisposing younger patients to fracture. FAI, resulting from a cam and/or pincer deformity, is common, affecting 25% of asymptomatic males and 5% of asymptomatic females, and has been linked to hip pain and early osteoarthritis. However, the relationship between FAI morphology and acetabular fracture pattern remains unclear.

**METHODS**: Patients, 18-55 years old, treated between 2005 and 2023 for acetabular fracture, hip dislocation, or femoral head fracture were reviewed for FAI morphology using the Judet and Letournel classification systems. Statistical comparisons were conducted using Fisher's exact tests and unpaired t-tests, with significance set at p < 0.05.

**RESULTS**: A total of 294 patients (72%) exhibited plain radiographic FAI morphology, while 115 (28%) served as controls. The most common fracture pattern in both groups was posterior wall (PW) fractures (23.1% FAI, 31.3% control). Male FAI patients were significantly more likely to experience transverse fractures (p = 0.032, OR=4.6) and posterior column plus PW fractures (p = 0.035, OR=2.5) than controls. Among FAI patients, posterior column fractures were significantly more likely to occur in females (p = 0.011, OR=19). A total of 31 (27.0%) control patients and 63 (21.4%) FAI patients experienced complications.

**CONCLUSIONS**: In our data set, FAI patients accounted for 72% of patients undergoing acetabular fracture ORIF. FAI patients most commonly sustained posterior wall fractures, but male FAI patients had a significantly higher rate of transverse and posterior column plus PW. FAI patients experienced a complication rate of 21.4% compared to 27.0% in non-FAI patients.

articles.title: Robotic navigation-assisted versus conventional freehand placement of the infra-acetabular screw in acetabular fracture surgery: A retrospective comparative study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: The infra-acetabular screw (IAS) is an important component of fixation constructs for complex acetabular fractures, but accurate freehand placement is technically demanding, and evidence on robotic navigation-assisted IAS placement remains limited. This study compared robotic navigation-assisted (RA) and conventional fluoroscopic freehand (CF) IAS placement in acetabular fracture surgery.

**METHODS**: In this retrospective study, 53 patients with acetabular fractures who underwent IAS fixation between June 2022 and July 2024 were included, 28 underwent RA placement using the HoloSight robotic navigation system and 25 underwent CF placement. The primary outcome was screw-placement accuracy, graded on postoperative CT according to the Lonstein criteria. Secondary outcomes included the number of guide-wire adjustments, fluoroscopy frequency, IAS insertion time, total operative time, intraoperative blood loss, fracture reduction quality, hip function, and complications.

**RESULTS**: The grade 0 (no cortical penetration) rate was higher in the RA group than in the CF group (96.4% [27/28] vs. 60.0% [15/25], p = 0.005). RA placement was associated with fewer guide-wire adjustments (0.07 ± 0.26 vs. 3.60 ± 1.15), fewer fluoroscopies (9.32 ± 1.66 vs. 21.28 ± 3.18), shorter IAS insertion time (10.36 ± 2.50 vs. 26.68 ± 4.11 min), shorter total operative time (134.54 ± 15.46 vs. 155.80 ± 18.48 min), and less intraoperative blood loss (468.21 ± 84.68 vs. 588.40 ± 80.76 mL) (all p < 0.001). The mean follow-up duration was 15.7 ± 2.0 months (range, 13-22 months). Reduction quality, hip function, and complication rates did not differ significantly between the two groups.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Robotic navigation-assisted IAS placement was associated with significantly higher screw-placement accuracy and greater procedural efficiency than the conventional freehand technique, without compromising fracture reduction quality, hip function, or safety.

articles.title: Risk factors for complications following surgical fixation of pelvic ring fractures: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Surgical fixation of pelvic ring fractures carries a substantial risk of postoperative complications, particularly surgical site infection, yet the relative contribution of fracture pattern and associated soft tissue injury to this risk remains incompletely defined.

**OBJECTIVE**: To describe the rate and spectrum of complications following surgical fixation of pelvic ring fractures and to identify factors independently associated with these complications, with particular attention to acute surgical site infection.

**METHODS**: Retrospective, single-center cohort study of 126 patients who underwent surgical fixation of pelvic ring fractures between December 2014 and November 2024, reported in accordance with the STROBE statement. Candidate demographic, injury-related, and treatment-related exposures were compared against a composite primary outcome (any postoperative complication) and against acute infection using Fisher's exact test, Pearson chi-square test, the Mann-Whitney U test, and multivariable logistic regression.

**RESULTS**: Overall, 39 of 126 patients (31.0%) experienced at least one postoperative complication; chronic pain (22.2%) and acute surgical site infection (16.7%) were the most frequent individual components. In bivariate analysis, the presence of a Morel-Lavallée lesion at baseline was significantly associated with both the composite outcome (OR 12.65, 95% CI 1.42-112.27, p = 0.011) and acute infection (OR 12.12, 95% CI 2.06-71.37, p = 0.007); Young-Burgess fracture pattern was also associated with infection (p = 0.018). After multivariable adjustment for infection, a Morel-Lavallée lesion (adjusted OR 17.69, 95% CI 2.46-126.95, p = 0.004) and combined-mechanism fracture pattern (adjusted OR 8.25 versus anteroposterior compression, 95% CI 1.91-35.58, p = 0.005) remained independently associated with infection. Neither the presence, technique, nor surgical approach of posterior ring fixation was associated with any complication type, and time from injury to definitive fixation (median 13 days) showed no significant association with either outcome.

**CONCLUSION**: A Morel-Lavallée lesion identified at initial evaluation was associated with postoperative complications in bivariate analysis and, together with a combined-mechanism fracture pattern, remained an independent predictor of surgical site infection after multivariable adjustment. No statistically significant association was identified between posterior fixation technique and complication risk.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: III, retrospective cohort study.

articles.title: Long-term functional and orthopaedic outcomes in patients with severe pelvic ring injury requiring REBOA: A two-center matched cohort study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) is used for life-threatening hemorrhage, but evidence has largely focused on acute outcomes. Long-term functional and orthopaedic outcomes among survivors treated with REBOA remain poorly characterized.

**METHODS**: This retrospective two-center matched cohort included 98 adults with severe, hemodynamically unstable pelvic ring injuries who survived at least 24 h; hospital survivors required at least 12 months of follow-up. Forty-nine REBOA-treated patients were matched 1:1 to 49 non-REBOA patients by major Young-Burgess category, Injury Severity Score, and age. The primary outcome was functional status among hospital survivors, categorized as good/fair/poor. Deep surgical site infection (SSI) after definitive pelvic fixation was the key secondary outcome, and nonunion was exploratory. Main models used a propensity-score linear predictor based on age, Injury Severity Score, initial systolic blood pressure, and lactate.

**RESULTS**: Seventy-five patients survived hospitalization (30 REBOA; 45 non-REBOA); median follow-up was 19 months. Good/fair/poor outcomes were 16.7%/46.7%/36.7% in REBOA survivors and 51.1%/37.8%/11.1% in non-REBOA survivors. REBOA exposure was associated with worse functional status after adjustment (common odds ratio [cOR], 3.14; 95% CI, 1.11-8.92; P = 0.032). Among 68 definitive-fixation survivors, deep SSI occurred in 44.0% versus 9.3% (adjusted OR, 7.01; 95% CI, 1.88-31.07; P = 0.003); all observed events occurred within 60 days. Nonunion occurred in 26.7% versus 6.7% (adjusted OR, 9.09; 95% CI, 2.00-53.71; P = 0.004). Sensitivity analyses for deep SSI were directionally consistent.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Among hospital survivors, REBOA exposure was associated with poorer long-term functional recovery and a higher burden of deep SSI. Nonunion was more frequent but remained exploratory. These findings characterize a high-risk orthopaedic survivor phenotype but do not establish a direct causal effect of REBOA.

articles.title: The prevalence of mental health service use after long-term minor-to-moderate motor vehicle crash injury: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Minor to moderate motor vehicle crash (MVC) injuries can lead to persistent psychological distress, yet evidence regarding mental health service (MHS) use is limited. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence and characterise the determinants of MHS use after minor to moderate MVC injury.

**METHODS**: This retrospective cohort study examined Australians with work-related, MVC injuries and workers' compensation claims exceeding 24 months duration. Claims and services data were linked with healthcare records to capture MHS use before and after injury. The injured group was divided into severity sub-groups based on hospital admission status (hospitalised, non-hospitalised). A community comparator group was matched to the non-hospitalised group based on gender and injury year. The primary outcome was MHS period prevalence within 24 months. Determinants of MHS were identified through binomial logistic regression.

**RESULTS**: There were 574 non-hospitalised, 293 hospitalised, and 8294 community comparators included in the study cohort. The prevalence of MHS use at 24 months post injury was highest for the hospitalised group (36.9%), followed by the non-hospitalised group (31.5%) and community comparators (13.5%). The non-hospitalised group had 3.14 times greater odds (95% CI 2.53, 3.88) of MHS use compared to community comparators, and had the highest prevalence of publicly-funded MHS (18.8%). Hospitalised participants (28.3%) had a higher prevalence of workers' compensation funded MHS compared to non-hospitalised participants (19.3%). The adjusted odds of MHS use were higher among females (OR 2.05 [1.42, 2.97]), and people who had used MHS in the 12 months prior to injury (OR 4.66 [2.41, 9.50]).

**CONCLUSION**: People with non-hospitalised MVC injuries had a significantly higher prevalence of MHS use compared with their matched community comparator group, and people with hospitalised MVC injuries had the highest prevalence at 24 months-follow up. The highest proportion of people assessing publicly funded MHS was by people in the non-hospitalised group. These findings highlight the ongoing mental health needs of people with minor to moderate MVC injury. Monitoring for the early post injury psychological signs and symptoms, and timely referral to MHS, could reduce psychological burden following MVC injury.

articles.title: Progressive outer midbrain lesion associated with repetitive mild traumatic brain injury: a study of 52 professional wrestlers.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVE**: Finite element modeling studies suggest that the midbrain is susceptible to mechanical strain during mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), but clinical neuroimaging characterization of midbrain alterations associated with mTBI remains limited. In 2018, the authors identified lesions on T2-weighted MRI consistently localized in the lateral midbrain tegmentum of some veteran professional Japanese wrestlers. These lesions were termed outer midbrain lesions (OMLs). This study aimed to elucidate the relationship between mTBI and OMLs.

**METHODS**: The study included 52 male Japanese professional wrestlers who underwent brain MRI examinations in 2022. An OML was defined as a lesion with a diameter ≥ 2 mm. Longitudinal changes in OMLs were examined in wrestlers who had undergone MRI before 2022. As a control group, brain MRI data from 91 patients with spinal cord injury or central poststroke pain from the authors' prior study were reviewed for the presence of OMLs. Wrestling career length was investigated as a surrogate for the period of repetitive head impact. Histories of concussion and symptomatic mTBI were reviewed from the records maintained by exclusive trainers.

**RESULTS**: OMLs were identified in 12 wrestlers (23.1%). Traumatic lesions were not observed in other parts of the brain. OMLs were identified only in wrestlers older than 40 years, whereas they were absent in the control group, even among older individuals. OMLs exhibited progressive growth over time on longitudinal MRI. The presence of OMLs was not associated with a documented history of symptomatic mTBI, but with career length. Each additional year of participation in professional wrestling was associated with a 14% increase in the prevalence of OMLs (prevalence ratio 1.14, 95% CI 1.08-1.19).

**CONCLUSIONS**: OMLs are neural structural alterations strongly suggested to be associated with repeated asymptomatic mTBI. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate the susceptibility of the midbrain to mTBI based on real-world clinical findings.

articles.title: Calculating trauma undertriage rates: Are we using the wrong formula-and the wrong definition?
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Undertriage (UT) is central to trauma center quality improvement, yet UT definitions vary, and no data-driven consensus target exists for interfacility benchmarking. We compared facility-level UT rates across four methods and assessed the impact on facility benchmarking.

**METHODS**: This retrospective study included patients aged 18 to 89 from Level I & II trauma centers in the ACS TQP Files (2021-2023). Facility-level UT was calculated using the Cribari Matrix Method (CMM), modified Cribari Matrix Method (mCMM), Standardized Triage Assessment Tool (STAT), and High-Intensity Time-Sensitive (HITS) intervention-based definition representing trauma team actions. Paired facility-level UT rates were compared across methods. To estimate benchmarking impact, we calculated within-facility rank change (higher rank = higher UT) relative to CMM.

**RESULTS**: 2,643,881 patients and 515 facilities were included. Median facility-level UT significantly differed by method: CMM 11% [interquartile range: 9-14], mCMM 60% [50-67], STAT 6% [5-8], and HITS 30% [22-40] (all P<0.001). At individual hospitals, the median range of maximum UT values between methods was 53% [44-60]. The median absolute facility rank change between the CMM method and other tools was 129 [54.5-236.5] for mCMM, 48 [17-90] for STAT, and 142 [62.5-252.5] for HITS.

**CONCLUSIONS**: These UT data highlight a concerning level of variation and uncertainty in the calculation and interpretation of a key trauma center performance metric. Until a UT definition is standardized and data-driven UT target goals established, cross-center benchmarking using UT should be interpreted cautiously and may be better suited for within-center trending.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Level III, therapeutic/care management.

articles.title: Bougie guided versus Endotracheal tube with Stylet guided intubation in critically injured patients with Difficult airway characteristics (BEST trial): randomised clinical trial.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Emergency airway management in critically injured trauma patients is frequently complicated by distorted anatomy, airway contamination, cervical spine immobilisation, and prior airway manipulation. Although bougie and stylet are commonly used adjuncts for tracheal intubation, evidence comparing their effectiveness in difficult trauma airways remains limited. We aimed to compare first-pass intubation success between bougie-guided and stylet-guided tracheal intubation in critically injured trauma patients with predefined difficult airway characteristics.

**METHODS**: In this prospective randomised clinical trial, 188 adult critically injured trauma patients requiring emergency tracheal intubation and having at least one predefined difficult airway characteristic were randomised to bougie-guided intubation (Group B, n = 94) or stylet-guided intubation (Group S, n = 94). All first-attempt intubations were performed by trauma anaesthesia senior residents using video laryngoscopy and a standardised drug-assisted delayed sequence intubation protocol. The primary outcome was first-pass intubation success. Secondary outcomes included time to intubation, rescue airway interventions, need for alternate adjunct or front-of-neck access, and peri-intubation complications.

**RESULTS**: First-pass intubation success was achieved in 67 of 94 patients (71.3%) in Group B and 63 of 94 patients (67.0%) in Group S, corresponding to an absolute difference of 4.3% points (95% CI, - 8.9 to 17.2; p = 0.53). Time to successful first-attempt intubation was similar between groups (39.55 ± 11.72 s in Group B versus 37.97 ± 13.54 s in Group S; mean difference 1.58 s, 95% CI - 2.80 to 5.97; p = 0.48). Emergency front-of-neck access was required in one patient in Group B. Oesophageal intubation occurred in five patients (5.3%) in Group S and in none in Group B; this difference did not reach statistical significance using Fisher's exact test (p = 0.059). On multivariable logistic regression, polytrauma with facial fractures was associated with increased odds of first-pass intubation failure (adjusted OR 2.54, 95% CI 1.10-5.83; p = 0.028).

**CONCLUSION**: In selected trauma patients with predefined difficult-airway characteristics undergoing protocolised delayed sequence intubation with video laryngoscopy, no statistically significant difference in first-pass success was observed between bougie-guided and stylet-guided intubation. Oesophageal intubation occurred only in the stylet group, an exploratory finding that requires confirmation in larger studies.

**TRIAL REGISTRATION**: The trial was approved by the Institute Ethics Committee (IEC-INT-2022/MD-543) and registered with the Clinical Trials Registry of India (CTRI/2022/11/047043).
articles.journal: Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med

articles.title: Development and validation of methods to predict ground- and helicopter-based emergency medical service travel times.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Helicopter-based Emergency Medical Services (EMS) are a costly and finite resource and should only be deployed when they provide substantial benefits to patients. One such benefit is a more rapid response to incidents and transport to hospital compared to Ground-based EMS. This study evaluates methods for estimating travel times for the purpose of optimizing the selection of helicopter vs. ground EMS.

**METHODS**: Ground EMS travel times were estimated using an open-source routing tool, the estimates of which were adjusted using linear regression and gradient boosting models based on historical travel times. Helicopter travel times were similarly estimated based on great circle distances adjusted by historical data. Models were evaluated using several measures of predictive accuracy to enable comparison with other studies.

**RESULTS**: In validation data collected after finalization of the methods, the best performing prediction models for Ground EMS travel times explained a substantial portion of variation in drive times to location and to hospital (R2 0.79 and 0.70 respectively), and less for helicopter flight times (R2 0.46 and 0.38 respectively). Mean average percentage error was 18-20% for all investigated estimation techniques and time intervals.

**CONCLUSION**: Integrating tools based on the open-source code provided with this study has the potential to improve the ability of dispatchers to estimate relative travel times and assess the potential time benefit of directing the most appropriate resources to a given patient.
articles.journal: Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med

articles.title: The association of ABO Rh blood groups with 30-day mortality following traumatic injury - A retrospective observational study in the East of England.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: ABO and RhD antigens are expressed on the surface of red blood cells; ABO antigens are also expressed on the surface of endothelial and some epithelial cells. Associations between ABO blood groups and disease have been reported in numerous areas of medicine. Recently there have been conflicting reports of an association between blood group O and mortality following trauma, none of which examine a combination of ABO and RhD groups. The aim of our study was to identify associations between all ABO RhD groups and trauma mortality.

**METHODS**: A retrospective analysis of trauma patients ≥ 16-years-old admitted to the East of England Major Trauma Centre, and who were included in the Trauma, Audit, & Research Network (TARN) database, 2016-2019. The primary outcome was a comparison of 30-day all-cause mortality between all eight ABO RhD groups. Secondary outcomes included injury pattern analysis on outcome.

**RESULTS**: 4188 patients were included; median age 59.3 [IQR 39.0-77.9] years old, and 2634 (62.9%) were male. The median injury severity score was 19.0 [10.0-25.0]. 30-day mortality was 9.3%, and there were significant differences in mortality across groups (p = 0.0094). O negative was associated with greater 30-day mortality compared to all other seven ABO RhD groups combined: 15.1% vs 8.8%; relative risk (RR) 1.7 (95%CI 1.3-2.2), p = 0.0002.

**CONCLUSIONS**: In this UK study we have demonstrated that blood group O negative is associated with a greater risk of 30-day all-cause mortality in undifferentiated trauma patients. Future trauma studies should consider including ABO RhD blood group as a baseline characteristic to ensure this does not confound results.

articles.title: Thoracic epidural versus paravertebral blockade for reducing chronic post-thoracotomy pain (TOPIC-2): open label, parallel group, superiority, multicentre, randomised controlled trial.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: To evaluate the effectiveness of paravertebral blockade versus thoracic epidural during the perioperative period in reducing chronic post-thoracotomy pain.

**DESIGN**: Open label, parallel group, superiority, multicentre, randomised controlled trial.

**SETTING**: 15 thoracic centres in the UK.

**PARTICIPANTS**: Adult patients undergoing thoracotomy randomised (1:1) to either paravertebral blockade or thoracic epidural using a web based service between January 2019 and September 2023.

**INTERVENTIONS**: Participants in the paravertebral group received three single-shot paravertebral injections of local anaesthetic before incision 

**MAIN OUTCOME MEASURE**: The primary outcome was incidence of chronic post-thoracotomy pain at six months after randomisation, defined as a 100 mm visual analogue score greater than or equal to 40 mm (indicating moderate pain) when considering worst chest pain over the past week. Secondary outcomes included acute pain (visual analogue score of 100 mm) and complications.

**RESULTS**: 770 patients were enrolled, of which 428 (56%) were male (mean (standard deviation, SD) age 66.6 (11.0) years). After 33 exclusions of patients after randomisation who did not proceed to thoracotomy, 737 remained in the modified intention-to-treat population (364 in the paravertebral group, 373 in the epidural group). Six months after randomisation, 59 (22%) of 272 participants in the paravertebral group and 47 (16%) of 292 participants in the epidural group developed chronic post-thoracotomy pain (adjusted risk ratio 1.32 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.93 to 1.86), adjusted risk difference 0.05 (95% CI -0.01 to 0.11), P=0.12). During the acute phase, worst and average pain was greater on day 1 with paravertebral blockade (adjusted mean difference 7.7 mm (95% CI 2.8 to 12.5 mm) and 7.0 mm (95% CI 2.7 to 11.2 mm), respectively), but no different on days 2-3. Hypotension was less common in the paravertebral group than the epidural group (12% 

**CONCLUSIONS**: Paravertebral blockade did not reduce chronic post-thoracotomy pain at six month follow-up compared to thoracic epidural. Thoracic epidural provided marginally better acute pain relief one day after the operation, but showed no difference thereafter. Postoperative complications were comparable between groups. The findings support the ongoing use of both techniques.

**TRIAL REGISTRATION**: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03677856.

articles.title: Is surgeon technique a modifiable risk factor for heterotopic ossification after posterior acetabular fracture fixation? A multi-surgeon study.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: Heterotopic ossification (HO) is a well-recognized complication following operative fixation of acetabular fractures through a posterior approach. Established risk factors largely reflect nonmodifiable patient and injury characteristics. Whether surgeon-controlled aspects of operative technique influence HO remains poorly defined. The purpose of this study was to determine if the individual surgeon and specific technique variables are associated with HO after accounting for established patient and injury factors.

**METHODS**: We retrospectively reviewed 1292 patients who underwent acetabular fracture fixation through a Kocher-Langenbeck approach at two Level 1 trauma centers between 2010 and 2025 by 14 fellowship-trained orthopaedic traumatologists. Patients receiving any form of HO prophylaxis were excluded. Four surgeon-controlled variables were examined: aggressiveness of gluteus minimus debridement, trochanteric osteotomy, thrombin gel use, and closed suction drainage. HO was graded on final radiographs by two independent reviewers using the Brooker classification, with third-reader adjudication for disagreements, and categorized as little-to-no (grade 0-I), moderate (grade II), or severe (grade III-IV). Mixed-effects logistic regression models with surgeon as a random effect were used to assess the associations between patient, injury, and surgeon-controlled technique variables, as well as the individual surgeon, with severe and moderate HO formation.

**RESULTS**: Little-to-no HO occurred in 1132 patients (87.6%), moderate HO in 96 (7.4%), and severe HO in 64 (5.0%). Aggressive gluteus minimus debridement was not associated with HO severity. For severe HO, the surgeon did not contribute meaningfully to model performance, and no surgeon-controlled technique variables were significant; severe head injury, mechanical ventilation beyond 72 h, African-American race, and dual surgical approaches were associated with severe HO. For moderate HO, the surgeon contributed moderately, and both trochanteric osteotomy (odds ratio [OR] 3.7, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.1-12) and closed suction drainage (OR 1.8, 95% CI 1.0-3.1) were associated with increased odds of moderate HO.

**CONCLUSION**: Severe HO following posterior acetabular fracture fixation is predominantly driven by patient and injury characteristics rather than surgeon technique. Aggressive gluteus minimus debridement does not appear to reduce HO risk, and prevention efforts should prioritize patient-level risk stratification.

articles.title: Association between mechanical ventilation with positive end-expiratory pressure and outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
articles.abstract:
**AIM**: The effect of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) during intermittent positive pressure ventilation in patients undergoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) on outcome is unknown. The aim of this study was to evaluate the association between the use of PEEP during cardiopulmonary resuscitation and clinical outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients.

**METHODS**: We conducted a single-centre observational cohort study using a retrospective analysis of data collected prospectively within a dedicated research registry of adult OHCA patients managed by a physician-staffed prehospital emergency medical team. All included patients were intubated and ventilated either with mechanical ventilation using PEEP or with manual ventilation without PEEP. Intratracheal pressure was continuously recorded via a catheter connected to a portable device, allowing objective verification of PEEP application and ventilation rate. The association between mechanical ventilation with PEEP use and clinical outcomes was evaluated using multivariable logistic regression adjusted for relevant confounders.

**RESULTS**: 362 patients were included, with a median age of 65 years (54-79), of whom 250 (69.1%) were male. Median ventilation rate was 15 breaths/min (10-19). Of all patients, 149 (41.2%) achieved Return Of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC) and 31 (8.6%) survived to hospital discharge. The adjusted odds ratio (OR) of mechanical ventilation with PEEP for achieving ROSC was 1.58 (95% CI 1.01-2.50, p = 0.048). The unadjusted OR of mechanical ventilation with PEEP for survival to hospital discharge was 2.22 (95% CI 1.03-4.78; p = 0.037).

**CONCLUSION**: The use of mechanical ventilation with PEEP during CPR in OHCA patients was associated with higher likelihood of ROSC.

articles.title: Calcium in trauma resuscitation: Transfusion volume or measurement-guided replacement?
PIEZO1 activation alters membrane remodeling and aggregability of stored red blood cells.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Transfused red blood cells (RBCs) actively contribute to post-injury hemostasis due to surface phosphatidylserine (PS) exposure. We hypothesized that storage sensitizes erythrocytes to the PIEZO1-induced, calcium‑dependent, PS externalization through calcium and protein kinase C (PKC) dependent activation of the phospholipid scramblase TMEM16F.

**METHODS**: Five units of type O whole blood were obtained for analysis at days 21 and 42 of storage. RBC PS was quantified by annexin V staining on flow cytometry at increasing extracellular CaCl₂ concentrations (0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 5.0 mmol/L), with and without the PIEZO1 agonist Yoda1 (0.2 μM), PKC agonist Phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA; 6 μM) and antagonist chelerythrine chloride (CC; 10 μM), and the TMEM16 family inhibitor niclosamide (2 μM). RBC aggregometry was assessed by multiplate. Data were analyzed by analysis of variance and mixed-effects modeling.

**RESULTS**: PS exposure increased in a Ca²⁺‑dependent manner in both day 21 and 42 RBCs (p<0.001). PIEZO1 stimulation enhanced this response to a greater extent in day 42 RBCs, with greater change in PS at 1 mmol/L (2.21% vs. -0.44%, p=0.021), 2 mmol/L (7.36% vs. 0.53%, p<0.001), and 5 mmol/L (12.09% vs. 6.40%, p<0.001) CaCl2. Compared with calcium alone, Yoda1 and PMA (+61.3%, p<0.001 for both) produced similar increases in PS externalization, whereas PKC inhibition (-45.6%, p=0.009) and TMEM16F inhibition (-4.6%, p=0.99) negated the PIEZO1 response. Yoda1 agonism preserved RBC aggregability after 42 days of storage (51.2±39.0 vs. 2.0±3.5 area under the curve, p<0.001).

**CONCLUSION**: Storage sensitizes RBCs to PIEZO1-mediated, calcium-dependent, PS externalization through PKC- and TMEM16F-dependent signaling. Given its endogenous mechanosensitive properties, pharmacologic PIEZO1 activation highlights a potential mechanism by which mechanical stress encountered during trauma and transfusion through the injured microcirculation may promote erythrocyte phospholipid membrane remodeling and aggregability, contributing to the procoagulant activity of transfused RBCs.

articles.title: Persistent gaps in health-related quality of life measures for older adult trauma patients: A systematic review.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Older adults experience persistent functional and psychosocial consequences after trauma, but it remains unclear whether commonly used health-related quality of life (HRQoL) instruments adequately measure recovery in this population. This systematic review appraised psychometric evidence and risk of bias for HRQoL instruments used in United States trauma cohorts that included adults aged 65 years or older.

**METHODS**: MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL were searched from inception through January 28, 2026. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Risk of bias was evaluated using an adapted Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies-of Interventions (ROBINS-I) assessment. Studies evaluating an HRQoL instrument as the target measure underwent Consensus-based Standards for the Selection of Health Measurement Instruments (COSMIN) Risk of Bias assessment for each reported measurement property. Results were rated as sufficient, insufficient, or indeterminate and synthesized by instrument.

**RESULTS**: Of 17,195 records, 19 studies were included. Studies most often examined isolated orthopedic trauma (n=7, 36.8%), spinal cord injury (n=6, 31.6%), other injury populations (n=3, 15.8%), polytrauma or systemic injury (n=2, 10.5%), and burns (n=1, 5.3%). Frequently evaluated domains included physical functioning (n=16), emotional or mental health (n=13), overall life satisfaction (n=13), social functioning (n=11), and physical symptoms (n=10). Although all studies used at least one previously developed patient-reported measure, none explicitly adapted or comprehensively validated an eligible HRQoL instrument for older adult trauma patients. Ten studies evaluated a target HRQoL instrument, contributing 33 COSMIN measurement property assessments: 19 sufficient, 10 indeterminate, and 4 insufficient. Overall risk of bias was low in six studies, moderate in eight, serious in three, and unclear in two.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Existing studies show that HRQoL instruments have been used in trauma cohorts including older adults, but they do not establish validity for older adult trauma patients specifically. Future studies should evaluate promising instruments in cohorts designed around older adults' recovery priorities and clinical characteristics after trauma.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Systematic Review; Level III.

articles.title: Blood-Based Biomarkers and Traumatic Intracranial Hypertension: A Transforming Research and Clinical Knowledge in Traumatic Brain Injury Study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES**: The role of blood-based biomarkers in guiding the acute management of patients with established traumatic brain injury is unclear. We sought to determine whether concentrations of glial fibrillary acid protein (GFAP) or ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCH-L1) on hospital day 1 are associated with intracranial pressure (ICP) and therapeutic intensity level (TIL).

**METHODS**: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Transforming Research and Clinical Knowledge in Traumatic Brain Injury data set, including patients age 17 years and older with traumatic brain injury and invasive ICP monitoring, excluding those undergoing decompressive craniectomy on admission. Patients were stratified into biomarker quartiles, and the relationships with ICP and TIL were analyzed descriptively. Multivariable linear regressions were performed to test the hypothesis that GFAP and UCH-L1 concentrations were independently associated with ICP and TIL after adjusting for a priori defined covariates.

**RESULTS**: Two hundred twenty-nine patients with a median age of 39 years (IQR 26-56) were included. Geometric mean concentrations for GFAP and UCH-L1 were 4423 and 989 pg/mL, respectively. Patients in the lowest GFAP quartile had a median of 7.3% of ICP readings >22 mm Hg vs 23.2% in the highest quartile (P < .001); secondary decompressive craniectomy was performed in 16% of the lowest quartile, compared with 39% of the highest quartile (P = .008). After adjusting for covariates, GFAP was significantly associated with ICP burden (B = 8.05, P = .014) and median TIL over 5 days (B = 1.65, P = .009). No significant relationship was seen for UCH-L1.

**CONCLUSION**: Day 1 blood concentration of GFAP is associated with elevated ICP and may be a useful adjunct when risk-stratifying patients for intracranial hypertension.

articles.title: Severity and resource utilisation among trauma patients undergoing trauma team activation in four Danish trauma units: a prospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Evidence on trauma epidemiology and outcomes largely originates from major trauma centres, while data from regional trauma units remain limited. The aim of this study was to describe the epidemiology, management, and outcomes of patients undergoing trauma team activation in the trauma units of Region Zealand, Denmark.

**METHODS**: We conducted a prospective multicentre observational study across four regional trauma units in Region Zealand, Denmark, between 1 March 2024 and 28 February 2025. All consecutive patients undergoing trauma team activation were included. Data included demographics, injury mechanisms, injury severity, in-hospital management, and mortality. Analyses were descriptive.

**RESULTS**: A total of 1611 patients were included. Median age was 38 years [IQR 20-58], and 60.5% were male. The most common injury mechanisms were traffic-related injuries (53%), falls (22%), and equestrian-related accidents (13%). Median Injury Severity Score was 1 [IQR 0-5] and 94% had Injury Severity Score < 16. Secondary transfer to a major trauma centre occurred in 3.8% of cases, and 90-day mortality was 2.6%. Trauma admissions occurred predominantly outside regular daytime workflow, with a peak in the late afternoon and early evening. Median TTA duration was 58 minutes [IQR 43-76] and CT imaging was performed in 86.7% of cases. Following trauma team activation, 55.2% of patients were discharged directly and 4.6% required intensive care unit admission.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Most patients undergoing trauma team activation in regional trauma units had minor injuries, were discharged directly from the emergency department, and infrequently required intensive care unit admission or secondary transfer. Despite this, trauma team activation had a median duration around one hour and showed marked diurnal variation, with a peak in the late afternoon and early evening when staffing and clinical resources are typically more limited. These findings highlight opportunities to optimise trauma team activation criteria and organisational structures to better align resource utilisation with patient acuity.

**TRIAL REGISTRATION**: Not applicable.
articles.journal: Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med

articles.title: Physiological determinants of piperacillin and cefazolin clearance in septic and trauma patients.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Physiological alterations in patients with sepsis and trauma can influence antibiotic clearance, yet reliable predictors remain poorly defined. We aimed to investigate the determinants of piperacillin and cefazolin clearance in these populations to identify bedside indicators of subtherapeutic exposure.

**METHODS**: Prospective physiological and pharmacokinetic study in patients receiving piperacillin/tazobactam for sepsis or prophylactic cefazolin post-trauma. articles.title: Eleven questions on Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome management in the ICU.
articles.abstract: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) due to Andes virus (ANDV) is a fulminant yet potentially reversible cause of respiratory and circulatory failure requiring timely critical care. This article addresses eleven practical questions on ICU management, drawing on clinical experience and research from the Chilean healthcare system. The recommendations cover early recognition, diagnostic workup, haemodynamic monitoring, cautious fluid and vasoactive support, respiratory management, VA-ECMO referral, daily ICU care, recovery, common pitfalls, and therapies with limited evidence. Because no antiviral or immunomodulatory therapy has consistently improved outcomes, survival relies on early suspicion, physiology-guided supportive care, and rapid escalation to ECMO-capable centres when severe cardiopulmonary failure develops.

articles.title: Influencing factors of the long-term predictive accuracy of the ocular trauma score.
articles.abstract:
**PURPOSE**: To evaluate the performance of the Ocular Trauma Score (OTS) in predicting long-term visual outcomes after mechanical ocular trauma and to identify the key factors influencing its accuracy.

**METHODS**: This retrospective study enrolled 106 patients with mechanical ocular trauma, with a median follow-up of 14 months. Retrieved variables included demographic characteristics and clinical data after the injury. The distribution of final best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was compared between the actual outcomes and the OTS-predicted outcomes. A weighted average predicted BCVA was calculated based on the BCVA probability distribution for each OTS category to classify patients into Better (actual BCVA better than OTS predicted) and Non-Better groups. Factors associated with OTS prediction discrepancies were identified using univariate analyses. Multivariable Firth logistic regression with bootstrap internal validation was performed to identify factors independently associated with better-than-predicted outcomes.

**RESULTS**: The OTS demonstrated a clear severity-dependent predictive pattern. Predictive accuracy was highest for mild injuries (OTS category 5) but showed a systematic pessimistic bias in severe injuries (OTS category 1), overestimating poor outcomes (NLP) and underestimating recovery potential (BCVA grades 3-5). For intermediate injuries (OTS categories 2-3), the likelihood of achieving moderate vision (20/200-20/50) was underestimated. Multiple surgeries were associated with better-than-predicted outcomes in the univariate analysis (p = 0.021). In the multivariable analysis, endophthalmitis (odds ratio [OR] = 2.95, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.08-8.29, p = 0.034) and penetrating injury (OR = 3.71, 95% CI: 1.17-12.94, p = 0.026) were independently associated with better-than-predicted outcomes, whereas initial BCVA grade 2, despite a significant univariate association, did not retain statistical significance after adjustment (OR = 2.01, 95% CI: 0.79-5.10, p = 0.144).

**CONCLUSION**: The OTS remains a useful prognostic tool but demonstrates limited accuracy in severe mechanical ocular trauma. Endophthalmitis and penetrating injury were identified as independent modifiers, while initial BCVA grade 2 and multiple surgeries were associated with better-than-predicted outcomes in the univariate analysis. Contextualising its predictions with contemporary surgical factors and clinical modifiers may improve the individualised application of the OTS.

articles.title: Focus Where It Matters: Design and Implementation of a Physiology-Based Care Pathway for Traumatic Shock.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVE**: Traumatic shock lacks a consensus definition, and in blunt-predominant systems its causes are heterogeneous. Simple physiological parameters remain the most universally available basis for early recognition. We describe the design and staged implementation of a physiology-based care pathway for traumatic shock and evaluate its implementation through staff experience.

**METHODS**: Single-centre quality-improvement and implementation project at an Australian Level 1 trauma centre, reported per SQUIRE 2.0. The pathway comprised physiology-based activation (systolic blood pressure ≤ 90 mmHg, shock index > 1, prehospital blood or senior clinician concern), structured pre-arrival preparation, trauma bay and equipment standardisation, task-based team roles, prioritised life-saving interventions and senior-led disposition, supported by simulation and embedded quality improvement. Components were implemented between June and November 2022. Evaluation comprised pre-intervention (2021) and post-implementation (2025) staff surveys, summarised as top-box favourability, with cross-sectional characterisation of the shocked cohort. Clinical effectiveness was not assessed.

**RESULTS**: Of 3667 major trauma patients, 324 (8.8%) met shocked trauma criteria; these patients were younger, more severely injured and had markedly higher mortality (emergency department death 6.8% vs. 0.4%). Favourable ratings of trauma bay equipment and environment rose from approximately one-quarter to 87.0%. Post-implementation, staff reported high favourability for timely life-saving interventions (88.9%), pathway embedding (85.2%) and role confidence (86.5%). Leadership clarity, communication and reliable debriefing did not improve and were identified as ongoing targets.

**CONCLUSIONS**: A physiology-based traumatic shock pathway was feasibly implemented and embedded, with high staff-reported readiness and clear targets for refinement. Effectiveness remains to be established.

articles.title: Lumbopelvic fixation for high-energy sacral fractures and spinopelvic dissociation: A systematic review and meta-analysis of complications, unplanned revision and implant removal.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: Secondary procedures after lumbopelvic fixation (LPF) include planned implant removal, removal for symptoms and revision for complications. Their differing indications, together with limited comparative evidence, complicate counselling and surgical planning.

**METHODS**: PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched to May 2026 (PROSPERO CRD420251036375) for comparative and single-arm studies (≥10 LPF patients). High-energy injuries and fragility fractures were considered separately. Random-effects models summarised complications, unplanned revision, implant removal and within-study comparisons of surgical approaches and fixation strategies.

**RESULTS**: Twenty-five studies were included (22 high-energy, 3 fragility). Across 19 high-energy LPF cohorts (564 patients), pooled surgical-site infection was 9.3% (95% CI 6.1-14.1), implant loosening or failure was 5.3%, nonunion occurred in 4 of 389 patients (1.0%) and loss of reduction in 2 of 355. Pooled unplanned revision was 11.9% (95% CI 8.7-16.0; prediction interval 5.3-24.3), most often for infection or wound complications. Implant removal was 79.0% in routine-removal series and 17.3% in selective-removal series. Four studies compared minimally invasive and open LPF. Pooling three studies showed less blood loss with minimally invasive LPF (mean difference -271 mL, 95% CI -367 to -175) and shorter operative time (-51 min, -97 to -5); the operative-time association did not persist with Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Infection (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.09-1.83) and revision (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.09-1.43) estimates were inconclusive. Four cohorts comparing LPF with posterior pelvic-ring fixation alone reported higher odds of revision after LPF (OR 3.96, 95% CI 1.63-9.60), with substantial potential for confounding by indication. Certainty was very low.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Nonunion and loss of reduction were infrequent after LPF, while unplanned revision most often involved infection or wound complications. Implant removal varied with institutional policy and warrants separate counselling. Minimally invasive LPF was associated with less blood loss, but comparative evidence remains insufficient to establish lower complication rates, equivalent mechanical outcomes or superiority of either fixation strategy.

articles.title: Impact of sarcopenic obesity phenotype on long-term survival in geriatric trauma: A nationwide cohort study using weight-adjusted waist index.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: As the global population ages, identifying effective prognostic markers for elderly trauma patients has become crucial. While Body Mass Index (BMI) is commonly used, its utility is limited by the "obesity paradox," failing to differentiate between muscle and fat. This study aimed to evaluate the Weight-Adjusted Waist Index (WWI), a surrogate marker for sarcopenic obesity, as a predictor of 20-year mortality following heavy trauma in the elderly.
