**METHODS**: We analyzed a nationwide cohort of 18,366 elderly patients (age≧65) from the National Health Insurance Service-National Sample Cohort (NHIS-NSC) who experienced heavy trauma (hospitalization, surgery, or ICU admission) between 2002 and 2022. Patients were categorized into WWI tertiles. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) for 20-year mortality, adjusting for demographics, lifestyle factors, comorbidities, and laboratory findings.

**RESULTS**: During the 20-year follow-up, the highest WWI tertile (T3) was associated with significantly higher mortality compared to the lowest tertile (T1). In the fully adjusted model, the HR for 20-year mortality in the T3 group was 1.72 (95% CI 1.55-1.91). Notably, the risk was more pronounced in obese patients (BMI≧25 kg/m2, HR 2.15) and those with low physical activity. Furthermore, high WWI was associated with a higher prevalence of hip and femur fractures (26.0% vs. 15.0%) and prolonged ICU stays.

**CONCLUSIONS**: WWI is a superior and independent predictor of long-term mortality compared to BMI in elderly trauma patients. By effectively identifying the high-risk sarcopenic obesity phenotype, WWI provides a practical and powerful tool for risk stratification in geriatric trauma management.

articles.title: Tachycardia and rhabdomyolysis after use of melanotan and an uncommon synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonist.
articles.abstract: Various medicinal and non-medicinal substances are available on the internet for a variety of intended effects such as recreational use, performance enhancement, and modification of body appearance. Melanotans are synthetic agonists of melanocyte stimulating hormone (a-MSH) used to promote tanning. We describe a young adult male presenting to the ED with tachycardia and tremors reportedly following melanotan injection. Clinical suspicion and laboratory confirmation led to detection of an undisclosed synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonist (SCRA) seldom reported in the US. We discuss the likely contributions of both substances to the findings in this case.

articles.title: Hollow viscus injury (HVI) score in adult patients sustaining non-motor vehicle collision blunt trauma: A single-center retrospective validation study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Delayed diagnosis of hollow viscus injury (HVI) from blunt trauma (BT) carries increased morbidity. An HVI prediction tool (HVI Score), incorporating vital signs, physical examination, and computed tomography (CT) findings has been validated in patients injured by motor vehicle collision (MVC) with an abdominal seatbelt sign. This study investigated the HVI Score performance in patients with non-MVC blunt trauma.

**METHODS**: This retrospective single-center study conducted between 2020 and 2024 included adult (>18-years-old) patients sustaining non-MVC BT who underwent CT imaging of the abdomen/pelvis prior to any abdominal operation. The primary outcome was operatively confirmed HVI. HVI Score model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC) curve and by calibration (ratio of observed to expected events, calibration-in-the-large, and calibration slope).

**RESULTS**: Of 752 non-MVC BT patients admitted, 19 (2.5%) were high-risk (scores >10), 105 (14.0%) moderate-risk (scores 6-9), and 628 (83.5%) low-risk (scores <5), with 19 (2.5%) having an HVI. The high-risk cohort had increased rates of abdominal tenderness (36.8% vs. 27.6% vs. 12.1%) as well as increased CT findings of free fluid (100.0% vs. 89.5% vs. 6.1%), soft tissue contusion (73.7% vs. 46.7% vs. 28.8%), mesenteric stranding (36.8% vs. 21.0% vs.7.6%), mesenteric hematoma (42.1% vs. 13.3% vs. 7.8%), bowel wall thickening (47.4% vs. 5.7% vs. 3.3%), and pneumoperitoneum (26.3% vs. 1.9% vs. 0.0%) compared to moderate and low-risk patients (all p < 0.001). The HVI Score achieved an AUROC of 0.96 (CI 0.94-0.98). Observed events numbered 19 against 26 expected (observed-to-expected ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.47-1.15), with a calibration slope of 0.96 (95% CI 0.64-1.28). At the low-risk threshold, sensitivity and NPV were both 100%; at the high-risk threshold, specificity was 99% and PPV 47%.

**CONCLUSION**: The HVI Score, which was originally validated for MVC patients with a seatbelt sign, had excellent performance in predicting HVI among patients with non-MVC BT.

**SOCIAL MEDIA SUMMARY**: The Hollow Viscus Injury (HVI) prediction score has excellent performance in predicting HVI among patients with non-MVC blunt abdominal trauma, thus extending its utility to all blunt trauma patients.

articles.title: Comparative trends of musculoskeletal injury in pickleball and tennis: An 11-year analysis of U.S. emergency department visits.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Pickleball participation continues to surge, with many recreational tennis players transitioning to the sport due to perceived ease of play and social appeal. The aim of this study was to compare 11-year injury patterns between patients presenting to the Emergency Department (ED) for pickleball and tennis injuries.

**HYPOTHESIS**: We hypothesized that (1) pickleball-related ED visits would increase over time while tennis-related visits would remain stable or decrease; (2) injury patterns would differ between sports by anatomical site, diagnosis, and mechanism; and (3) older adults would account for a higher proportion of fall-related injuries requiring hospital admission.

**STUDY DESIGN**: Retrospective comparative epidemiologic study LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III METHODS: National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (NEISS) data between 2014 and 2024 were sorted for pickleball (product code 3235) and tennis (product code 3284). Cases were manually reviewed to confirm sport participation and exclude non-musculoskeletal injuries. Anatomical site, diagnosis, injury mechanism, treatment disposition, and date of ED visit were extracted. Group comparisons used t-tests and chi-square tests, and linear regression evaluated annual trends.

**RESULTS**: A total of 4141 cases were included (pickleball n = 1442; National Estimates (NE) 80,553; tennis n = 2699; NE 110,480). Pickleball-related ED visits increased over time, while tennis-related visits remained stable. Pickleball players were older than tennis players (60.1 (SD 16.7) yr vs. 40.9 (SD 23.3) yr; p < 0.01), with individuals ≥ 65 years accounting for 52.1% of pickleball-related injuries. Wrist injuries were the most common in pickleball (17.0%) and ankle injuries were most common in tennis (18.3%). Fractures were more frequent in pickleball (43.1%), while sprains/strains were more common in tennis (46.4%, p < 0.01). Falls were the leading mechanism in both sports (Pickleball 52.2%, Tennis 33.8%). Pickleball injuries occurred most frequently in the Winter (30.3%) while tennis injuries occurred most frequently in Summer (29.1%). Hospital admissions were more frequent for pickleball players (7.8% vs 3.9%).

**CONCLUSIONS**: The rapid rise in pickleball-related injuries necessitates proactive efforts in education, conditioning, and injury prevention to safeguard participants, particularly older adults.

**CLINICAL RELEVANCE**: As participation in pickleball grows, especially among older adults, targeted conditioning, emphasizing neuromuscular control and safety education may help reduce injury rates.

articles.title: Epidemiological characteristics and comparison of clinical outcomes between conservative and surgical treatment for rib fractures in South China: A 10‑year retrospective cohort study of 4085 cases with propensity score‑matching analysis.
articles.abstract:
**PURPOSE**: To systematically describe the epidemiological characteristics of rib fractures in South China and compare the clinical characteristics, hospital stay, and total costs between patients receiving conservative versus surgical treatment, thereby providing evidence‑based support for clinical decision‑making and public health prevention.

**METHODS**: A retrospective analysis was performed on 4085 hospitalized patients with rib fractures admitted to the Fifth Affiliated Hospital of Southern Medical University between January 2014 and December 2023. Data on gender, age, injury mechanism, fracture type, complications, blood group, and occupational distribution were collected. A subgroup analysis comparing conservative (n = 586) versus surgical treatment (n = 137) was conducted among 723 patients admitted between January 2021 and December 2023. Propensity score matching was used to balance baseline characteristics between the two groups, and differences in hospital stay, total costs, and injury mechanisms were compared.

**RESULTS**: (1) Epidemiological characteristics: Of the 4085 patients, 68.13% (2783/4085) were male, and the 41-60 year age group accounted for the highest proportion (50.35%). Autumn and winter were the peak seasons for injury (54.71%). Traffic accidents were the leading cause of injury (51.18%), followed by falls (21.82%) and height‑related falls (19.13%). Multiple fractures predominated (75.52%). The most common complication was pulmonary contusion (45.14%), followed by traumatic pneumothorax/hemothorax/hemopneumothorax/pleural effusion (40.02%). Among occupations, freelancers were the largest group (34.37%), followed by farmers (23.18%). Blood group O was the most prevalent (42.15%), while blood group B was the least common (5.55%, P < 0.001), suggesting that blood group O may be a potential risk factor for rib fractures. (2) Comparison of treatment modalities: The conservative group had a significantly shorter hospital stay than the surgical group [3 (2-6) days vs. 17 (13-26) days, P < 0.001] and significantly lower total costs [5879 (2570-8877) RMB vs. 69,588 (54,499-89,845) RMB, P < 0.001]. The distribution of injury mechanisms differed significantly between the two groups (P < 0.001): the conservative group was mainly injured by falls/slips (44.4%), whereas the surgical group was mainly injured by height‑related falls/ground‑level falls (30.7%). The proportion of concomitant hemopneumothorax was higher in the surgical group than in the conservative group (21.9% vs. 3.4%, P < 0.001).

**CONCLUSION**: Based on a large sample of 4085 cases, this study is the first to systematically delineate the full epidemiological profile of rib fractures in South China, with a sample size more than ten times larger than the previous largest regional report. The results indicate that middle‑aged males, freelancers, and farmers are high‑risk populations, with traffic accidents and multiple fractures being predominant, and a unique autumn peak seasonal pattern in South China is reported for the first time. Treatment strategies should be tailored according to injury mechanism and fracture severity. The novel association between blood group O and increased rib fracture risk, reported here for the first time, provides a new perspective for precision prevention; the potential mechanism may involve impaired hemostatic response due to lower baseline levels of von Willebrand factor and factor VIII in individuals with blood group O.

articles.title: Fracture characteristics in coronal shear fractures of the distal humerus: Clinical significance of medial trochlear involvement.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Coronal shear fractures of the distal humerus exhibit diverse fracture-extension patterns that are not fully characterized by conventional classification systems. The clinical significance of fracture extension into the medial or lateral column remains incompletely understood. This study investigated fracture-extension patterns beyond the conventional Dubberley classification and evaluated their associations with clinical outcomes and bone-related complications.

**METHODS**: This multicenter retrospective study included surgically treated coronal shear fractures of the distal humerus with a minimum follow-up of 12 months at four affiliated institutions between 2012 and 2024. Fractures were classified using the AO/OTA and Dubberley systems. Computed tomography (CT) images were reviewed to assess medial trochlear involvement, lateral column involvement without posterior condylar comminution, and isolated trochlear fractures. Clinical outcomes included elbow range of motion (flexion, extension, and arc of motion) and postoperative complications. Univariate logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors associated with bone-related complications.

**RESULTS**: Among 374 surgically treated distal humeral fractures, 35 coronal shear fractures were included in the final analysis. Medial trochlear involvement was identified in 8 fractures (23%) and was most frequently observed in Dubberley type 3 fractures. Patients with medial trochlear involvement had significantly greater loss of elbow extension at final follow-up than those without medial trochlear involvement (-29° vs. -16°, P = 0.042). Bone-related complications were more frequent in fractures with medial trochlear involvement than in those without (50% vs. 7%, P = 0.016). In univariate logistic regression analysis, medial trochlear involvement was significantly associated with bone-related complications (odds ratio, 12.5; 95% confidence interval, 1.69-92.3; P = 0.013). Neither the AO/OTA nor the Dubberley classification was significantly associated with bone-related complications.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Medial trochlear involvement was significantly associated with greater loss of elbow extension and bone-related complications at final follow-up in coronal shear fractures of the distal humerus. Preoperative CT assessment of medial trochlear involvement may provide clinically useful information complementary to conventional fracture classification systems and may aid surgical planning.

articles.title: Machine learning models with SHAP explanations for predicting neurosurgical intervention and six month functional outcome after traumatic brain injury.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Admission information can help describe surgical treatment and subsequent functional outcomes following traumatic brain injury (TBI). We developed interpretable machine learning models to address these two tasks.

**METHODS**: This retrospective study included 673 adults evaluated at a single center between December 2018 and December 2023. Outcomes recorded were neurosurgical intervention and six-month Glasgow Outcome Scale status, dichotomized as favorable (scores 4-5) or unfavorable (scores 1-3). Patients were randomly allocated to training and internal validation sets in a 7:3 ratio. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used to select predictors for the XGBoost and random forest models. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, along with classification and prediction error metrics, was employed for model evaluation. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) were used to interpret model predictions.

**RESULTS**: There were 75 unfavorable outcomes and 66 surgical interventions. The reported validation accuracy for XGBoost was 87.56% for predicting functional outcomes and 95.02% for surgical interventions. Validation Brier scores were 0.083 and 0.035, respectively. The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), pupillary light reflex, and blood glucose levels contributed significantly to functional outcome predictions, while GCS, fibrinogen, and white blood cell count were key predictors for surgical interventions. Interpretation of threshold-dependent measures is limited by class imbalance and incomplete specification of outcome coding.

**CONCLUSION**: The models combined routinely collected admission variables to characterize the treatment received and functional outcomes in a selected traumatic brain injury (TBI) cohort. These findings require confirmation through analysis replication and independent validation before they can be applied clinically.

articles.title: Articular compliance and tolerance to residual incongruity after intra-articular fracture: A hypothesis-driven narrative review.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Residual articular incongruity after intra-articular fracture is widely held to cause post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA), yet tolerance of a given step-off differs between joints and between regions of the same joint. Reduction targets are nonetheless expressed as uniform millimetre thresholds, and no tissue-level mechanism has been offered for the variation.

**HYPOTHESIS**: The compliance of the osteochondral unit - cartilage thickness, cartilage material properties and subchondral bone stiffness together - modulates tolerance of residual incongruity, and incongruity is more informatively expressed relative to local cartilage thickness than in absolute millimetres.

**METHODS**: Narrative review with a documented search of PubMed/MEDLINE (inception to 14 October 2026) covering cartilage and subchondral properties of opposing surfaces, experimental and computational studies of articular incongruity, and clinical studies relating residual displacement to outcome. Four searches returned 3928 records, 3579 after deduplication; 54 sources informed the synthesis. This is not a systematic review; reporting follows SANRA.

**FINDINGS**: Small, localised contact-stress elevations appear tolerable; step-offs remodel less completely as their height increases; and cumulative contact-stress exposure above a threshold predicts PTOA after tibial plafond fracture. Opposing surfaces differ measurably in cartilage thickness, modulus and subchondral bone thickness, but the direction of the difference reverses between joints and between regions of one joint, so curvature is not a usable proxy for compliance. Clinically, the acetabulum and tibial plafond appear least tolerant, the meniscus-covered tibial plateau more tolerant, and distal radius incongruity predicts radiographic arthrosis more strongly than functional loss.

**CONCLUSIONS**: The evidence is consistent with, but does not establish, a contribution of osteochondral compliance; joint-level factors confound the clinical data. We set out a Compliance Framework defining measurable determinants, propose relative incongruity as a testable metric, and state four falsifiable predictions with the designs that would test them. Current joint-specific reduction standards should guide practice until those predictions are tested.

articles.title: Global research on cricket injuries (1982-2025): A bibliometric analysis.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Cricket is one of the most widely played sports worldwide and carries a significant burden of musculoskeletal injuries, particularly among fast bowlers. Over the past four decades, research in cricket injury epidemiology, biomechanics, workload monitoring, and surveillance has expanded substantially.

**OBJECTIVE**: To conduct a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of global cricket injury research, identifying growth trends, influential publications, leading contributors, collaboration networks, and major thematic domains.

**METHODS**: Publications from 1982 to 2025 were systematically analyzed using bibliometric indicators including annual growth, authorship productivity, institutional and country contributions, citation impact, total link strength (TLS), and co-authorship networks. The top 100 cited papers and the top 10 highly cited papers (HCPs) were examined in detail to identify landmark contributions and research priorities.

**RESULTS**: A sharp rise in publications occurred after 2003, with nearly 90% of output produced in the last two decades. Australia, the United Kingdom, and South Africa led in productivity, citation impact, and collaborative link strength. The top 10 HCPs accounted for 10% of papers but 37.25% of total citations, underscoring concentrated scholarly influence. Fast bowlers consistently demonstrated the highest injury incidence, particularly lumbar spine and lower limb injuries. Workload spikes were strongly associated with increased injury risk, establishing load monitoring as a central preventive strategy. Biomechanical factors such as mixed bowling action, trunk rotation, and front-knee mechanics were linked to lumbar stress injuries. Standardized injury definitions and international consensus surveillance frameworks significantly improved research quality and comparability.

**CONCLUSION**: Cricket injury research has evolved into a mature, collaborative, and high-impact domain centered on fast bowling biomechanics, workload regulation, and surveillance standardization. Expanded global participation and integration of advanced analytics are essential for future injury prevention strategies.

articles.title: Transcutaneous Pacing in the Prehospital Setting: A Retrospective Cohort Study of Electrical Capture.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: Transcutaneous pacing (TCP) treats hemodynamically unstable bradycardia refractory to pharmacologic management. Effective TCP requires electrical and mechanical capture to augment perfusion. Little is known about prehospital TCP and capture incidence.

**METHODS**: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients treated with prehospital TCP by an emergency medical services agency between 2017 and 2024. Continuous electrocardiogram recordings from cardiac monitors were reviewed. Electrical capture was the primary outcome, defined as a widened QRS with a distinct T wave following a TCP spike. Secondary measures included capture duration, clinician-verbalized pulse during pacing, plethysmograph waveform alignment, and changes in systolic blood pressure (SBP), pulse oximetry, and end-tidal carbon dioxide.

**RESULTS**: Fifty-six patients received attempted TCP. Median age was 70 years (interquartile range [IQR] 58-85), and 34% were female. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) was administered in 59% of patients. Electrical capture was achieved in 18 patients (32%). Among patients who achieved electrical capture, complete capture occurred a mean of 27% (standard deviation 30%) of attempted pacing duration. The median SBP change was +22 (IQR: -2-82) mmHg in patients with electrical capture and 0 (IQR: -29-7) mmHg in those with only rare-to-absent capture (

**CONCLUSIONS**: Electrical capture during prehospital TCP occurred in a minority of patients and was often intermittent. Prehospital identification of mechanical capture using routine clinical indicators was difficult and unreliable. Future work should standardize capture definitions and physiologic measurements to determine when TCP produces clinically meaningful perfusion.

articles.title: The Accuracy and Precision of Gravity-Driven Infusions.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: When infusion pumps are unavailable in the prehospital setting, clinicians must estimate fluid flow by counting drops in a drip chamber. We aimed to assess the accuracy and precision of gravity-driven infusions and to estimate the magnitude of inaccuracy and imprecision attributable to human and non-human factors.

**METHODS**: We recruited 55 paramedics to participate in a structured, experimental, simulated study under controlled laboratory conditions, in which each participant set nine drip rates as accurately as possible on a standardized setup. Measurements of flow were made visually (drip rate) and volumetrically (delivered fluid). Volumetric measurements were used to represent overall error, visual measurements were used to represent human error, and the difference was used to represent non-human error. We measured accuracy (percentage error) and precision (mean absolute deviation) using the natural log of error factor to represent the multiplicative decomposition of human and non-human error additively. Mixed effect models were used to assess accuracy and precision across targeted drip rates.

**RESULTS**: Inaccuracy and imprecision varied by targeted drip rate. Overall inaccuracy ranged from -45.3% (95%CI, -52.7% to -36.8%) to 5.8% (95%CI, -8.5% to 22.3%). Human inaccuracy ranged from -38.8% (95%CI, -46.0% to -30.8%) to 44.1% (95%CI, 27.1% to 63.4%). Non-human inaccuracy ranged from -26.7% (95%CI, -30.1% to -23.2%) to -6.8% (95%CI -11.1% to -2.3%). Imprecision was primarily driven by human factors. The degree of human variation between trial participants ranged from 24.2% (95%CI, 15.3% to 33.7%) to 43.7% (95%CI, 33.4% to 54.9%) across targeted rates. The targeted drip rate of 1gtt/s was more accurate than the pool of all other targeted rates (absolute error 31.1% versus 48.5%). Targeted drip rates of whole numbers were more accurate than targeted drip rates of fractional numbers (absolute error 40.7% versus 54.1%). Targeted drip rates below 1gtt/s were more accurate than rates above 1gtt/s (absolute error 35.3% versus 63.1%).

**CONCLUSIONS**: Gravity-driven fluid delivery exhibits inaccuracy and imprecision, which varies by targeted rate. While potentially modifiable human factors may improve the accuracy of this technique, non-human error contributes substantially to inaccuracy. There is a need to assess whether this inaccuracy and imprecision adversely affect patient outcomes.

articles.title: Fixation of patellar fractures using bioabsorbable hydroxyapatite/poly-L-lactide cannulated screws and subperiosteal nonabsorbable sutures.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: Bioabsorbable implants offer a promising alternative to metallic fixation for patellar fractures, potentially avoiding hardware-related complications. In 2023, a new generation of bioabsorbable hydroxyapatite/poly-L-lactide (HA/PLLA) cannulated screws was introduced, featuring a low-profile (2 mm) trident-shaped head and increased root diameter for enhanced strength. This study evaluates the clinical outcomes of a surgical technique combining these redesigned screws with subperiosteal nonabsorbable sutures.

**MATERIALS AND METHODS**: Between April 2023 and May 2025, 19 consecutive patients with transverse patellar fractures (AO/OTA 34-C1/C2) underwent open reduction and internal fixation. Two bioabsorbable cannulated screws were used. High-strength nonabsorbable sutures were passed through the screw channels and a central bone tunnel using a double-loop sliding knot for compression. The sutures were systematically routed subperiosteally to minimize tissue irritation. Full weight-bearing with a brace began on postoperative day one. Clinical and radiographic outcomes were assessed. This study was approved by the institutional review board of Kainan Hospital.

**RESULTS**: The mean maximum articular surface gap was 8.7 ± 5.2 mm. The mean follow-up was 8.6 ± 3.0 months. Bone union was achieved in all cases. At the final follow-up, the mean knee flexion was 138.7° ± 13.0° and extension was - 1.6° ± 3.4°. No postoperative complications, including infection, loss of reduction, screw breakage, or symptomatic hardware irritation, were observed during the follow-up period. No reoperations were required during the follow-up period.

**CONCLUSIONS**: All patients achieved bone union. No major complications or reoperations were observed during the follow-up period. These preliminary findings suggest that this technique may be feasible for transverse patellar fractures.

articles.title: Two Decades of Neurosurgical Device Innovation: A Comprehensive Analysis of FDA Authorization Trends From 7800 Approvals by Subspecialty, Regulatory Pathway, and Approval Time.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES**: Technological progress has accelerated neurosurgical care, yet a panoramic view of these innovations remains lacking. This study aims to analyze all US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) authorizations issued from 2000 to 2023 to map neurosurgical device output by subspecialty, compare regulatory pathways and approval times, and identify factors affecting market entry.

**METHODS**: All devices cleared or approved by the FDA Neurology and Orthopedic Review Panels (January 2000-December 2023) were extracted from publicly available 510(k), De Novo, Humanitarian Device Exemption, and Premarket Approval databases. Devices were assigned to 1 of 9 neurosurgical subspecialties and stratified by regulatory pathway, device class, company maturity, and geographic origin. Descriptive statistics, analysis of variance, and Welch t-tests assessed temporal and categorical differences.

**RESULTS**: Of 16 064 devices reviewed by the FDA Neurology and Orthopedic panels, 7873 (49.0%) were neurosurgical, rising 172.1% over the period. Spine and peripheral nerve (5227 devices) and stereotactic and functional (1378) dominated volume and number of new market entries, while cerebrospinal fluid disorders (n = 149) and cranial trauma (n = 111) had fewer approvals. Cerebrovascular and endovascular (95.5%) and cranial trauma (200.0%) showed the largest growth rates, while cerebrospinal fluid disorders (-54.2%) and general cranial surgery (-34.5%) declined over time. Mean approval time varied by subspecialty (P < .001), the shortest for spine and peripheral nerve (119.0 ± 102.7 days) and the longest for stereotactic and functional (158.7 ± 121.5 days). Approval or clearance times were strongly influenced by regulatory pathway and device class (both P < .001), with Premarket Approval devices (584.8 ± 323.3 days) the longest. Mature companies achieved faster approvals compared with startups (114.9 ± 97.0 vs 174.5 ± 133.9 days, P < .001).

**CONCLUSION**: Neurosurgical device output has more than doubled, but volume concentrates where predicates are rich and reimbursement established, not where clinical need or novelty is the greatest. Pathway architecture, device complexity, and sponsor experience influence approval efficiency more than novelty.

articles.title: Coagulopathy and anticoagulation management in adult ECPR patients.
articles.abstract: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) has emerged as a lifesaving strategy for refractory cardiac arrest, restoring systemic perfusion when conventional cardiopulmonary resuscitation fails. However, ECPR profoundly disrupts haemostasis, driven by the combined effects of whole-body ischaemia-reperfusion injury, systemic inflammation, endothelial activation, platelet dysfunction, and blood contact with extracorporeal surfaces. Together, these processes create a highly dynamic and unstable thromboinflammatory milieu, marked by the simultaneous risk of thrombosis and life-threatening bleeding. Systemic anticoagulation is required to maintain circuit patency and prevent thromboembolic complications, yet optimal strategies remain uncertain. Haemostasis during ECPR is highly dynamic, shaped by the underlying aetiology of cardiac arrest, patient-specific characteristics, and circuit-related factors. This complexity underscores the limitations of fixed anticoagulation targets and the need for individualized, context-sensitive management guided by continuous clinical and laboratory assessment. Despite the increasing global adoption of ECPR, high-quality evidence to guide anticoagulation practices remains scarce. Current strategies are largely extrapolated from other extracorporeal life support populations, contributing to substantial inter-centre variability. This review synthesizes the available evidence on coagulopathy and anticoagulation in adult patients receiving ECPR and discusses emerging approaches to monitoring and anticoagulation management.

articles.title: Assessing Swedish guidelines for prehospital bleeding control: a cross-sectional appraisal using AGREE II.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: High-quality clinical practice guidelines are essential for safe and consistent prehospital bleeding control, particularly in settings with variable geography and transport times. This study appraised the methodological quality of Swedish regional prehospital guidelines for traumatic external haemorrhage using the AGREE II instrument.

**METHODS**: This cross-sectional study included clinical practice guidelines requested from all 21 Swedish healthcare regions. Guideline quality was assessed independently by two appraisers using AGREE II, which evaluates 23 items across six domains. Domain scores were calculated as percentages of the maximum possible score.

**RESULTS**: Complete responses were obtained from 15 of 21 regions. Overall methodological quality was low across the included guidelines. The highest median domain score was observed for clarity of presentation, whereas rigour of development, stakeholder involvement, applicability, and editorial independence scored poorly. Most guidelines lacked explicit descriptions of evidence search strategies, criteria for selecting evidence, links between recommendations and supporting evidence, update procedures, and declarations of editorial independence.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Swedish regional prehospital guidelines for traumatic external bleeding control showed limited methodological quality when assessed using AGREE II. Future guideline development should prioritise transparent evidence linkage, multidisciplinary stakeholder involvement, clear implementation considerations, scheduled updating, and adaptation to regional differences in transport and evacuation times.

**TRIAL REGISTRATION**: Not applicable.
articles.journal: Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med

articles.title: Differentiated effect of hypothermia versus normothermia after cardiac arrest by neurological status and clinical correlates of ischemic burden.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: The optimal temperature target after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains uncertain, as major randomized trials have not demonstrated a clear benefit of lower-target hypothermia compared with normothermia. Despite this, patients with differing degrees of ischemic burden or early neurological injury may hypothetically respond differently to temperature targets, raising the possibility of heterogeneous treatment effects. This study aimed to determine whether outcomes differ after OHCA with 33 °C versus controlled normothermia (36.0-37.7 °C) according to correlates of ischemic burden and neurological findings at hospital admission.

**METHODS**: This secondary analysis of the TTM and TTM2 trials employed effect-based machine learning to probe for heterogeneous treatment effects. Causal forests and Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) estimated individualized treatment effects (ITE) based on ischemia duration, prehospital factors, and neurological examination findings at hospital admission. Treatment effect modifier variable importance parameter (TEM-VIP) analysis ranked the baseline variables most likely to modify effect. The primary outcome was six-month all-cause mortality, and the secondary outcome was poor functional outcome (modified Rankin scale score 4-6). Primary analyses evaluated potential heterogeneity within each trial, while secondary analyses pooled all participants.

**MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS**: All 2789 adult OHCA patients from the trials' primary analyses were included (median age 65 years (IQR 56-73), 79.9% male). Death occurred in 49.4% of patients in the 33 °C group, and in 47.9% in the controlled normothermia group. Variation in six-month mortality ITEs estimated from ischemic burden correlates and initial neurological findings was minimal, and no significant heterogeneity of treatment effect was identified across all methods and analysis populations. In the pooled analysis, estimated conditional mean mortality risk difference ranged from - 1.2% to 2.1% in causal forest (p = 0.99), and from - 0.5% to 1.5% in BART, with posterior probabilities for hypothermia benefit ranging from 42% to 53%. Absolute subgroup estimates in TEM-VIP analysis were small and non-significant. Results were consistent for the six-month functional outcome.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Among TTM and TTM2 participants randomized to 33 °C versus controlled normothermia post-OHCA, no evidence of detectable heterogeneity of treatment effect based on available clinical correlates of ischemic burden or initial neurological findings was identified, with minimal estimated variation in treatment effect.

articles.title: Current models of emergency general surgery care delivery in Manitoba, Canada: a cross-sectional survey.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Emergency general surgery conditions result in disproportionately high rates of morbidity and mortality. Despite this, little is known about the resources available for related care in Canadian hospitals. Our aim was to describe the resources and structures dedicated to emergency general surgery in Manitoba, Canada.

**METHODOLOGY**: We developed a survey to examine institutional capabilities in providing emergency general surgical care. The survey was developed over three iterations using a modified Delphi technique and was then reviewed separately by community surgeons to ensure broad applicability. A cross-sectional survey of representatives at each of the fourteen hospitals reported to offer emergency general surgery care in Manitoba was performed in two iterations between March and December 2023. Findings were examined descriptively and stratified between tertiary, urban, and rural centres. Our aim was to describe the resources and structures in place for providing related care, including the proportion of hospitals with a dedicated emergency general surgery care model.

**RESULTS**: After exclusions and non-responses, we examined the resources and capabilities of nine institutions. Two tertiary, two urban community, and five rural community centres were evaluated. Of these institutions, 4/9 (44.4%) had an emergency general surgery model of care, including one rural centre. There was a large degree of variation in operative resources, specialty services, and physician learners between centre types. Allied health professionals were more consistently available across hospitals. Our survey results identified several pertinent gaps in care, including a lack of shared treatment protocols, transfer agreements, and quality improvement measures, even at large tertiary centres.

**CONCLUSIONS**: This study demonstrates a pressing need for collaboration between centres and involvement in quality improvement amongst practitioners to meet standards of care in emergency general surgery. The results also show that important aspects of emergency general surgical care can be quantified with our survey and will serve as the basis for expanding this to a country-wide study.

articles.title: Impact of the provider-in-triage model on computed tomography and ultrasound imaging in renal colic.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: Physician-in-Triage (PIT) models may influence diagnostic imaging decisions in the emergency department (ED). We evaluated the association between PIT exposure and imaging utilization among patients with renal colic and examined the influence of physician ultrasound training on imaging selection.

**METHODS**: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with an ED diagnosis of renal colic at a single tertiary ED from January 2024 through December 2025. A prespecified lower-risk subgroup included patients aged <51 years with prior nephrolithiasis, no infection, and normal creatinine. The primary exposure was PIT evaluation. Outcomes included computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis (CTAP), point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS), and radiology-performed renal ultrasound (RUS) utilization. Multivariable logistic regression was used to evaluate the association between PIT exposure and each imaging outcome after adjustment for age, gender, emergency severity index, admission, and race.

**RESULTS**: Of 1041 patients, 596 (57.3%) were exposed to PIT. CTAP utilization was higher among PIT-exposed patients than non-PIT patients (72.9% vs 66.1%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.40, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.07-1.85). PIT exposure was associated with lower POCUS utilization (10.3% vs 18.6%; aOR 0.49, 95% CI 0.34-0.70), while RUS utilization was similar (10.1% vs 9.0%; aOR 1.17, 95% CI 0.76-1.79). Overall ultrasound utilization (POCUS or RUS) was also lower among PIT-exposed patients (20.1% vs 26.7%; aOR 0.69, 95% CI 0.51-0.93). In the lower-risk subgroup, PIT exposure remained associated with greater CTAP utilization (63.6% vs 48.1%, p = 0.028) and lower POCUS utilization (14.4% vs 30.4%, p = 0.008). Ultrasound-trained attendings used CTAP less frequently than non-ultrasound-trained attendings (57.8% vs 71.8%; aOR for non-ultrasound-trained physicians 1.86, 95% CI 1.18-2.93).

**CONCLUSION**: PIT exposure was associated with greater CTAP and lower ultrasound utilization in patients with renal colic, including among a prespecified lower-risk cohort. Ultrasound-trained physicians used ultrasound more frequently and CTAP less frequently in renal colic patients.

articles.title: Long-term survival following extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a two-center five-year analysis.
articles.abstract: Randomized trials have shown short-term benefit of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but the long-term durability of survival and neurological recovery after hospital discharge remains poorly defined. We performed a retrospective cohort study of consecutive patients discharged alive after ECPR for refractory VT/VF OHCA from two academic centers (University of Minnesota, USA, and Charles University, Prague) from January 2013 through December 2022. The primary outcome was 5-year survival. Secondary outcomes included neurological status by Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) and associations of age and discharge disposition with long-term outcomes. Among 728 patients treated with ECPR, 211 (29.0%) survived to discharge; 138 from Minnesota and 73 from Prague. Median follow-up was 3.9 years; 68 patients (32%) completed 5 years. No patients were lost to follow-up. Among hospital survivors, 76.9% and 67.2% were alive at 1 and 5 years, respectively, with most deaths occurring within 90 days of discharge. CPC 1-2 was present in 78.7% at discharge and remained high among survivors beyond 1 year (93.4-94.2%). Five-year survival declined by age from 91.6% for those between 18-39 years and 52.9% for >70 years. Discharge disposition also strongly stratified long-term prognosis. Among patients discharged alive after ECPR for refractory OHCA, long-term survival was substantial, with approximately two-thirds alive at 5 years with favorable CPC in most. Younger age and discharge home or to acute rehabilitation identified subgroups with particularly favorable prognosis. These findings support the long-term durability of benefit among selected patients treated within established ECPR systems of care.

articles.title: Pediatric flexor tendon injuries: A 13-year retrospective review of injury characteristics, treatment, and outcomes.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Pediatric flexor tendon injuries are rare but potentially devastating. Due to low incidence, optimal perioperative management remains poorly defined, and evidence is scarce. This study evaluates the injury characteristics, surgical treatment, age-specific functional outcomes, and challenges in this population.

**METHODS**: A retrospective review was conducted on 79 pediatric patients (mean age 6.84 ± 4.27 years; 67.1% male) who underwent surgical repair for flexor tendon lacerations between 2010 and 2023. Outcomes were assessed using Total Active Motion (TAM), Strickland score, grip/pinch strength, Semmes-Weinstein monofilament, two-point discrimination, and QuickDASH questionnaire, with a mean follow-up of 59.9 ± 32.8 months.

**RESULTS**: Zone 2 was the most common injury site (45.6%), with glass being the predominant mechanism (67.1%). Nerve injury was present in 35.4% of cases. Overall, good/excellent results were achieved in 81.9% (TAM) and 89.0% (Strickland) of patients. The 0-5 years age group had significantly lower Strickland scores than the 6-12 years group (74.28% vs. 82.9%, p < 0.05). Zone 5 injuries demonstrated significantly better outcomes than Zone 2 and 3 (p < 0.001). The overall complication rate was low (5.1%), with a rerupture rate of 2.5%.

**CONCLUSION**: Pediatric flexor tendon repairs yield favorable functional outcomes with low complication rates. Age-related differences in functional outcomes should be interpreted cautiously because of developmental differences in patient cooperation and age-dependent rehabilitation strategies. Concomitant nerve injury was associated with poorer functional outcomes. The modified Kessler technique remains a reliable repair method.

articles.title: Limb preservation and optimization: A whole-patient approach to comprehensive care after catastrophic extremity injuries.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: The objective of this study was to describe the Limb Preservation and Optimization Center's (LPOC) components and mechanisms in treating catastrophic extremity injuries and report the initial patient demographics, indications, and outcomes using data from an established registry.

**METHODS**: A retrospective observational study was performed including all patients entered in the LPOC registry since January 1, 2014. Patient demographics, injury types and treatments, and outcomes, including functional outcomes. Descriptive statistics were calculated to determine proportions, means, standard deviations, and ranges.

**RESULTS**: 992 patients were included with a mean final follow-up of 20.5 months (SD:22.1, range 0-114); 178 (17.9%) underwent an amputation. Of those who reported RTW, 164 patients (71.6%) reporting RTW at full capacity. Lower extremity injuries were most common (74.9%). Demographic, health insurance, living setting, and presentation variables were similar among LPOC patients. Fractures and soft tissue injuries predominated across all injury categories with fracture fixation and wound coverage treatments most common. Upper extremity joint injuries and all types of combined injuries were associated with the highest reoperation rates. Treatment failure rates ranged from 11% to 100% with fracture and bone-related injuries being associated with the most favorable outcomes across categories.

**DISCUSSION**: Fractures and soft tissue injuries were the primary types of problems affecting all patients utilizing the LPOC. Fracture fixation and wound coverage treatments were the most performed procedures. Return to the operating room to address the limb preservation and optimization goal was extremely common across categories such that patients may expect at least 4 reoperations. Patients return to some type of work 75-88%. Treatment failure rates varied from 11% to 100%, with fracture and bone-related injuries being associated with the most favorable outcomes across categories. Overall, the results are encouraging and will help shape care in these patients.

articles.title: Geography matters: Variations in neck trauma between urban and rural level-II trauma centers.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Geodemographic factors create divergent clinical patterns between urban and rural settings. Level-II trauma centers are a vital trauma-care infrastructure for both urban and rural communities. This study compares neck trauma patterns, resource utilization, and outcomes at these distinct geodemographic nodes.

**METHODS**: Retrospective analysis (2014-2024) of neck trauma at an urban center (UC, n = 65) and a rural center (RC, n = 60). Demographics, mechanism, treatments, interventions, and outcomes were analyzed.

**RESULTS**: RC patients sustained more blunt, transport-related multisystem trauma with higher ISS. UC patients predominantly presented with localized penetrating injuries. Rural patients had higher ICU admission rates, longer ICU stays, more transfers to level-I centers yet underwent fewer operative interventions, invasive airway procedures, and CT angiogrophy.

**CONCLUSIONS**: There are significant variations in neck trauma between urban and rural level-II trauma centers. An "intervention paradox" exists were rural centers stabilize high-severity blunt trauma for transfer, while urban centers provide definitive care for penetrating wounds. These findings necessitate geodemographically tailored protocols. Understanding geodemographic variations is a critical aspect of optimizing trauma systems.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: II Retrospective cohort.

articles.title: Gabapentinoid-opioid co-prescription after long bone fracture fixation is associated with increased 1-year nonunion.
articles.abstract:
**PURPOSE**: Gabapentinoids are increasingly incorporated into multimodal analgesia after orthopaedic surgery, yet their impact on outcomes following fracture fixation remains unclear. This study evaluated the association between early postoperative gabapentinoid-opioid co-prescription and clinical outcomes after operative fixation of closed long bone fractures.

**METHODS**: Using TriNetX, we identified opioid-naïve and gabapentinoid-naïve adults undergoing intramedullary or plate-and-screw fixation of isolated closed diaphyseal tibia, humerus, or femur fractures. Patients prescribed gabapentin or pregabalin and opioids within three days after surgery were compared with patients receiving opioids alone. Propensity score matching (1:1) incorporated demographics, medical comorbidities, fracture location, fixation method, mental health disorders, and substance use disorders. Primary outcomes were prolonged (30-90 days) and chronic (90-180 days) postoperative opioid use. Secondary outcomes included 30-day emergency department (ED) visits and readmissions, and 1-year nonunion and reoperation.

**RESULTS**: After matching, each cohort consisted of approximately 2000 patients (range, 1946-2012). Gabapentinoid-opioid therapy was associated with higher rates of prolonged (21.0% vs 16.1%; RR 1.31; p < 0.001) and chronic (9.8% vs 7.4%; RR 1.33; p = 0.007) postoperative opioid use. Gabapentinoid-opioid therapy was associated with fewer 30-day ED visits (25.1% vs 42.5%; RR 0.59; p < 0.001), while 30-day readmission rates were similar between cohorts (p = 0.174). One-year rates of nonunion (4.3% vs 1.9%; RR 2.21; p < 0.001) and reoperation (7.1% vs 4.2%; RR 1.68; p < 0.001) were significantly higher among patients receiving gabapentinoid-opioid therapy. In a sensitivity analysis that defined the opioid-only cohort based on the absence of gabapentinoid prescriptions during the first 3 postoperative days, rather than the 1-year postoperative medication window used in the primary analysis, the associations with prolonged and chronic opioid use and reoperation were no longer statistically significant, whereas the association with nonunion remained significant (RR 1.62; p = 0.001).

**CONCLUSION**: Gabapentinoid-opioid therapy was associated with fewer ED visits and higher rates of prolonged and chronic opioid use, nonunion, and reoperation; in sensitivity analysis, ED visits and nonunion remained significant, whereas opioid use and reoperation did not. These findings suggest that potential short-term analgesic benefits may be offset by adverse long-term outcomes, warranting caution and further study of gabapentinoid-opioid prescribing for acute perioperative fracture pain.

articles.title: Timing matters: Delayed surgery increases mortality for blunt hollow viscus injury.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Immediate surgical exploration is recommended for suspected hollow viscus injury (HVI) following blunt trauma. However, diagnostic uncertainty can lead to delayed operative management. We aimed to evaluate if delayed bowel resection/repair (DBR), defined as ≥8 hours after emergency department arrival, was independently associated with increased mortality in blunt trauma patients. We also sought to identify risk factors associated with DBR.

**METHODS**: The Trauma Quality Improvement Program database (2017-2024) was queried for admitted adults with blunt abdominal trauma (abdomen abbreviated injury scale grade ≥2) who underwent bowel resection/repair. Patients who were transferred from another facility or died within 8 hours were excluded. Patients undergoing early bowel resection <8 hours (EBR) were compared with patients undergoing DBR (≥8 h). Multivariable logistic regression evaluated the association between DBR and mortality, controlling for age, severe head and thoracic injury, intubation within 1 hour of arrival, injury to the small bowel, colon, or rectum, and blood transfusion within 4 hours.

**RESULTS**: Of 33,728 patients undergoing bowel resection/repair, 16,010 (47.5%) underwent DBR. The DBR cohort had lower rates of small bowel (49.6% vs. 53.9%, p<0.001) and colon (46.7% vs. 49.7%, p<0.001) injuries, but similar rates of rectal injury (4.4% vs. 4.1%, p=0.166). Injuries to the liver (26.8% vs. 20.8%), spleen (28.2% vs. 23.4%), and kidney (12.9% vs. 9.0%) were more frequent in the DBR cohort (all p<0.001). DBR patients had an increased associated risk of mortality (13.0% vs. 8.5%, OR 1.21, 95% CI: 1.12-1.30, p<0.001). Small bowel injury was the only independent factor with decreased associated risk of DBR (OR 0.93, CI: 0.89-0.97, p=0.001).

**CONCLUSION**: Delayed operative management for blunt HVI occurs more often in patients with solid organ injuries and is independently associated with increased mortality. These findings highlight the importance of early detection and timely surgical management of HVI.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Therapeutic/Care Management, Level IV.

articles.title: Defining the therapeutic window for ADAMTS13 modulation in early trauma-induced coagulopathy.
Hypoxia Paradox in Middle Meningeal Artery Embolization for Chronic Subdural Hematoma: A Mechanistic Framework for Treatment Resistance.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES**: The clinical efficacy of middle meningeal artery embolization (MMAE) in chronic subdural hematoma (CSDH) is increasingly established; yet, recent landmark randomized controlled trials consistently report only a 30% to 50% reduction in recurrence, implying that middle meningeal artery occlusion alone does not fully resolve the pathological microenvironment of the outer hematoma membrane. The mechanistic basis of this incomplete treatment response remains undefined.

**METHODS**: To develop a mechanistic framework for this clinical paradox, we performed a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses-compliant systematic review. Of 876 records identified across PubMed, Embase, and ClinicalTrials.gov, 47 underwent full-text review and 18 studies (16 clinical studies and 2 registry records) published through October 2025 were included, integrating clinical outcomes with pathological and molecular insights. A secondary analysis of a publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing data set of normal human dural tissue was performed to map the cellular infrastructure underlying key molecular drivers.

**RESULTS**: CSDH progression is driven by an interconnected triad of inflammatory infiltration, pathological angiogenesis, and vascular hyperpermeability within the outer hematoma membrane. While MMAE suppresses these pathogenic programs by reducing middle meningeal artery-derived arterial supply, we propose that occlusion-induced ischemic stress may paradoxically stabilize hypoxia-inducible factor 1α, triggering compensatory angiogenesis in cases of incomplete devascularization, a mechanism we formally term the "hypoxia paradox". Secondary single-cell RNA sequencing analysis identified fibroblast-like and endothelial dural populations as the primary cellular platforms for this response, providing a translational cellular basis for the proposed framework.

**CONCLUSION**: The hypoxia paradox represents a testable mechanistic hypothesis, offering a coherent explanation for heterogeneous MMAE outcomes and generates specific, testable predictions regarding post-MMAE molecular signatures in the outer hematoma membrane. Prospective paired tissue sampling integrated with multimodal molecular analyses is essential to validate this model and advance CSDH management toward individualized, mechanism-guided therapy.

articles.title: Post-Traumatic Amnesia Testing for Suspected Concussion in the Emergency Department: A Retrospective Study.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVE**: Among patients discharged from the ED after mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), 16%-25% experience post-concussive symptoms for up to 3 months after injury. However, the assessment of mTBI in the ED is variable. A common tool for the assessment of mTBI in Australia is the Abbreviated Westmead Post-Traumatic Amnesia Scale (A-WPTAS). The aim of this study was to report the proportion of patients who were detected to have post-traumatic amnesia (PTA) following a head injury and whether this varied by reported loss of consciousness (LOC), age, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and mechanisms of injury.

**METHODS**: This was a single-centre, retrospective cohort study. Data were extracted from patients' electronic medical records. All patients presenting to the ED between 1 January 2019 and 31 December 2021 with a head injury, documented results of A-WPTAS, and aged ≥ 18 years were included for analysis.

**RESULTS**: There were 6259 patients included, and 5746 (91.8%, 95% CI: 91.1%-92.5%) passed the A-WPTAS. -PTA was more frequent among patients who presented with GCS 13 or 14, male patients, those with low falls and presenting after hours. Among patients with documented LOC, the pass rate was 90.6% (95% CI: 88.8%-92.4%), and among those without LOC, it was 92% (95% CI: 91.3%-92.8%); p = 0.13.

**CONCLUSION**: PTA was detected in a small proportion of patients tested in the ED. PTA was associated with low initial GCS, but not with reported LOC. Among patients discharged from the ED, follow-up for persistent post-concussion symptoms is indicated.

articles.title: Can posterolateral tibial plateau fractures be treated with an anterolateral approach? A biomechanical study on novel plating concepts in artificial tibia models.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: The aim of this study was to evaluate biomechanically whether fixation of posterolateral tibial plateau fractures (PLTPFs) through the more accessible modified anterolateral approach and by using a newly designed lateral plate with or without posterior plate extension or supplemental anteroposterior screw fixation, can provide comparable stability to direct posterolateral buttress plating.

**METHODS**: PLTPFs were simulated on 40 artificial tibiae and subsequently fixed with 5 different plating techniques (n = 8), namely using Variable Angle Locking Compression Plate (VA-LCP) Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 (VA Lateral), Variable Angle Optimized Locking Technology (VOLT) Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 (VOLT Lateral), VOLT Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 with Posterolateral Extension (Hug), VOLT Posterolateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 (PL), and VOLT Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 with two anteroposterior parallel 3.5 mm locking screws placed superiorly to the plate's lateral-to-medial rafting locking screws (Jail) using a dedicated guide block. Biomechanical testing was performed under progressively increasing cyclic loading to failure. Interfragmentary movements were monitored via motion tracking.

**RESULTS**: Fragment displacement and its posterior tilt over the first 40,000 cycles did not differ significantly between Hug, PL, and Jail (all p > 0.999). Hug, PL, and Jail outperformed VA Lateral significantly in terms of fragment displacement over 40,000 cycles (p ≤ 0.004). In addition, Hug was associated with significantly less fragment displacement versus VOLT Lateral (p = 0.018). Posterior fragment tilting over 40,000 cycles was significantly lower in Hug, PL, and Jail versus VA Lateral and VOLT Lateral (p ≤ 0.014). Hug, PL, and Jail demonstrated significantly higher cycles to clinical failure and corresponding loads at clinical failure than VA Lateral and VOLT Lateral (p < 0.001), with no significant differences among Hug, PL, and Jail (p > 0.999). For catastrophic failure, Hug demonstrated significantly higher values than all other groups (p ≤ 0.045).

**CONCLUSION**: From a biomechanical perspective, VOLT Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 with Posterolateral Extension and VOLT Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate with supplemental jail screw fixation provide fixation stability comparable to VOLT Posterolateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 with respect to fragment displacement, posterior tilt, and clinical failure. Whether PLTPFs could be addressed via the more accessible anterolateral approach without compromising the biomechanical stability of fracture fixation remains yet to be clinically validated. Standalone Lateral Proximal Tibia Plate 3.5 (VA-LCP or VOLT) performed inferiorly to their augmented alternatives.

articles.title: Where is trauma care delivered in New York state? A statewide analysis of distribution and outcomes by trauma center level.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Understanding where and how trauma care is delivered is critical to preventing and managing its disease burden. This study identified patterns in trauma care delivery by characterizing the relationship between trauma presentations and outcomes as a function of trauma center level, including trauma presentations at non-trauma centers.

**METHODS**: A retrospective review of trauma inpatients aged ≥ 15 years across New York State from 2016 through 2020 was performed, utilizing a comprehensive New York State all-payer data reporting system, the Statewide Planning and Research Cooperative System (SPARCS). The primary endpoint for this study was mortality. Secondary endpoints included overall complications, discharge dispositions, and hospital length of stay.

**RESULTS**: A total of 361,141 patients were included with 42.1% presenting to Level 1 and 37.3% to Non-Trauma Centers. Older adults were more frequently treated at Level 3 and Non-Trauma Centers, while younger patients and high-energy mechanisms (motor vehicle crashes and penetrating injuries) were more commonly managed at Level 1 and Level 2 Centers. The association between trauma-center group and mortality varied by severity of illness (SOI) (interaction p < 0.0001). Compared with Level 3 and Non-Trauma Centers, Level 1 and 2 Centers had higher adjusted mortality odds among hospitalizations with major SOI (aOR 1.43, 95% CI 1.12-1.83) and extreme SOI (aOR 1.39, 95% CI 1.18-1.62), with no significant difference in moderate SOI (aOR 0.83, 95% CI 0.62-1.11).

**CONCLUSIONS**: Differences in outcomes across trauma center levels are strongly influenced by case mix and severity. These findings highlight opportunities to improve triage, resource allocation, and system-level performance.

articles.title: Variations in hip fracture management at trauma vs. non-trauma centers.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Hip fractures represent a growing public health burden. Optimal management relies on timely surgical intervention coordinated by multidisciplinary care and appropriate resource availability, all of which may vary between hospital settings. Differences between trauma hospitals and non-trauma hospitals may influence outcomes, yet these variations have not been well characterized.

**METHODS**: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of hip fracture cases over a 2-year period (October 2022 to August 2024), comparing patient and procedural characteristics between a Level II trauma hospital (TH) (n = 104) and a non-trauma hospital (NTH) (n = 31). Polytrauma patients were excluded. Data were extracted from the electronic medical record (EMR). Primary outcomes were hospital length of stay (LOS) and time from admission to surgery. Group comparisons utilized chi-square or Fisher's exact tests for categorical variables and Mann-Whitney U or Welch t-tests for continuous variables, as appropriate. A multivariable random forest model was used to evaluate predictors of operative duration.

**RESULTS**: ASA physical status distribution differed significantly between facilities (p = 0.03), with more ASA > 2 patients at the NTH (76.6% vs. 65.7%). Osteosynthesis was performed in 73.3% of NTH cases and 82.2% of TH cases; arthroplasty comprised 26.7% and 17.8%, respectively. LOS differed significantly by facility (p < 0.01), with a shorter mean stay at the NTH (4.3 vs. 5.9 days; mean difference, -1.73 days). Time to surgery also differed significantly (p < 0.001): mean 846 min (95% CI, 615-1078) at the NTH vs. 2686 minutes (95% CI, 2391-2981) at the TH. In multivariable modeling, procedure type was the dominant predictor of operative duration (permutation importance 0.686), followed by payer type (0.216); facility identity contributed minimally (0.034) after accounting for case mix.

**CONCLUSION**: Hip fracture care differed meaningfully between the TH and NTH within the same health care system. The NTH demonstrated significantly shorter time to surgery and LOS despite treating a proportionally higher-acuity patient population by ASA classification. These findings highlight opportunities for optimizing timeliness and resource allocation in hip fracture management across hospital settings and questions whether THs are the optimal location to treat these injuries.

articles.title: Segmental phase angle as predictor of activities of daily living and muscle health in patients with osteoporotic fracture A retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
**PURPOSE**: This study aimed to determine whether the segmental phase angle is associated with clinical outcomes such as activities of daily living (ADL), muscle strength, and skeletal muscle mass in patients with osteoporotic fractures.

**METHODS**: This was a retrospective cohort study of patients with osteoporotic fractures admitted to convalescent rehabilitation wards. The primary outcome was a Functional Independence Measure motor (FIM-motor) score at discharge, and secondary outcomes were handgrip strength and skeletal muscle mass index (SMI) at discharge. Multivariate analysis was used to adjust for confounders and to examine the association between segmental phase angle and outcome.

**RESULTS**: A total of 115 subjects (97 women, age 81.0 ± 10.0 years) were included in the study. The median baseline phase angle was 3.6°. Multiple regression analysis adjusted for confounders showed that arm phase angle was independently positively associated with handgrip strength (β=0.250, P < 0.001) and SMI (β=0.215, P < 0.001) at discharge. Leg phase angle was independently positively associated with FIM-motor score (β=0.077, P = 0.045), handgrip strength (β=0.174, P < 0.001), and SMI (β=0.154, P < 0.001) at discharge.

**CONCLUSIONS**: The leg phase angle was associated with ADL, muscle strength, and skeletal muscle mass in patients with osteoporotic fractures at discharge. Segmental phase angle may be a useful indicator for considering intervention methods in patients with osteoporotic fractures.

articles.title: Province-wide assessment of emergency care capacity and skills in a rural provincial health system: A facility-based cross-sectional assessment in Battambang, Cambodia.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Emergency care capacity remains critically limited in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), particularly in rural areas where specialists and infrastructure are scarce. In Cambodia, stroke and ischemic heart disease are leading causes of mortality, and trauma burdens are increasing alongside rapid infrastructure development. Evidence on emergency equipment availability and frontline provider skills at the facility level in rural provinces remains limited.

**METHODS**: A facility-based cross-sectional assessment was conducted across all seven public referral hospitals in Battambang Province, Cambodia, in January 2023. Emergency equipment availability was evaluated through structured interviews and direct visual confirmation against the World Health Organization (WHO) Guidelines for Essential Trauma Care. Clinical skill examinations were administered to physicians (two scenario-based cases: acute stroke with airway compromise; traumatic injury with tension pneumothorax and intra-abdominal bleeding) and nurses (a Basic Life Support [BLS] scenario assessed in pairs). Hospitals were stratified by Complementary Package of Activities (CPA) level: CPA1 (basic care only), CPA2 (including surgery and intensive care), and CPA3 (highest provincial level).

**RESULTS**: At Complementary Package of Activities (CPA)1 (basic care only) hospitals, intubation equipment and 12-lead electrocardiogram were each available in only 25% of facilities. None had a crash cart, blood transfusion capacity, basic metabolic panel, or coagulation testing. In the stroke scenario, airway patency was confirmed by 28.6% of physicians at CPA1 hospitals, compared with 70.0% at CPA2 hospitals (including surgery and intensive care), 57.1% at the CPA3 hospital (highest provincial level), and 75.0% at the Provincial Health Department. In the trauma scenario, no physician at CPA1 hospitals correctly performed spinal immobilization with the spine kept straight or thoracentesis at the correct anatomical location. Among 38 nurse pairs, 97.4% initiated chest compressions promptly, but only 21.1% demonstrated correct compression technique, and 13.2% provided effective bag-valve-mask ventilation. Deficiencies in equipment and clinical skills were most pronounced at CPA1 hospitals.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Emergency care capacity in Battambang Province was substantially limited, with the greatest deficiencies at CPA1 hospitals. Recurrent low-cost training and targeted strengthening of basic emergency care should be prioritized at lower-level facilities.

articles.title: A scoping review evaluating artificial intelligence applications across various injury prevention domains.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly utilized for injury prevention across diverse clinical and community settings including machine learning (ML). This scoping review aimed to synthesize the current literature on the applications and predictive performance of AI across multiple injury prevention domains.

**METHODS**: This scoping review searched five major databases, including PubMed, Embase, ScienceDirect, ProQuest, and the Cochrane Library, to identify studies evaluating AI applications for injury prevention published through May 2026. Eligible studies included original U.S.-based, English-language research across self-harm and suicide, abuse and violence, fall prevention, and sports injury prediction. Studies were excluded if they lacked measurable prevention outcomes or sufficient methodological detail, or focused on injury treatment rather than prevention, to ensure relevant and interpretable evidence for synthesis.

**RESULTS**: Nineteen studies met the inclusion criteria. ML models generally outperformed or matched traditional screening methods for self-harm and suicide prediction (AUC 0.81-0.82), while multimodal approaches achieved the highest predictive accuracy (AUC 0.90). In abuse and violence prevention, AI predicted intimate partner violence with an AUC of 0.88 and identified cases before formal disclosure. AI also improved fall risk assessment by accurately categorizing patient risk levels, predicting future falls, and mitigating fall injuries through wearable airbag technology. ML models predicted future sports-related injuries (AUC 0.76-0.84), while identifying modifiable risk factors including workload, strength deficits, prior injury burden, and concussion history.

**CONCLUSION**: ML-based prediction showed promise for risk stratification in self-harm, suicide, intimate partner violence, and recurrent victimization. Additionally, AI predicted fall risk and identified athletes at risk for future sports-related injuries while detecting modifiable risk factors, including workload, prior injury burden, and strength deficits. Although these findings suggest that AI and ML may have potential applications in supporting earlier risk identification, informing targeted prevention strategies, and facilitating more personalized approaches to injury prevention, the limited available evidence warrants careful interpretation.

articles.title: Enhanced wound healing potential of a carboxymethyl cellulose/gelatin-based hydrogel containing decellularized amniotic membrane and Matricaria chamomilla extract: A multifunctional composite dressing.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Chronic wound healing remains a complex biological process influenced by excessive inflammation, oxidative stress, microbial invasion, and insufficient tissue regeneration. Therefore, the design of multifunctional biomaterials that integrate structural support with biological regulation has emerged as a promising strategy in advanced wound care. This study sought to develop a composite hydrogel incorporating decellularized amniotic membrane (dAM)-derived extracellular matrix components alongside Matricaria chamomilla extract, with the goal of achieving enhanced regenerative and therapeutic outcomes.

**METHODS**: A CMC/GEL-Chamomilla-dAM hydrogel was prepared using decellularized dAM and subsequently evaluated in terms of its physicochemical and biological characteristics. The effectiveness of the decellularization process and preservation of ECM components were first examined, followed by characterization of hydrogel morphology, rheological properties, swelling and degradation behavior, and pH stability. Its biological performance was further assessed through hemocompatibility, cytocompatibility, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial assays, as well as a full-thickness wound model.

**RESULTS**: Incorporation of dAM and chamomile extract resulted in a stable hydrogel with favorable physicochemical and biological characteristics. The decellularization procedure removed 97.9% of the DNA. The resulting composite hydrogel exhibited an average pore size of 78.3 ± 9.8 µm, and all hydrogel formulations showed hemolysis rates below the 5% threshold accepted for blood-contacting biomaterials, with values ranging from 3.8% to 4.5%. The composite hydrogel also supported enhanced fibroblast viability (109.6 ± 11.3%) and demonstrated antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial activities against wound-associated pathogens. In vivo, treatment with CMC/GEL-Chamomilla-dAM accelerated wound closure (85.7 ± 6.3% at day 14) and supported tissue regeneration, outperforming both the dAM-containing hydrogel (78.9 ± 9.9%) and the commercial DuoDERM dressing (58.9 ± 4.5%), as evidenced by improved re-epithelialization, collagen deposition, angiogenesis, and early signs of tissue remodeling.

**CONCLUSION**: The CMC/GEL-Chamomilla-dAM hydrogel combines a dAM-containing extracellular matrix scaffold with chamomile-derived bioactive compounds, creating a favorable microenvironment for tissue repair. The addition of chamomile extract to the dAM-containing scaffold was associated with improved wound closure and tissue regeneration. While the present study design does not permit a definitive assessment of synergy between dAM and chamomile, these findings support the potential of this formulation as a multifunctional biomaterial platform for advanced wound healing applications.
